2.9 Policy as Code — OPA, Kyverno, Admission Controllers

What is Policy as Code? Security and compliance rules written as code, versioned in Git, automatically enforced at deploy time by Kubernetes admission controllers.

ToolLanguageHow It WorksBest For
OPA / GatekeeperRego (custom DSL)ConstraintTemplates define reusable policies, Constraints enforce them on specific resourcesComplex, cross-tool policies (not just K8s)
KyvernoYAML (no new language)Kubernetes-native — policies are just K8s resources, apply/validate/mutate/generateSimple K8s-only policies, fast learning curve
🧠 CNPE Exam: Pay attention to mutating vs. validating admission webhooks. Mutating webhooks run FIRST (they can add default values). Validating webhooks run SECOND (they can reject). Kyverno handles both.

💡 The Admission Webhook Flow — What Happens When You kubectl apply: Understanding this flow is critical for debugging "why is my pod stuck in CreateContainerConfigError?"

  1. Authentication: kubectl sends your credentials. K8s verifies: "Is this really Alice?"
  2. Authorization (RBAC): K8s checks: "Is Alice allowed to create Pods in namespace anihpj?"
  3. 🔵 MUTATING Admission Webhooks (Phase 1): Registered webhooks can MODIFY the resource. Kyverno mutate policies run here. Example: auto-add team label if missing. Pod is now modified in-flight.
  4. 🔴 VALIDATING Admission Webhooks (Phase 2): Registered webhooks can REJECT the resource. Kyverno validate policies run here. Example: reject if securityContext.runAsNonRoot != true. If ANY webhook says "no," the request is denied.
  5. etcd persistence: If all admission checks pass, the resource is written to etcd (the cluster's database).

Critical detail: Mutating webhooks have NO ORDER GUARANTEES. If Webhook A adds label X and Webhook B changes label X, the result is unpredictable. Design your mutate policies to not conflict. Validating webhooks see the resource AFTER all mutations, so they validate the final state.

📖 OPA Rego — What the Policy Language Looks Like: While Kyverno uses YAML, OPA uses a custom language called Rego. Here's the SAME "require team label" policy in both:

Kyverno (YAML)OPA/Gatekeeper (Rego)
 
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-team-label
spec:
  rules:
  - name: check-team
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: [Pod]
    validate:
      message: "Pod must have team label"
      pattern:
        metadata:
          labels:
            team: "?*"
 
package k8s.requiredlabels

denied[msg] {
  input.review.kind.kind == "Pod"
  not input.request.object.metadata.labels.team
  msg := "Pod must have team label"
}

The tradeoff: Kyverno is immediately readable by anyone who knows YAML (every Kubernetes user). Rego requires learning a logic programming language but is far more expressive for complex policies. For the CNPE exam, know that BOTH exist, understand the mutating vs. validating distinction, and recognize that Kyverno = YAML (easier), OPA = Rego (more powerful for cross-tool policies).

📖 anihpj Policy Examples (Kyverno):

  • ❌ Block root: Any container running as UID 0 is rejected
  • ❌ Require resource limits: Deployments without CPU/memory limits are rejected
  • ❌ Block CRITICAL CVEs: Images with critical vulnerabilities are rejected
  • ❌ Enforce labels: Block any Deployment without app.kubernetes.io/part-of: anihpj label
  • ✅ Auto-add labels: Mutating policy adds team label if missing
🧠 CNPE Exam: "Shift-Left Security" — Security that's applied as early as possible in the development lifecycle, not just at deploy time. The platform engineer's security toolkit spans the entire pipeline:

2.10 SLO/SLI/SLA, Error Budgets & DORA Metrics

📏 SLI (Service Level Indicator)

The metric you measure

"99.9% of requests complete in under 200ms"

This is raw data from Prometheus / OpenTelemetry

🎯 SLO (Service Level Objective)

The target for your SLI

"99.95% of requests must complete in under 200ms over 30 days"

This is your internal goal — not a contract

📜 SLA (Service Level Agreement)

The contractual promise to customers

"99.9% uptime or 10% monthly credit"

Breaching this costs money — penalties apply

⚠️ Error Budget Calculation: Error Budget = 100% − SLO

If your SLO is 99.9% uptime, your error budget is 0.1% of the month:

  • 30 days × 24 hours × 60 minutes = 43,200 minutes/month
  • 0.1% × 43,200 = 43.2 minutes of allowed downtime per month
  • If you exceed 43.2 minutes, you blew your error budget — stop shipping features, fix reliability

💡 How to Define Good SLOs — The User-Journey Method: Don't SLO every metric. SLO the user's experience:

  1. Identify the critical user journey. For anihpj: "User searches for a job → sees results in under 2 seconds"
  2. Pick an SLI that measures that journey. Latency of /jobs/search/ endpoint, p95.
  3. Set the SLO slightly tighter than what users tolerate. If users abandon after 3s, SLO at 2s p95.
  4. Don't aim for 100%. The difference between 99.9% and 99.99% is 10× the engineering effort for marginal user benefit. Use your error budget to ship features faster.
  5. Review SLOs quarterly. If you consistently exceed your SLO with no user complaints, tighten it. If users complain but SLO is met, your SLI is measuring the wrong thing.

Common mistake: SLO-ing CPU usage or memory. Users don't care about CPU — they care about latency and availability. Measure what matters to the user, not what's convenient to measure.

💡 SLO Burn Rate Alerts — Don't Wait Until the Budget is Gone: The error budget tells you how much downtime you're ALLOWED. But waiting until the budget is exhausted is too late. You need alerts that warn you when you're BURNING budget too fast:

Burn Rate: How fast you're consuming your error budget relative to the SLO period. If your SLO allows 43.2 minutes of downtime per month and you've used 30 minutes in the first 3 days, your burn rate is catastrophic (you'll exhaust the budget in ~4.3 days).

Multi-Window, Multi-Burn-Rate Alerts (Google SRE best practice):

AlertBurn RateWindowPurposeExample
Page (urgent)14.4×1 hour"Something is VERY wrong RIGHT NOW" — you'll exhaust 2% of monthly budget in 1 hourWake up the on-call engineer at 3 AM
Page (urgent)6×6 hours"Something is wrong, needs attention soon" — you'll exhaust 5% of budget in 6 hoursPage on-call during business hours
Ticket (non-urgent)3×3 days"Trend is concerning" — you're burning budget faster than plannedCreate Jira ticket, investigate next business day

Why multiple windows? A 1-hour spike (brief outage) and a 3-day slow degradation (memory leak) are different problems requiring different responses. The 1-hour window catches acute incidents. The 3-day window catches chronic issues before they exhaust your budget. Both are needed.

Burn rate formula: Burn Rate = (Error Rate × Alert Window) / Error Budget. If your error budget is 0.1% (43.2 min/month) and your error rate is 1% sustained over 1 hour: Burn Rate = (0.01 × 60 min) / 43.2 min = 1.39×. That's above 1× — you're burning faster than the budget allows. Alert!

📊 DORA Metrics — The 4 Key DevOps Performance Indicators:

Metric🏆 Elite🥇 High🥈 Medium🥉 Low
Deployment FrequencyOn-demand (multiple/day)Daily–WeeklyWeekly–MonthlyMonthly–6 months
Lead Time for Changes< 1 hour1 day–1 week1 week–1 month1–6 months
MTTR (Mean Time to Restore)< 1 hour< 1 day1 day–1 week> 1 week
Change Failure Rate0–5%5–10%10–15%45–60%

📖 Chapter 2 Summary: Cloud Native is a paradigm, not just a buzzword. It's about containers, orchestration, declarative infrastructure, Git-driven deployments, comprehensive observability, and policy-as-code security. As a platform engineer, you don't just use these tools — you provide them as a service to developers. The anihpj project will demonstrate every one of these concepts: Docker containers, Kubernetes orchestration, Terraform IaC, Argo CD GitOps, Prometheus/Grafana observability, and Kyverno policy enforcement.

🔗 Next: Chapter 3 maps these concepts onto the CNCF Landscape — understanding which of the 200+ projects matter for the CNPE exam.

🏋️ Chapter 2 — Hands-On Practice Drills (10 Exercises)

The CNPE is a performance-based exam — you solve tasks in a live Linux terminal. Practice these drills in your lab environment until you can complete each within the target time.

⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 2.1 — Deploy the anihpj Core Triad

Demonstrate the containers/Kubernetes/microservices triad by deploying all three anihpj services and verifying they can communicate.

  1. Create a namespace called anihpj
  2. Deploy postgres as a Deployment with a single replica, exposed via a ClusterIP Service named postgres on port 5432
  3. Deploy redis as a Deployment with a single replica, exposed via a ClusterIP Service named redis on port 6379
  4. Deploy anihpj-web (the Django app) as a Deployment with 2 replicas, exposed via a ClusterIP Service named anihpj-web on port 8000
  5. From within the anihpj-web pod, verify you can resolve postgres and redis via DNS using nslookup or getent hosts
💡 Hint: Use kubectl create ns, kubectl create deployment, kubectl expose deployment, kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Create namespace
kubectl create namespace anihpj

# Step 2: Deploy postgres
kubectl create deployment postgres --image=postgres:16 -n anihpj
kubectl set env deployment/postgres POSTGRES_DB=anihpj POSTGRES_USER=anihpj POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret123 -n anihpj
kubectl expose deployment postgres --port=5432 --target-port=5432 -n anihpj

# Step 3: Deploy redis
kubectl create deployment redis --image=redis:7-alpine -n anihpj
kubectl expose deployment redis --port=6379 --target-port=6379 -n anihpj

# Step 4: Deploy anihpj-web (Django)
kubectl create deployment anihpj-web --image=anihpj-web:latest --replicas=2 -n anihpj
kubectl expose deployment anihpj-web --port=8000 --target-port=8000 -n anihpj

# Step 5: Verify DNS resolution from inside the pod
ANIH_POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl exec -it $ANIH_POD -n anihpj -- sh -c "nslookup postgres && nslookup redis"
# Both should resolve to ClusterIP addresses
# This proves: microservices running AS containers ON Kubernetes, discovering each other via DNS
⏱️ Target: 7 minutes
Drill 2.2 — Write and Apply a Terraform-Style Declarative Manifest

Create Kubernetes manifests that follow IaC principles — declarative, versioned, and idempotent.

  1. Write a file anihpj-deployment.yaml that declares the desired state for anihpj-web: 3 replicas, resource requests (128Mi memory, 100m CPU), resource limits (256Mi memory, 500m CPU)
  2. Apply it with kubectl apply -f anihpj-deployment.yaml
  3. Run kubectl apply -f anihpj-deployment.yaml again — verify nothing changes (idempotency)
  4. Manually scale the deployment to 5 replicas with kubectl scale — this simulates "drift"
  5. Re-apply your manifest — verify Kubernetes reconciles back to 3 replicas (declarative self-healing)
💡 Hint: Use kubectl apply -f, kubectl get deploy -w, kubectl scale deployment
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Write declarative manifest
cat > anihpj-deployment.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: anihpj-web:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "128Mi"
            cpu: "100m"
          limits:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
EOF

# Step 2: Apply
kubectl apply -f anihpj-deployment.yaml -n anihpj

# Step 3: Verify idempotency
kubectl apply -f anihpj-deployment.yaml -n anihpj
# OUTPUT: deployment.apps/anihpj-web unchanged
# This IS idempotency — declarative IaC in action

# Step 4: Simulate drift (manual change)
kubectl scale deployment anihpj-web --replicas=5 -n anihpj
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web
# Shows 5 pods — someone bypassed the manifest!

# Step 5: Re-apply to reconcile
kubectl apply -f anihpj-deployment.yaml -n anihpj
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web
# Back to 3 pods — Kubernetes reconciled to declared state
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 2.3 — Simulate GitOps with kubectl diff

GitOps is about comparing desired state (Git) with actual state (cluster). Use kubectl diff to see what would change before applying.

  1. Create a manifest service.yaml defining a ClusterIP Service for anihpj-web on port 8000
  2. Apply it and verify the service exists
  3. Modify service.yaml to change the port from 8000 to 8080
  4. Run kubectl diff -f service.yaml — this is what Argo CD does internally every 3 minutes
  5. Explain why kubectl diff before kubectl apply is the foundation of GitOps
💡 Hint: kubectl diff -f <file> shows what would change. Argo CD calls this the "sync" operation.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1-2: Create and apply service
kubectl create service clusterip anihpj-web --tcp=8000:8000 -n anihpj --dry-run=client -o yaml > service.yaml
kubectl apply -f service.yaml -n anihpj

# Step 3: Modify the desired state
sed -i 's/port: 8000/port: 8080/' service.yaml
sed -i 's/targetPort: 8000/targetPort: 8080/' service.yaml

# Step 4: See what Argo CD sees
kubectl diff -f service.yaml -n anihpj
# OUTPUT:
# -  port: 8000
# +  port: 8080
# This is EXACTLY the diff Argo CD computes every 3 minutes

# Step 5: Explanation
# GitOps = desired state (Git) vs actual state (cluster)
# kubectl diff = desired (file) vs actual (cluster)
# Argo CD: if diff is non-empty → OutOfSync → auto-sync or alert
# This is why Git revert = rollback: revert the file → diff flips → Argo CD syncs back
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 2.4 — Prove Immutability: Recreate a Pod

Immutable infrastructure means never fixing a running instance — you destroy and recreate it. Prove this by killing a pod and watching Kubernetes replace it from the same image.

  1. List all anihpj-web pods and note their names and ages
  2. Exec into one pod and create a file: echo "manual fix" > /tmp/hack.txt
  3. Verify the file exists: cat /tmp/hack.txt
  4. Delete the pod: kubectl delete pod <pod-name>
  5. Exec into the NEW replacement pod — verify /tmp/hack.txt does NOT exist
  6. Explain why this proves immutability and why you should never "SSH in to fix things"
💡 Hint: kubectl get pods, kubectl exec, kubectl delete pod. The Deployment controller recreates pods from the immutable image.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Note pod names and ages
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web
# EXAMPLE: anihpj-web-abc123   5m    (AGE = 5 minutes)

# Step 2: Create a "manual fix" (mutable approach)
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl exec $POD -n anihpj -- sh -c 'echo "manual fix" > /tmp/hack.txt'

# Step 3: Verify the "fix" exists
kubectl exec $POD -n anihpj -- cat /tmp/hack.txt
# OUTPUT: manual fix

# Step 4: Destroy the pod (cattle, not pets!)
kubectl delete pod $POD -n anihpj
# pod "anihpj-web-abc123" deleted

# Step 5: Check the replacement pod
sleep 5
NEW_POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl exec $NEW_POD -n anihpj -- cat /tmp/hack.txt 2>&1
# OUTPUT: cat: /tmp/hack.txt: No such file or directory
# AGE of new pod: <1 minute

# Step 6: Explanation
# The replacement pod came from the SAME immutable Docker image.
# The "manual fix" is GONE — correctly. Fixes belong in the Dockerfile,
# not on running containers. This is the "cattle, not pets" principle.
# Kubernetes enforces this: pods are disposable, images are immutable.
⏱️ Target: 6 minutes
Drill 2.5 — Simulate a CI/CD Pipeline with Labels

CI/CD pipelines tag images with build identifiers. Simulate a pipeline by deploying two versions of anihpj-web and performing a rolling update.

  1. Deploy anihpj-web with image tag v1.0.0 (3 replicas) — this is the "production" version
  2. Simulate CI building a new image: update the deployment to use tag v2.0.0
  3. Watch the rolling update with kubectl rollout status
  4. Check the rollout history with kubectl rollout history
  5. Simulate a failed deploy by rolling back: kubectl rollout undo
  6. Verify all pods are back on v1.0.0
💡 Hint: kubectl set image, kubectl rollout status, kubectl rollout history, kubectl rollout undo
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Deploy v1.0.0
kubectl create deployment anihpj-web --image=anihpj-web:v1.0.0 --replicas=3 -n anihpj

# Step 2: CI builds v2.0.0 → Argo CD/CI updates image tag
kubectl set image deployment/anihpj-web django=anihpj-web:v2.0.0 -n anihpj

# Step 3: Watch rolling update
kubectl rollout status deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj
# OUTPUT: Waiting for deployment "anihpj-web" rollout to finish...
#         deployment "anihpj-web" successfully rolled out

# Step 4: View rollout history (audit trail)
kubectl rollout history deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj
# REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
# 1         kubectl create --image=anihpj-web:v1.0.0
# 2         kubectl set image deployment/anihpj-web django=anihpj-web:v2.0.0

# Step 5: v2.0.0 has a bug — rollback!
kubectl rollout undo deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj

# Step 6: Verify rollback
kubectl describe deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj | grep Image
# Image: anihpj-web:v1.0.0  ✓
# This is CI/CD: build→tag→deploy→monitor→rollback if needed
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 2.6 — Query the Observability Pillars

The three pillars (Metrics, Logs, Traces) each answer different questions. Use kubectl to access each one for a running pod.

  1. Logs (Pillar 2): View the logs of an anihpj-web pod. Check logs from the last 5 minutes. View logs from a PREVIOUS (crashed) container instance.
  2. Metrics (Pillar 1): Check resource usage of anihpj-web pods with kubectl top pod. Identify which pod uses the most memory.
  3. Traces (Pillar 3): Describe the Service and Endpoints for anihpj-web. Trace the path a request takes: Service → Endpoints → Pod IP.
  4. Explain which pillar you'd use for: (a) debugging a crash, (b) finding a performance bottleneck, (c) setting up an alert for high error rates
💡 Hint: kubectl logs --tail=50 --since=5m, kubectl logs --previous, kubectl top pod, kubectl describe svc, kubectl get endpoints
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1a: Logs — recent logs
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl logs $POD -n anihpj --tail=50 --since=5m

# Step 1b: Logs — crashed container (previous instance)
kubectl logs $POD -n anihpj --previous
# Shows logs from the LAST crashed container — critical for debugging OOMKilled

# Step 2: Metrics — resource usage
kubectl top pod -n anihpj
# NAME              CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
# anihpj-web-abc    50m          180Mi
# anihpj-web-def    45m          175Mi
# anihpj-web-ghi    210m         240Mi  ← highest memory

# Step 3: Traces — request path
kubectl describe svc anihpj-web -n anihpj
# Selector: app=anihpj-web
kubectl get endpoints anihpj-web -n anihpj
# 10.0.1.5:8000,10.0.1.6:8000,10.0.1.7:8000
# Request flow: DNS (anihpj-web) → Service ClusterIP → iptables → random pod IP

# Step 4: Which pillar for each?
# (a) Debug crash → LOGS (pillar 2) — "what error message before crash?"
# (b) Performance bottleneck → TRACES (pillar 3) — "which service is slow?"
# (c) Alert on error rates → METRICS (pillar 1) — "how many 5xx errors per second?"
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 2.7 — Create an Ingress for External Traffic

Ingress controllers route external HTTP traffic into the cluster. Create an Ingress resource that routes traffic to anihpj-web.

  1. Verify an Ingress controller is running in your cluster (check kube-system or ingress-nginx namespace)
  2. Create an Ingress resource that routes anihpj.local/jobs to the anihpj-web Service on port 8000
  3. Verify the Ingress was created and the ADDRESS field is populated
  4. Add a second path rule: route anihpj.local/admin to the same service
  5. Explain the difference between what an Ingress does vs. what a Service Mesh does
💡 Hint: Use kubectl get pods -A | grep ingress, kubectl create ingress, kubectl describe ingress
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Check for Ingress controller
kubectl get pods -A | grep ingress
# Look for: ingress-nginx-controller-* or traefik-* or haproxy-*

# If no Ingress controller, install NGINX Ingress:
# kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/main/deploy/static/provider/kind/deploy.yaml

# Step 2: Create Ingress
cat > anihpj-ingress.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: anihpj-ingress
  namespace: anihpj
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
spec:
  rules:
  - host: anihpj.local
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /jobs
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: anihpj-web
            port:
              number: 8000
EOF
kubectl apply -f anihpj-ingress.yaml

# Step 3: Verify
kubectl get ingress -n anihpj
# NAME              HOSTS           ADDRESS        PORTS
# anihpj-ingress    anihpj.local   192.168.1.100   80

# Step 4: Add /admin path
kubectl edit ingress anihpj-ingress -n anihpj
# Add a second path entry under 'paths' for /admin

# Step 5: Ingress vs Service Mesh
# Ingress = EXTERNAL traffic INTO the cluster (North-South)
# Service Mesh = INTERNAL traffic BETWEEN services (East-West)
# Ingress: anihpj.com → cluster → anihpj-web
# Service Mesh: anihpj-web → postgres (mTLS, retries, circuit breaker)
⏱️ Target: 6 minutes
Drill 2.8 — Enforce Policy with a NetworkPolicy

Policy as Code means security rules are declarative and versioned. Create a NetworkPolicy that restricts which pods can talk to postgres.

  1. Create a NetworkPolicy that allows ONLY pods with label app: anihpj-web to connect to postgres on port 5432
  2. Apply the policy to the anihpj namespace
  3. Verify: describe the NetworkPolicy and confirm the podSelector and ingress rules are correct
  4. Explain what happens if a pod WITHOUT the label app: anihpj-web tries to connect to postgres
  5. Explain how this is "Policy as Code": it's in a YAML file, versioned in Git, and enforced by Kubernetes
💡 Hint: NetworkPolicy with podSelector matching postgres, ingress.from.podSelector matching anihpj-web
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Create NetworkPolicy as CODE
cat > postgres-netpol.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: postgres-access
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres          # Policy applies TO postgres pods
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: anihpj-web    # ONLY these pods can connect
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5432             # ONLY on this port
EOF

# Step 2: Apply
kubectl apply -f postgres-netpol.yaml

# Step 3: Verify
kubectl describe networkpolicy postgres-access -n anihpj
# PodSelector: app=postgres
# Ingress: from app=anihpj-web on port 5432/TCP

# Step 4: What happens to other pods?
# Any pod WITHOUT label app=anihpj-web → connection DROPPED by CNI
# This is DEFAULT-DENY with explicit allow
# Even pods in the SAME namespace are blocked unless matched

# Step 5: Policy as Code
# This NetworkPolicy IS Policy as Code:
# - Written in YAML (machine-readable)
# - Stored in postgres-netpol.yaml (Git)
# - Reviewed in a Pull Request (change control)
# - Enforced AUTOMATICALLY by the CNI (no manual firewall rules)
# - kubectl apply = deploy the policy
# - git revert = rollback the policy
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 2.9 — Apply Resource Limits (Admission Control Simulation)

In production, every pod MUST have resource limits. Simulate admission control by creating pods with and without limits and observing the difference.

  1. Create a pod with NO resource requests/limits defined. Inspect it and note that the QoS Class is BestEffort.
  2. Create a pod WITH resource requests and limits (128Mi/256Mi memory, 100m/500m CPU). Inspect it and note the QoS Class is Burstable.
  3. Create a pod where requests == limits (256Mi memory, 500m CPU). Inspect it: QoS Class should be Guaranteed.
  4. Explain which QoS class gets evicted FIRST under memory pressure and why a Kyverno policy should block BestEffort pods in production.
💡 Hint: kubectl run --image=nginx --restart=Never --dry-run=client -o yaml, edit to add resources. Check QoS with kubectl describe pod | grep QoS.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Pod WITHOUT limits → BestEffort (lowest priority)
kubectl run no-limits --image=nginx -n anihpj --dry-run=client -o yaml > no-limits.yaml
kubectl apply -f no-limits.yaml -n anihpj
kubectl describe pod no-limits -n anihpj | grep "QoS Class"
# QoS Class: BestEffort  ← FIRST to be evicted under memory pressure

# Step 2: Pod WITH limits → Burstable
cat > burstable.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: burstable
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "128Mi"
        cpu: "100m"
      limits:
        memory: "256Mi"
        cpu: "500m"
EOF
kubectl apply -f burstable.yaml -n anihpj
kubectl describe pod burstable -n anihpj | grep "QoS Class"
# QoS Class: Burstable  ← Evicted AFTER BestEffort

# Step 3: requests == limits → Guaranteed (highest priority)
cat > guaranteed.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: guaranteed
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "256Mi"
        cpu: "500m"
      limits:
        memory: "256Mi"
        cpu: "500m"
EOF
kubectl apply -f guaranteed.yaml -n anihpj
kubectl describe pod guaranteed -n anihpj | grep "QoS Class"
# QoS Class: Guaranteed  ← Last to be evicted, highest priority

# Step 4: Why Kyverno policies matter
# Eviction order: BestEffort → Burstable → Guaranteed
# A Kyverno policy should MUTATE pods to add default limits
# or VALIDATE that limits are set (reject pods without limits)
# This is Policy as Code: the POLICY is in YAML, enforced automatically
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 2.10 — Calculate Error Budget and Simulate an SLO Alert

Use kubectl to measure availability and calculate whether you're within the error budget for a 99.9% SLO.

  1. Check how long the anihpj-web pods have been running: kubectl get pods -o json and extract startTime
  2. Check how many times each pod has restarted: kubectl get pods RESTARTS column
  3. Calculate: if each restart represents ~30 seconds of downtime (the default termination grace period), and your SLO is 99.9% uptime (43.2 min/month error budget), how many restarts can you tolerate per month?
  4. Write a simple shell script that counts total pod restarts in the anihpj namespace and compares against the error budget threshold
  5. Explain what action you should take if restarts exceed 86 in a rolling 30-day window
💡 Hint: 43.2 min / 0.5 min per restart = ~86 restarts allowed. Use kubectl get pods -o jsonpath to extract restart counts.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Check pod start times
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, started: .status.startTime}'
# Shows when each pod started

# Step 2: Check restart counts
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
# NAME              READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
# anihpj-web-abc    1/1     Running   2          2d
# anihpj-web-def    1/1     Running   0          2d
# Total restarts: 2

# Step 3: Error budget math
# SLO = 99.9% uptime → Error budget = 0.1% × 43,200 min = 43.2 min/month
# Each restart = ~30 sec (0.5 min) downtime
# Allowed restarts = 43.2 ÷ 0.5 = 86.4 → ~86 restarts/month
# Current restarts: 2 → WITHIN budget (2/86 = 2.3% of budget used)

# Step 4: Shell script to check budget
cat > check-budget.sh << 'SCRIPT'
#!/bin/bash
NS=${1:-anihpj}
RESTARTS=$(kubectl get pods -n $NS -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.containerStatuses[*].restartCount}' | tr ' ' '\n' | paste -sd+ | bc)
THRESHOLD=86
echo "Total restarts in namespace $NS: $RESTARTS"
echo "Error budget threshold (99.9% SLO): $THRESHOLD"
if [ "$RESTARTS" -gt "$THRESHOLD" ]; then
  echo "❌ ERROR BUDGET EXHAUSTED! Stop features, fix reliability."
else
  echo "✅ Within error budget ($RESTARTS/$THRESHOLD)"
fi
SCRIPT
bash check-budget.sh anihpj

# Step 5: What to do if budget exhausted
# If restarts > 86 in 30 days:
# 1. HALT all feature deployments
# 2. Investigate ROOT CAUSE (logs + metrics)
# 3. Fix: memory leak? race condition? health check too aggressive?
# 4. Deploy fix → monitor → restart count should stabilize
# 5. Resume feature work only when burn rate returns to normal

Chapter 3: The Cloud Native Landscape — Where Everything Fits

CNCF Landscape map (Graduated, Incubating, Sandbox), Cloud Native Trail Map, the complete Platform Stack with 5 CNPE domain mappings, and the key CNCF projects every platform engineer must know.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~1.5 hours🗺️ Landscape

📖 Chapter Overview: The CNCF Landscape has over 200 projects. It can feel like walking into a massive library where every book claims to solve your problems. This chapter gives you a navigation system — the CNCF maturity levels (Graduated / Incubating / Sandbox), the Cloud Native Trail Map adoption path, and the Platform Stack model that maps every tool to one of 5 layers. By the end, you'll know which projects matter for the CNPE exam and how they fit together into a coherent platform.

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Categorize CNCF projects by maturity level: Graduated, Incubating, Sandbox
  • Trace the Cloud Native Trail Map adoption path from containerization to security
  • Map each layer of the Platform Stack to its corresponding CNPE exam domain and weight
  • Identify the 9 must-know CNCF projects for platform engineers
  • Select the right CNCF tool for each platform layer with reasoning
  • Explain why platform engineers own steps 2-6 while developers only need step 1
📋 CNPE Domain Mapping: Chapter 3 introduces the Platform Stack — the organizing framework for the entire exam. Every subsequent chapter maps to one of these 5 layers. Domain 3 (Platform APIs — 25%) and Domain 2 (GitOps & CD — 25%) together are 50% of the exam. Understanding WHERE each tool fits is your first step toward passing.

3.1 CNCF Landscape Map — Graduated, Incubating, Sandbox

The CNCF organizes projects into three maturity levels based on adoption, community health, and production readiness. Think of these as "proven," "promising," and "experimental."

📖 Why Does the CNCF Exist? — A Brief History

The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) was founded in 2015 as a sub-foundation of the Linux Foundation. Google donated Kubernetes 1.0 to the CNCF at launch. The motivation: after Docker popularized containers (2013), an ecosystem of tools exploded around it — but there was no neutral body to govern them. Companies were hesitant to adopt tools controlled by a single vendor (what if they changed the license? abandoned it? went bankrupt?).

The CNCF solves this by providing:

  • 🛡️ Vendor-neutral governance: No single company controls a CNCF project. Multiple maintainers from different companies share responsibility. Even if one company drops support, the project lives on.
  • 📋 Standardized maturity: The Graduated/Incubating/Sandbox levels give you a clear signal: "Is this ready for my production platform?" Without this, every tool claims to be production-ready — and you have to evaluate them all from scratch.
  • 🤝 Community & events: KubeCon + CloudNativeCon (the CNCF's flagship conference) draws 10,000+ attendees. It's where the ecosystem collaborates, standards are debated, and best practices emerge.
  • 🔓 Open governance: CNCF projects must have open governance. No CLA (Contributor License Agreement) that assigns copyright to one company. This protects contributors and users alike.

The CNCF is NOT: (1) A standards body like W3C or IETF — it doesn't create standards, it hosts projects. (2) A funding source — the CNCF provides infrastructure and marketing, not direct funding. (3) A certification authority for individuals — that's the Linux Foundation's training arm (which runs the CNPE exam).

🎓Graduated

Production-ready. Battle-tested.

Widely adopted by major enterprises. Strong governance, security audits, diverse maintainers.

Examples: Kubernetes, Prometheus, Envoy, Helm, etcd, containerd, Argo CD, Linkerd, Cilium, Falco

When to use: Default choice for production platforms. These projects have proven themselves at scale.

🥚Incubating

Growing fast. Maturing rapidly.

Increasing adoption, active development, working toward graduation criteria.

Examples: Backstage, Crossplane, Knative, OpenTelemetry, Flux, Kyverno, cert-manager

When to use: Production-ready for most use cases. Evaluate against graduated alternatives.

🧪Sandbox

Experimental. Early-stage.

New ideas, niche solutions, proof-of-concepts. May or may not graduate.

Examples: 150+ projects — too many to list. Most will never reach Incubation.

When to use: Evaluate carefully. Only if no Graduated/Incubating alternative exists.

Maturity LevelKey Criteriaanihpj Would UseCNPE Exam Relevance
🎓 GraduatedSecurity audit passed, multiple maintainers, 250+ contributors, used in production by 3+ end usersKubernetes, Prometheus, Argo CD, Helm, Envoy (via Istio), CiliumHIGH — The exam expects you to know these tools and when to use them
🥚 IncubatingGrowing adoption, 3+ maintainers, 50+ contributors, documented usersBackstage, Crossplane, OpenTelemetry, Kyverno, cert-manager, FluxMEDIUM — Know the major Incubating projects and their use cases
🧪 SandboxExperimental, early adopters, 2+ maintainers, open governanceNiche tools only if no alternative existsLOW — The exam won't test specific Sandbox projects
🧠 CNPE Exam: The exam expects you to know which tools solve which problems — you don't need to memorize 200+ projects, just the key Graduated and Incubating ones. For each project, know: what problem it solves, its maturity level, and its anihpj equivalent. If a question mentions a Sandbox project, a Graduated alternative probably exists.

📖 How Does a Project Enter the CNCF? — The TOC and Acceptance Process: Understanding this helps you evaluate WHY some projects graduate and others don't:

  1. Submission: A project applies to the CNCF Technical Oversight Committee (TOC) with a proposal explaining what problem it solves and why it belongs in the cloud native ecosystem.
  2. TOC Review: The TOC (9 elected technical leaders from companies like Google, Red Hat, VMware) evaluates the proposal. They look for: open governance, diverse maintainers, community health, and alignment with cloud native principles.
  3. Sandbox Acceptance: If accepted, the project enters Sandbox. The CNCF provides: neutral hosting (GitHub), marketing support, and community events (KubeCon). No funding yet.
  4. Incubation Application: The project must demonstrate: growing adoption, 3+ maintainers from different companies, regular releases, documented security practices, and user case studies.
  5. Graduation Application: The highest bar: security audit by a 3rd party (costs ~$50K, CNCF pays), 250+ contributors, multiple production users at scale, formal governance with a steering committee.

Why this matters: When you see "CNCF Graduated," it means the project has survived years of scrutiny, passed a security audit, and is trusted by major enterprises. This is why platform teams default to Graduated projects.

CNCF PROJECT MATURITY LIFECYCLE — Sandbox → Incubating → Graduated
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    CNCF PROJECT MATURITY JOURNEY                          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🧪 SANDBOX                    🥚 INCUBATING                  🎓 GRADUATED
  ┌────────────────┐           ┌────────────────┐           ┌────────────────┐
  │  Submit to CNCF │    ───►  │  3+ maintainers│    ───►  │  Security audit │
  │  2+ maintainers │           │  50+ contributors│        │  passed          │
  │  Open governance│           │  Growing users  │        │  250+ contributors│
  │  Early adopters │           │  Maturing docs  │        │  Production use  │
  │                 │           │                 │        │  at scale        │
  └────────────────┘           └────────────────┘        └────────────────┘
         │                            │                          │
         ▼                            ▼                          ▼
  "Interesting idea"          "Gaining traction"         "Battle-tested standard"
  Example: KubeVela          Example: Backstage         Example: Kubernetes

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  ⏱️ TYPICAL TIMELINE: Sandbox → Incubating: ~1-2 years
                       Incubating → Graduated: ~2-4 years
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
💡 The Stories Behind Key Graduated Projects — What Graduation Really Means

Graduation isn't just a badge. It represents years of proving a project can survive and thrive independently. Here are the journeys of the projects you'll use most:

ProjectDonated ByYear Entered CNCFYear GraduatedJourney Highlights
☸️ KubernetesGoogle2015 (founding)2018 (first graduate)Google donated K8s 1.0 at CNCF launch. Based on Google's internal Borg system (ran Google Search, Gmail for 10+ years). First CNCF project to graduate. Now maintained by thousands across 500+ companies.
📊 PrometheusSoundCloud20162018 (2nd graduate)Created at SoundCloud in 2012 because existing monitoring tools (Nagios, Graphite) couldn't handle their scale. Born from real production pain. Now the de facto monitoring standard for K8s.
🔗 EnvoyLyft20172018 (3rd graduate)Lyft built Envoy to solve their microservice networking problems. Originally a monolithic app → microservices migration created chaos. Envoy became the universal data plane. Now powers Istio, AWS App Mesh, and Cloudflare.
🔄 ArgoIntuit / Akuity20202022Intuit needed a workflow engine for their K8s-based data pipelines. Argo CD (GitOps) became more popular than Argo Workflows (pipelines). Now 4 sub-projects: CD, Workflows, Rollouts, Events.
🛡️ FalcoSysdig20182024 (newest!)Sysdig built Falco to detect runtime threats using eBPF (a Linux kernel technology). Reads kernel syscalls without modifying the kernel. The newest CNCF graduate — proves the graduation pipeline is still active.

Pattern to notice: Every Graduated project was born from a real company's production pain (Google's Borg, SoundCloud's monitoring, Lyft's networking). They weren't built by committees — they were built by engineers who needed something that didn't exist. Then they were donated to the CNCF so the community could own and evolve them. This is the cloud native pattern: build for yourself, open-source for everyone, CNCF for neutral governance.

3.2 The Cloud Native Trail Map — Step-by-Step Adoption

The CNCF published the Cloud Native Trail Map as a step-by-step guide for organizations adopting cloud native. It's a sequential path — each step builds on the previous one. The key insight: platform engineers implement steps 2-6 so developers only need step 1.

THE CLOUD NATIVE TRAIL MAP — 6 Steps to Cloud Native

😰 Life WITHOUT the Trail Map — The "Just Use Docker Compose" Startup
  • 🔴 "We deploy by SCP-ing files to an EC2 instance and running docker compose up -d. Our one server handles 50 users fine."
  • 🔴 "We hit the front page of Hacker News. The server melted. We were down for 6 hours while we frantically set up a second server."
  • 🔴 "We have no metrics. We found out about the outage from a Twitter DM."
  • 🔴 "The second server has different package versions because someone manually installed things. Production is inconsistent."
  • 🔴 "We need to roll back a deploy but we overwrote the old files. We're restoring from last week's backup."
🎉 Life WITH the Trail Map — Following Each Step Deliberately
  • ✅ Step 1 (Containerize): Dockerfile defines the exact environment. Same image on dev laptop and production. No "works on my machine."
  • ✅ Step 2 (CI/CD): GitHub Actions builds and tests on every push. Broken code never reaches users. Pipeline catches issues in minutes.
  • ✅ Step 3 (Orchestrate): Kubernetes scales from 2 to 50 replicas in seconds when Hacker News traffic hits. HPA handles it automatically.
  • ✅ Step 4 (Observe): Prometheus alerts within 30 seconds of latency spike. Grafana dashboard shows exactly which endpoint is slow. No Twitter DM needed.
  • ✅ Step 5 (Service Mesh): mTLS encrypts all service-to-service traffic. Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures. Retries handle transient errors.
  • ✅ Step 6 (Security): Kyverno blocks containers running as root. Falco detects anomalous processes. Trivy scans images for CVEs before deployment.

💡 Why This Trail Map Matters for Platform Engineers: Each step represents a service you provide to developers. Think of it as building a highway:

  • Step 1 (Containerization): You provide base images, Dockerfile templates, and a container registry. Developers write their Dockerfile and push. This is the only step developers do themselves.
  • Step 2 (CI/CD): You provide pipeline templates, build infrastructure, and artifact promotion. Developers commit code; the pipeline handles the rest.
  • Step 3 (Orchestration): You provide the Kubernetes cluster, namespaces, RBAC, and resource quotas. Developers don't think about nodes or scheduling.
  • Step 4 (Observability): You provide dashboards, alerting rules, and log aggregation. Developers just expose /metrics and log to stdout.
  • Step 5 (Service Mesh): You provide mTLS, retries, circuit breakers, and traffic splitting. Developers don't implement these in their code — the mesh does it.
  • Step 6 (Security & Policy): You provide admission policies, image scanning, runtime security, and compliance checks. Developers may not even know these exist — they're transparent.
📖 The Trail Map Scales — From Startup to Enterprise

The Cloud Native Trail Map is not all-or-nothing. Different organizations adopt different steps at different times based on their scale and needs:

Organization SizeTypical Trail Map AdoptionWhat They Skip (at first)
🏠 Startup (3-10 engineers)Steps 1-3: Containerize + CI/CD + K8s cluster (maybe managed like EKS/GKE). Basic monitoring (CloudWatch/Grafana Cloud).Service Mesh (Step 5) — 3 microservices don't need a mesh. Security (Step 6) — basic RBAC + cloud firewall is enough.
🏢 Scale-up (20-100 engineers)Steps 1-5: Full CI/CD pipeline, K8s with multiple namespaces, Prometheus/Grafana, service mesh for mTLS.Full Policy as Code (Step 6) — starting to add Kyverno for critical policies but not comprehensive yet.
🏙️ Enterprise (200+ engineers)ALL 6 steps, fully automated. Self-service platform layer on top. Multiple clusters, multi-tenancy, compliance frameworks.Nothing. At this scale, skipping any step creates unacceptable risk.

anihpj's position: We're designing for the Scale-up level — assuming 20-100 engineers, growing fast. That means we invest in Steps 1-5 now, with Step 6 (Policy as Code) designed for easy adoption when the team grows. The platform should be ready before the pain arrives.

⚠️ The Reverse Trail Map — What Happens When You SKIP a Step

The Trail Map is sequential for a reason. Skipping steps creates compounding problems:

  • 🔴 SKIP Step 1 (Containerize): You're deploying JARs/WARs directly to VMs. No isolation. "But it works on my machine" becomes a daily excuse. Rollback means "restore the VM snapshot from 3 days ago."
  • 🔴 SKIP Step 2 (CI/CD): Developers build and deploy manually. Human error is your deployment pipeline. One typo in a deploy command takes down production. Rollback means "who has the last working JAR?"
  • 🔴 SKIP Step 3 (Orchestrate): You manage containers with bash scripts and docker-compose. Scaling = manually SSH into 5 servers and run docker run. One server goes down = 20% of your capacity gone until a human notices.
  • 🔴 SKIP Step 4 (Observe): You have NO idea how your app is performing. Users tweet about the outage before you know. Debugging = SSH into servers and tail -f /var/log/syslog. MTTR measured in hours, not minutes.
  • 🔴 SKIP Step 5 (Service Mesh): Every service implements retries, timeouts, and circuit breakers differently (if at all). One slow service causes a cascading failure. Debugging why = tracing through 5 different retry implementations.
  • 🔴 SKIP Step 6 (Security): Containers run as root. No network segmentation. One compromised container → lateral movement to the entire cluster. Audit? "Check the CloudTrail logs from 3 months ago — oh wait, we don't have those."
TRAIL MAP DECISION TREE — Which Step Should You Tackle Next?
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    TRAIL MAP SKIP-RISK DECISION TREE                       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  START: "We want to go cloud native"
  │
  ├─► Are your apps containerized? ──NO──► DO STEP 1 FIRST (non-negotiable)
  │
  ├─► Do you automate builds/tests? ──NO──► DO STEP 2 (biggest ROI for small teams)
  │
  ├─► Running on K8s? ──NO──► DO STEP 3 (but you need Steps 1-2 first)
  │
  ├─► Can you see metrics/logs? ──NO──► DO STEP 4 (you're flying blind)
  │
  ├─► Do you need mTLS/circuit breakers? ──NO──► SKIP Step 5 (revisit at 10+ services)
  │
  └─► Is security automated? ──NO──► DO STEP 6 (at minimum: no root, image scanning)

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  GOLDEN RULE: Never skip Step 1-2. Everything else depends on them.
               Step 5 is OPTIONAL until you have 10+ microservices.
               Step 6 is NON-NEGOTIABLE for any production system.
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

3.3 The Platform Stack — Self-Service → Delivery → Orchestration → Observability → Security

The Platform Stack is a layered model that organizes every cloud native tool into one of five layers. This is the organizing framework for the ENTIRE CNPE exam. Each layer maps to a CNPE domain with a specific exam weight.

THE CLOUD NATIVE PLATFORM STACK (Mapped to CNPE Domains)
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              THE CLOUD NATIVE PLATFORM STACK (Mapped to CNPE)       │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  ─┐

  │  Backstage/Port | CRDs | Operators | Developer CLI | Golden      │   │
  │  Paths | Self-Service DB/NS/TLS Provisioning                     │   │  TOP
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │  (What
                               │                                         │  developers
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │  SEE)
  │  🚀 DELIVERY LAYER (Domain 2: GitOps & CD — 25%)                 │   │
  │  Argo CD/Flux | CI/CD Pipelines | Progressive Delivery           │   │
  │  Helm/Kustomize | Container Registries | Image Signing           │   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
                               │                                         │
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  ⚙️ ORCHESTRATION (Domain 1: Platform Architecture — 15%)        │   │
  │  Kubernetes | Service Mesh | Ingress/Gateway API                 │   │
  │  Multi-Tenancy | Cost Management | Storage | Scheduling          │   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
                               │                                         │
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  📊 OBSERVABILITY (Domain 4: Observability & Ops — 20%)          │   │
  │  Prometheus/Grafana | OpenTelemetry | Loki | Tempo               │   │
  │  SLOs/SLIs | Alerting | Incident Management | DORA Metrics       │   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
                               │                                         │
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  🔒 SECURITY (Domain 5: Security & Policy — 15%)                 │   │  BOTTOM
  │  OPA/Kyverno | Falco | Trivy | mTLS | RBAC | Audit              │   │  (Invisible
  │  SBOM | Cosign/Sigstore | SLSA | CIS Benchmarks                  │   │  foundation)
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  ─┘

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  TOP = Developer-facing (they see and interact with these layers)
  BOTTOM = Platform-internal (developers benefit without knowing details)
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

💡 Why the Stack Order Matters: Each layer depends on the layer below it. You can't do GitOps (Delivery) without a Kubernetes cluster (Orchestration). You can't secure services (Security) without observability to detect anomalies. The stack is built bottom-up but consumed top-down: developers interact with the Self-Service layer, which delegates to Delivery, which orchestrates on K8s, which is monitored by Observability, which is protected by Security.

📖 The Platform Stack as a Restaurant Kitchen — An Analogy for Non-Technical Stakeholders: This analogy helps explain the platform layers to anyone:

Platform LayerRestaurant EquivalentWhat It Means
👨‍💻 Self-ServiceThe Menu & WaitstaffThis is what customers (developers) interact with. They don't need to know how the kitchen works — they just order from the menu. The menu defines what's available (golden paths). The waitstaff takes the order (developer CLI/portal).
🚀 DeliveryThe Pass (Expediter)The expediter coordinates between the dining room and the kitchen. They make sure orders get to the right table, in the right order, at the right time. This is what CI/CD and Argo CD do — they move code from "ordered" to "delivered."
⚙️ OrchestrationThe Kitchen & ChefsThe kitchen takes raw ingredients (containers) and turns them into dishes (running services). The head chef (Kubernetes scheduler) decides which stove (node) cooks which dish. If a stove breaks, the chef moves the dish to another stove.
📊 ObservabilityThermometers & Tasting SpoonsHow do you know the food is right? Thermometers (metrics) measure temperature. Taste tests (health checks) verify quality. Ticket times (traces) track how long each dish takes. Without these, you're cooking blind.
🔒 SecurityHealth Inspector & Food SafetyThe health inspector (Kyverno) ensures the kitchen follows safety rules. Hairnets (RBAC) restrict who can touch the food. Refrigeration logs (audit trails) prove compliance. Customers never see this — but they'd get sick without it.

Key takeaway: When a developer says "I just want to deploy my app," they're saying "I just want to order from the menu." The platform engineer's job is to build the entire restaurant behind that menu so every order comes out perfect — even when the restaurant is serving 500 tables at once.

💡 The Developer Contract — What Each Layer Promises

Every platform layer makes an implicit promise to developers. When you build the platform, you're signing this contract:

LayerThe Platform's Promise to DevelopersThe Developer's Responsibility
👨‍💻 Self-Service"You can get a database, namespace, or TLS certificate in <5 minutes without filing a ticket."Specify what you need (size, region, backup policy). Don't ask Ops to do it for you.
🚀 Delivery"Push to main. We'll build, test, scan, and deploy. If it fails, we'll roll back automatically."Write tests. Keep the pipeline green. Don't bypass it.
⚙️ Orchestration"Your app will stay running. If a node dies, your pods move. If traffic spikes, you auto-scale."Set resource requests/limits. Define health checks. Design for ephemeral pods.
📊 Observability"You'll know about problems before users do. Dashboards, alerts, and logs are ready — just instrument your app."Expose /metrics. Log to stdout as structured JSON. Pass trace context in headers.
🔒 Security"Your app is protected by default. No root containers, no unsigned images, no unexpected network access."Don't request unnecessary permissions. Keep dependencies updated. Report security issues.

This contract is the heart of platform engineering. If either side breaks it — platform doesn't deliver on its promises, or developers bypass the platform — the whole model collapses. The CNPE exam tests whether you understand this two-way relationship.

3.4 Key CNCF Projects Every Platform Engineer Must Know

From 200+ projects, here are the 9 essential CNCF projects that appear again and again in platform engineering — and on the CNPE exam.

ProjectCategoryMaturityWhat It Doesanihpj Use
☸️ KubernetesOrchestration🎓 GraduatedSchedules and manages containers across a cluster. The foundation everything else runs on.Runs all anihpj workloads (web, postgres, redis, monitoring, GitOps)
📦 HelmPackage Management🎓 Graduated"apt-get for Kubernetes." Packages, versions, and distributes K8s manifests as Charts.Install Prometheus, Grafana, cert-manager via community charts
📊 PrometheusMonitoring🎓 GraduatedMetrics collection and alerting. Pull-based, time-series DB. The gold standard for K8s monitoring.Scrapes /metrics from anihpj-web. Alerts on 5xx errors, high latency.
🔗 EnvoyProxy🎓 GraduatedHigh-performance L7 proxy. Powers Istio's sidecar, API Gateways, and Ingress controllers.Istio sidecar (Envoy) handles mTLS between anihpj-web → postgres
🔄 ArgoGitOps / Workflows🎓 GraduatedArgo CD (GitOps sync), Argo Workflows (DAG pipelines), Argo Rollouts (progressive delivery).Argo CD syncs k8s/base/ → cluster. Argo Rollouts for canary deploys.
🛡️ FalcoRuntime Security🎓 GraduatedDetects anomalous behavior at the kernel level using eBPF. Alerts on unexpected syscalls.Alerts if anyone runs kubectl exec in production. Detects crypto miners.
🔍 OpenTelemetryObservability🥚 IncubatingStandard for collecting traces, metrics, and logs. One SDK for all observability backends.Auto-instruments Django. Sends traces → Tempo, metrics → Prometheus.
🔐 cert-managerSecurity🥚 IncubatingAutomates TLS certificate issuance and renewal. Integrates with Let's Encrypt, HashiCorp Vault.Auto-provisions TLS certs for anihpj.com Ingress. Renews before expiry.
📋 KyvernoPolicy🥚 IncubatingKubernetes-native policy engine. Policies written in YAML. Mutate, validate, generate.Blocks pods without resource limits. Auto-adds team labels. Enforces image registry.

💡 The 4-Step Tool Evaluation Framework: When you encounter a new CNCF project (or any tool), use this framework to decide whether to adopt it for your platform:

  1. 🧭 MATURITY CHECK: Is it Graduated? Incubating? Sandbox? Default to Graduated. Evaluate Incubating if no Graduated alternative exists. Avoid Sandbox for production unless there's truly no other option and you're willing to accept the risk.
  2. 🎯 FIT CHECK: Does it solve a REAL problem for your platform? Don't adopt a tool just because it's popular. If your team has 3 microservices, you don't need a service mesh yet. Start with the problem, not the tool.
  3. 👥 COMMUNITY CHECK: Are there multiple active maintainers from different companies? Is the project's GitHub healthy (responses to issues, regular releases)? A single-company project is a risk — if that company loses interest, the project dies.
  4. 🔌 INTEGRATION CHECK: Does it integrate with your existing stack? If you're already using Prometheus, adding Grafana is natural (same ecosystem). If a tool requires replacing 3 existing tools, that's a migration project — not a simple adoption.

anihpj example: We chose Argo CD (Graduated ✓, solves GitOps ✓, active community ✓, integrates with K8s natively ✓). We rejected Flux for anihpj not because it's bad, but because Argo CD's Web UI is essential for our multi-team platform (Fit Check).

📖 Tools NOT in CNCF — But Essential for Platform Engineers

Not every critical tool lives under the CNCF umbrella. Here are tools that every platform engineer must know that are NOT CNCF projects:

ToolCategoryGoverned ByWhy It's Essentialanihpj Use
🐳 DockerContainer EngineDocker Inc. (now part of Mirantis)Built the container revolution. Still the most common way to build OCI images locally. Docker Hub is the default public registry.docker build -t anihpj-web . — every developer's first step
🏗️ TerraformIaCHashiCorp (BSL license since 2023)Provision cloud infrastructure (EKS clusters, RDS databases, VPCs). Terraform provisions what Kubernetes runs ON.Provision EKS cluster, RDS for anihpj, VPC networking
⚡ GitHub ActionsCI/CDMicrosoft/GitHubThe most popular CI/CD platform. Tightly integrated with GitHub repositories. Free for public repos.anihpj CI pipeline: lint → test → build → push to ECR
📊 GrafanaVisualizationGrafana LabsWhile Prometheus (CNCF Graduated) collects metrics, Grafana visualizes them. They're a pair — you need both. Grafana also visualizes Loki logs and Tempo traces.Unified dashboards for metrics, logs, and traces

Why this matters: The CNPE exam is NOT limited to CNCF projects. It tests your ability to design and operate a platform using the RIGHT tools, regardless of governance. A platform that only uses CNCF tools is incomplete — you need Terraform (HashiCorp), Docker (Mirantis), and GitHub Actions (Microsoft) too. The skill is knowing which tool solves which problem, CNCF or not.

📖 Deep Profiles — What Makes Each of the 9 Projects Unique

Beyond the basic "what it does," here's what makes each project special and where it fits in the ecosystem:

ProjectArchitectureKey DifferentiatorMain CompetitorWhen NOT to Use
☸️ KubernetesControl plane (API server, scheduler, controller-manager, etcd) + worker nodes (kubelet, kube-proxy, CRI runtime)Only orchestrator with 500+ integrations. The "Linux of the cloud" — it won because it's extensible, not because it's simple.Nomad (HashiCorp) — simpler but far less ecosystemIf you run <3 containers on a single VM. K8s overhead isn't worth it at tiny scale.
📦 HelmClient (helm CLI) + Charts (templated YAML) + Repository (chart storage). No server-side component."apt-get for K8s" — one command installs complex stacks (e.g., helm install prometheus prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack installs Prometheus + Grafana + AlertManager + node-exporter).Kustomize (simpler, template-free) or Timoni (OCI-native)For your own apps where you want full control over every YAML line. Use Kustomize instead.
📊 PrometheusSingle binary (Prometheus server) with local TSDB. Pull model scrapes HTTP endpoints. No distributed components (Thanos/Cortex add clustering).Pull model eliminates the "monitoring agent" concept. Every app is self-instrumenting via /metrics. No separate agent to install, configure, or debug.VictoriaMetrics (higher performance, PromQL compatible) or Datadog (SaaS)For long-term storage (>30 days) without Thanos/Cortex. Prometheus alone is NOT a long-term data warehouse.
🔗 EnvoySingle binary proxy. Runs as sidecar (alongside each app) or as edge proxy (at cluster boundary). Configured via xDS APIs from control plane.Universal data plane — same proxy binary handles ingress, egress, and service-to-service traffic. One technology to learn for all networking.NGINX (simpler, larger install base) or HAProxy (battle-tested TCP load balancer)For simple reverse proxy needs. NGINX is easier to configure. Envoy's power is its programmability.
🔄 ArgoArgo CD: controller in K8s + Web UI + CLI. Argo Workflows: CRD-based DAG engine. Argo Rollouts: superset of Deployment CRD.Argo CD's Web UI makes GitOps VISIBLE. Every app's sync status, health, and diff is one click away. Critical for multi-team platforms.Flux CD (CRD-only, no Web UI) — but Flux has better image update automationIf you prefer everything-as-CRDs with no Web UI, Flux is better. Argo is opinionated about visibility.
🛡️ FalcoKernel module or eBPF probe + userspace engine + rules engine. Reads syscalls in real-time without modifying the kernel.Detects UNKNOWN threats, not just known CVEs. If a container starts spawning shells, reading /etc/shadow, or making outbound connections on unusual ports — Falco alerts. It's behavioral, not signature-based.Tetragon (Cilium's eBPF-based security) or Aqua (commercial)For CVE scanning only (use Trivy). Falco complements CVE scanning — it catches what CVEs miss (zero-days, insider threats).
🔍 OpenTelemetrySDKs (per language) + Collector (agent/gateway) + OTLP protocol. Vendor-neutral — send to any backend.ONE standard for traces, metrics, AND logs. Before OpenTelemetry, you needed Jaeger SDK for traces + Prometheus SDK for metrics + Fluentd for logs. Now: one SDK, three signals.No direct competitor — it's THE standard. Older alternatives: OpenTracing + OpenCensus (merged into OTel)If all your observability is already Prometheus + Fluentd. Adding OTel adds complexity. Migrate when you need distributed tracing.
🔐 cert-managerController in K8s + CRDs (Certificate, Issuer, ClusterIssuer). Integrates with Let's Encrypt, HashiCorp Vault, Venafi, AWS PCA."Set and forget" TLS. Create a Certificate CRD → cert-manager provisions, renews, and rotates TLS certs automatically. Never manually renew a cert again.Manual certbot cron jobs (works but not K8s-native) or commercial CAs with their own automationFor internal-only services that don't need public TLS. Use k8s self-signed certs or an internal CA.
📋 KyvernoController in K8s + CRDs (ClusterPolicy, Policy). Uses dynamic admission webhooks. No external database.Policies are plain YAML. No new language to learn. Any K8s user can read a Kyverno policy. Compare: OPA requires learning Rego (a logic programming language).OPA/Gatekeeper (Rego language — more powerful but steeper learning curve)For policies that span beyond K8s (e.g., Terraform, Envoy, SSH). OPA is a general-purpose policy engine. Kyverno is K8s-only.

💡 What Each Domain Actually Tests — Task Type Breakdown

Knowing the weight percentages is helpful. Knowing what KINDS of tasks you'll face is actionable. Here's what each domain's exam tasks look like:

DomainWeightTypical Task TypesExample Task
Domain 1: Architecture15%Upgrade a cluster, configure etcd backup, troubleshoot control plane, set up multi-tenancy with namespaces and resource quotas"Configure RBAC so Team A can only deploy to namespace 'team-a' with max 4 CPUs and 8GB RAM."
Domain 2: GitOps & CD25%Create Argo CD Application, configure sync policies, set up Helm chart deployment, write a CI/CD pipeline, configure progressive delivery"Create an Argo CD Application that deploys the anihpj Helm chart from the 'main' branch with automated sync and pruning enabled."
Domain 3: Platform APIs25%Create a CRD, write an Operator, configure Backstage component, design a self-service workflow, expose a service via Gateway API"Create a CRD 'Database' with fields for engine, version, and size. Deploy an Operator that provisions an RDS instance when a Database CR is created."
Domain 4: Observability20%Configure ServiceMonitor, write PromQL queries, set up Grafana dashboard, configure Loki log pipeline, define SLO alerts"Create a Prometheus alert that fires when the anihpj-web error rate exceeds 5% over a 5-minute window. The alert must route to the 'platform-oncall' Slack channel."
Domain 5: Security15%Write Kyverno/OPA policy, configure NetworkPolicy, set up mTLS, scan images with Trivy, configure Falco rules, implement RBAC"Create a Kyverno ClusterPolicy that blocks any Pod using the 'latest' image tag and mutates deployments to add 'app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: platform' label."

Key insight: Notice that the highest-weighted domains (2 and 3) are the most automation-heavy — they test whether you can build systems that work without you. The exam isn't testing your ability to MANUALLY operate a cluster (that's CKA). It's testing your ability to BUILD PLATFORMS that make manual operation unnecessary.

💡 CNPE Exam Time Management — 2 Hours, ~25-30 Tasks

The CNPE is a 2-hour performance-based exam in a live terminal. Here's how to manage your time:

PhaseTimeWhat to Do
Setup (first 5 min)0:00–0:05Read ALL task descriptions first (don't solve yet). Flag easy tasks (ones you know immediately). Flag hard tasks (come back later). Set kubectl context. Verify cluster access.
Easy Tasks (next 30 min)0:05–0:35Solve all ~10 easy tasks first. These are typically: create a namespace, expose a service, label a resource, check logs. Build momentum and confidence. You should finish each in <3 min.
Medium Tasks (next 45 min)0:35–1:20Solve ~10-12 medium tasks: configure Argo CD sync, write a Kyverno policy, create a ServiceMonitor, set up an Ingress with TLS. These take 4-7 min each. If stuck for >5 min, flag and move on.
Hard Tasks (next 25 min)1:20–1:45Solve 3-5 hard tasks: create a CRD with validation schema, write an Operator reconciliation loop, configure multi-cluster GitOps. These test deep understanding. Use kubectl explain and --dry-run=client to verify YAML before applying.
Review (last 15 min)1:45–2:00Re-check ALL tasks: did you save output to the correct file? Did you use the right namespace? Did you apply (not just create) resources? The CNPE grades EXACT output — spelling and namespaces matter.

Critical exam tips:

  • 🔑 Use context switching carefully: Every task specifies a kubectl context. The WRONG context = WRONG cluster = ZERO points even if your commands are correct. Always run kubectl config current-context before starting a task.
  • 📝 Read output requirements: Some tasks say "save the output to /tmp/answer.txt." If you solve the task but don't save the output → ZERO points. Read the LAST LINE of each task first.
  • ⚡ Use imperative commands with --dry-run: kubectl create deployment my-app --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml generates correct YAML in seconds. Don't hand-write YAML unless required.
  • 📚 kubectl explain is your friend: Can't remember a CRD field? kubectl explain deployment.spec.template.spec.containers.resources shows the full schema. The exam terminal has this available.
  • ⏱️ Don't fixate: If you spend 7+ minutes on one task, you're losing time for 2-3 easier tasks. Flag it, move on, come back if time permits. Partial credit is rare — incomplete answers usually score 0.

🏋️ Chapter 3 — Hands-On Practice Drills (10 Exercises)

The CNPE is a performance-based exam — you solve tasks in a live Linux terminal. Practice these drills in your lab environment until you can complete each within the target time.

⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 3.1 — Classify CNCF Projects by Maturity

Create a sorted list of CNCF projects and classify them by maturity level.

  1. Run kubectl get pods -n argocd to see Argo CD components — this is a Graduated project
  2. Check if Kyverno is installed: kubectl get pods -n kyverno — an Incubating project
  3. Write a shell script that categorizes 5 CNCF projects into Graduated/Incubating/Sandbox and prints a summary table
💡 Hint: Use echo and printf to create a formatted table. Reference: K8s=Graduated, Prometheus=Graduated, OpenTelemetry=Incubating, Kyverno=Incubating, Backstage=Incubating.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Check Argo CD (Graduated)
kubectl get pods -n argocd 2>/dev/null || echo "Argo CD not installed (install with: kubectl create namespace argocd && kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml)"

# Step 2: Check Kyverno (Incubating)
kubectl get pods -n kyverno 2>/dev/null || echo "Kyverno not installed"

# Step 3: Maturity classification script
cat > classify-cncf.sh << 'SCRIPT'
#!/bin/bash
echo "PROJECT          MATURITY"
echo "──────────────────────────"
echo "Kubernetes       🎓 Graduated"
echo "Prometheus       🎓 Graduated"
echo "Argo CD          🎓 Graduated"
echo "Helm             🎓 Graduated"
echo "Envoy            🎓 Graduated"
echo "Falco            🎓 Graduated"
echo "OpenTelemetry    🥚 Incubating"
echo "Kyverno          🥚 Incubating"
echo "Backstage        🥚 Incubating"
echo "Crossplane       🥚 Incubating"
echo "cert-manager     🥚 Incubating"
SCRIPT
chmod +x classify-cncf.sh
./classify-cncf.sh
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 3.2 — Install Argo CD (Graduated GitOps Tool)

Install Argo CD in your cluster — the most important CNCF Graduated GitOps tool.

  1. Create the argocd namespace
  2. Install Argo CD from the official manifest
  3. Wait for all pods to be Running
  4. Get the initial admin password
  5. Port-forward the Argo CD server and access the UI at https://localhost:8080
💡 Hint: Argo CD install manifest is at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml. The admin password is stored in a Secret named argocd-initial-admin-secret.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Create namespace
kubectl create namespace argocd

# Step 2: Install Argo CD
kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml

# Step 3: Wait for pods
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n argocd --timeout=300s
kubectl get pods -n argocd
# EXPECTED: argocd-server, argocd-repo-server, argocd-application-controller, argocd-redis

# Step 4: Get admin password
kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret -o jsonpath="{.data.password}" | base64 -d
echo  # newline

# Step 5: Port-forward and access
kubectl port-forward svc/argocd-server -n argocd 8080:443 &
# Open: https://localhost:8080
# Username: admin
# Password: (from step 4)
⏱️ Target: 6 minutes
Drill 3.3 — Install Prometheus Stack (Graduated Monitoring)

Install the kube-prometheus-stack using Helm — the CNCF Graduated monitoring standard.

  1. Add the Prometheus Community Helm repo
  2. Install kube-prometheus-stack in the monitoring namespace
  3. Verify Prometheus, Grafana, and AlertManager pods are running
  4. Port-forward Grafana and log in (default: admin / prom-operator)
  5. Navigate to the Kubernetes/Compute Resources/Pods dashboard
💡 Hint: helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts, then helm install prometheus prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack -n monitoring --create-namespace
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Add Helm repo
helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update

# Step 2: Install kube-prometheus-stack
helm install prometheus prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack \
  -n monitoring --create-namespace

# Step 3: Verify pods
kubectl get pods -n monitoring
# EXPECTED: prometheus-prometheus-0, alertmanager-prometheus-0,
#           prometheus-grafana-*, prometheus-kube-state-metrics-*,
#           prometheus-prometheus-node-exporter-*

# Step 4: Access Grafana
kubectl port-forward svc/prometheus-grafana -n monitoring 3000:80 &
# Open: http://localhost:3000
# Username: admin
# Password: prom-operator

# Step 5: Explore dashboards
# In Grafana: Dashboards → Browse → Kubernetes / Compute Resources / Pod
# This shows CPU and memory usage for all pods — a CNPE exam skill
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 3.4 — Map anihpj Components to Platform Layers

Given hypothetical anihpj components, determine which Platform Stack layer each belongs to.

  1. Create a file layer-mapping.txt with columns: Component | Layer | Domain
  2. Classify: Argo CD Application for anihpj-web
  3. Classify: Prometheus ServiceMonitor for anihpj-web
  4. Classify: Kyverno ClusterPolicy blocking root containers
  5. Classify: Backstage Component representing anihpj-web in the developer portal
  6. Classify: Kubernetes Deployment for anihpj-web (with resource requests/limits)
💡 Hint: Use the Platform Stack table from 3.5. Each component maps to exactly one layer.
📝 View Solution 
# Create mapping file
cat > layer-mapping.txt << 'EOF'
COMPONENT                         | PLATFORM LAYER       | CNPE DOMAIN
──────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────────
Argo CD Application (anihpj-web) | 🚀 Delivery           | Domain 2: GitOps & CD
Prometheus ServiceMonitor         | 📊 Observability      | Domain 4: Obs & Ops
Kyverno ClusterPolicy (no-root)  | 🔒 Security           | Domain 5: Security
Backstage Component (anihpj-web) | 👨‍💻 Self-Service       | Domain 3: Platform APIs
K8s Deployment (anihpj-web)      | ⚙️ Orchestration      | Domain 1: Architecture
EOF
cat layer-mapping.txt

# KEY RULE:
# If a developer interacts with it directly → Self-Service (Domain 3)
# If it handles deployment/syncing → Delivery (Domain 2)
# If it's about running containers → Orchestration (Domain 1)
# If it monitors/measures → Observability (Domain 4)
# If it enforces rules/policies → Security (Domain 5)
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 3.5 — Install and Configure cert-manager (Incubating)

cert-manager automates TLS certificate management — an essential Incubating CNCF project.

  1. Install cert-manager using the static manifest
  2. Verify the cert-manager pods are running in cert-manager namespace
  3. Create a self-signed ClusterIssuer named selfsigned-issuer (for lab use)
  4. Create a Certificate resource for anihpj.local
  5. Verify the certificate was issued and the Secret exists
💡 Hint: kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/latest/download/cert-manager.yaml. For ClusterIssuer, use kind: ClusterIssuer with selfSigned: {}.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Install cert-manager
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.14.5/cert-manager.yaml

# Step 2: Verify pods
kubectl get pods -n cert-manager
# EXPECTED: cert-manager-*, cert-manager-cainjector-*, cert-manager-webhook-*

# Step 3: Create self-signed ClusterIssuer
cat > selfsigned-issuer.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: selfsigned-issuer
spec:
  selfSigned: {}
EOF
kubectl apply -f selfsigned-issuer.yaml

# Step 4: Create Certificate
cat > anihpj-cert.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: anihpj-local-tls
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  secretName: anihpj-local-tls
  issuerRef:
    name: selfsigned-issuer
    kind: ClusterIssuer
  dnsNames:
  - anihpj.local
EOF
kubectl apply -f anihpj-cert.yaml

# Step 5: Verify
kubectl get certificate -n anihpj
# anihpj-local-tls   True    anihpj-local-tls
kubectl get secret anihpj-local-tls -n anihpj
# Contains: tls.crt, tls.key
# This is automated TLS — a core platform engineering pattern
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 3.6 — Verify CNCF Project Status with kubectl

Check which CNCF projects are installed in your cluster and verify their components.

  1. List ALL namespaces in your cluster that contain CNCF project components
  2. For each CNCF project namespace, count how many pods are running
  3. Identify which Platform Stack layer each installed project belongs to
  4. Print a summary table: Project | Namespace | Pod Count | CNCF Maturity | Platform Layer
💡 Hint: kubectl get ns to find namespaces. Check for: argocd, monitoring, cert-manager, kyverno, istio-system. Count pods with kubectl get pods -n <ns> --no-headers | wc -l
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1-2: Find CNCF namespaces and count pods
for ns in argocd monitoring cert-manager kyverno istio-system falco; do
  if kubectl get ns $ns &>/dev/null; then
    COUNT=$(kubectl get pods -n $ns --no-headers 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
    echo "$ns: $COUNT pods"
  else
    echo "$ns: NOT INSTALLED"
  fi
done

# Step 3-4: Summary table
cat > cncf-summary.txt << 'EOF'
PROJECT        NAMESPACE       PODS   MATURITY     PLATFORM LAYER
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Argo CD        argocd          4      🎓 Graduated  🚀 Delivery
Prometheus     monitoring      5      🎓 Graduated  📊 Observability
Grafana        monitoring      1      🎓 Graduated  📊 Observability
cert-manager   cert-manager    3      🥚 Incubating 🔒 Security
EOF
cat cncf-summary.txt
# This is EXACTLY the kind of analysis the CNPE exam expects
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 3.7 — Implement the Trail Map: Containerize → CI → Orchestrate

Follow the Cloud Native Trail Map by deploying anihpj-web through steps 1-3.

  1. Step 1 (Containerize): Build a Docker image for anihpj-web with tag trail-map:v1
  2. Step 2 (CI/CD): Push the image to a registry and update the Deployment with the new tag
  3. Step 3 (Orchestrate): Deploy to Kubernetes and verify the pod is running with the correct image
💡 Hint: Use docker build -t anihpj-web:trail-map-v1 ., kubectl set image deployment/anihpj-web django=anihpj-web:trail-map-v1
📝 View Solution 
# STEP 1: Containerize (Developer responsibility)
cd /path/to/anihpj
docker build -t anihpj-web:trail-map-v1 .
# This is the ONLY step developers do

# STEP 2: CI/CD (Platform provides pipeline)
# In production: GitHub Actions builds and pushes
# For this drill, simulate CI:
docker tag anihpj-web:trail-map-v1 localhost:5000/anihpj-web:trail-map-v1
docker push localhost:5000/anihpj-web:trail-map-v1
kubectl set image deployment/anihpj-web django=localhost:5000/anihpj-web:trail-map-v1 -n anihpj

# STEP 3: Orchestrate (Platform provides K8s)
kubectl rollout status deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.containers[*].image}'
# Should show: localhost:5000/anihpj-web:trail-map-v1

# THE INSIGHT:
# Developer does Step 1 (docker build)
# Platform provides Steps 2-3 (registry + CI pipeline + K8s cluster)
# This is the Platform Engineering contract
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 3.8 — Compare Two CNCF Tools for the Same Problem

The CNCF often has multiple tools for the same use case. Compare Argo CD vs Flux for GitOps.

  1. List the key features of Argo CD (Graduated)
  2. List the key features of Flux (Incubating)
  3. Create a comparison table: Feature | Argo CD | Flux | Winner
  4. Write a recommendation for which to use in the anihpj platform with reasoning
💡 Hint: Argo CD has a rich Web UI. Flux has built-in image update automation. Both support Helm and Kustomize.
📝 View Solution 
# Create comparison file
cat > argo-vs-flux.txt << 'EOF'
FEATURE               ARGO CD (Graduated)     FLUX (Incubating)      WINNER
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Web UI                ✅ Rich dashboard       ❌ CLI-first            Argo CD
Multi-tenancy         ✅ Projects/AppProjects  ⚠️ Instance per team    Argo CD
Image auto-update     ⚠️ Separate component   ✅ Built-in CRDs         Flux
Helm support          ✅ Native               ✅ Native (HelmRelease)  Tie
Kustomize support     ✅ Native               ✅ Native                Tie
Sync frequency        Every 3 min (default)   Every 1-10 min          Flux (faster)
CNCF Status           🎓 Graduated            🥚 Incubating           Argo CD
Learning curve        Medium (Web UI helps)   Medium (CRDs only)      Argo CD
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
RECOMMENDATION FOR ANIHpj:
Use ARGO CD — Graduated status means production-proven, the Web UI

As a platform engineer, you don't need to master all 200+ projects — you need to know which Graduated and Incubating projects solve specific problems for each layer. The Cloud Native Trail Map shows the adoption order: Containerize → CI/CD → Orchestrate → Observe → Service Mesh → Security. Platform engineers own steps 2-6. The anihpj platform uses: K8s (orchestration), Argo CD (delivery), Backstage + CRDs (self-service), Prometheus + Grafana + Loki + Tempo (observability), and Kyverno + Falco (security).
