Image naming convention: <registry>/<namespace>/<image>:<tag>. Example: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:v1.0.0

💡 Image Pull Performance — Why Registry Choice Affects Pod Startup Time

When a K8s node pulls an image, speed depends on WHERE the registry is and HOW the image is structured:

FactorFastSlow
Network proximityRegistry in same region/cloud (ECR in us-east-1, node in us-east-1). Pull via VPC endpoint.Docker Hub from an AWS node (traverses public internet). Rate-limited on free tier.
Image size200MB multi-stage image (anihpj). Node pulls in <10 seconds.1.2GB single-stage image. Node pulls in >60 seconds. Slower pod starts.
Layer reuseSame base image across 50 services — only pull base ONCE. Subsequent services reuse cached layer.Every service uses a different base image. 50 unique pulls = 50× the time and bandwidth.
Pull policyIfNotPresent — only pull if image not cached locally. Standard for versioned tags.Always — pull every time, even if cached. Wastes bandwidth. Only needed for :latest tag.

Platform team best practice: Use ECR (or cloud-native registry) in the same region as your K8s cluster. Enable VPC endpoints for S3 and ECR — traffic stays on AWS backbone, not public internet. Standardize on a single base image (python:3.12-slim) across all Python services to maximize layer cache hits.

📖 Image Signing with Cosign — Prove the Image Hasn't Been Tampered With

Pushing an image to a registry proves it exists. But how do you prove it was built by YOUR CI pipeline and hasn't been replaced by an attacker? Cosign (part of the Sigstore project) signs images with a cryptographic signature:

# Generate a key pair (once)
cosign generate-key-pair
# Creates: cosign.key (private — KEEP SECRET) and cosign.pub (public)

# Sign the image after pushing (in CI pipeline)
cosign sign --key cosign.key 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:v1.0.0
# This creates a signature object in the registry alongside the image

# Verify the signature before deploying (in Argo CD or admission controller)
cosign verify --key cosign.pub 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:v1.0.0
# Returns: Verification for ... — the image is verified!

Kyverno integration: Kyverno can ENFORCE that only signed images are deployed. If an attacker pushes an unsigned image to your registry, Kyverno rejects it at admission time. The CNPE exam (Domain 5) tests image signing as part of the software supply chain security chain: build → sign → push → verify → deploy.

5.8 Image Scanning — Trivy, Grype, Docker Scout

⚠️ The Shocking Truth: 87% of container images have HIGH or CRITICAL vulnerabilities

Every time you docker pull python:3.12-slim, you're pulling an image with potentially hundreds of known vulnerabilities in the base OS packages. Scanning isn't optional — it's a non-negotiable part of the CI pipeline.

ToolSpeedWhat It ScansCI Integration
Trivy (Aqua)Fast (seconds)OS packages + language deps (Python, Node, Go) + IaC files + K8s manifeststrivy image --severity CRITICAL --exit-code 1 anihpj:latest — fails CI if CRITICAL found
Grype (Anchore)Fast (seconds)OS packages + language deps. Good SBOM generation.grype anihpj:latest --fail-on critical
Docker ScoutMediumOS + language deps. Built into Docker Desktop. Remediation suggestions.docker scout cve anihpj:latest
🧠 CNPE Exam — Domain 5 (Security): Image scanning in CI/CD is a tested skill. Know: (1) Trivy is the most common open-source scanner, (2) Scans should BLOCK the pipeline on CRITICAL CVEs, (3) Scanning should happen BEFORE pushing to the registry (scan the local image), (4) Remediation priority: update the base image first (most CVEs are in OS packages), then update language dependencies.
📖 SBOM — Software Bill of Materials

An SBOM is a machine-readable inventory of EVERY component in your image — every OS package, every Python dependency, every library. It's like a nutrition label for software. The US government now REQUIRES SBOMs for federal software (Executive Order 14028):

# Generate SBOM in CycloneDX format (industry standard)
trivy image --format cyclonedx --output anihpj-sbom.json anihpj:latest

# Generate SBOM in SPDX format (Linux Foundation standard)
trivy image --format spdx --output anihpj-sbom.spdx anihpj:latest

# What's inside the SBOM?
cat anihpj-sbom.json | jq '.components[] | {name, version, type}' | head -20
# libpq-dev, version: 15.2, type: library
# django, version: 5.0.1, type: application
# gunicorn, version: 21.2.0, type: application
# openssl, version: 3.1.4, type: library

Why this matters for the CNPE exam: (1) SBOMs enable fast vulnerability response — when Log4Shell hits, you search your SBOMs to find every image using the vulnerable version in seconds. (2) SBOMs are a Domain 5 requirement — know that Trivy and Syft can generate them. (3) SBOMs are checked into Git alongside the Dockerfile — they're part of the software supply chain.

💡 CVE Remediation Workflow — From Scan to Fix

Scanning finds vulnerabilities. But what do you DO about them? Here's the platform engineer's remediation workflow:

PriorityActionTime to FixExample
1. Update base imageChange FROM python:3.12-slim to the latest patch. Rebuild. 80% of CVEs are in OS packages — this fixes most of them at once.Immediate (<1 hour)python:3.12.0-slim → python:3.12.4-slim. Fixes 12 OS CVEs in one line change.
2. Update language depsRun pip install --upgrade django gunicorn. Update requirements.txt. Rebuild.Same daydjango==5.0.1 → django==5.0.7. Fixes Django CVE-2024-xxxxx.
3. Remove unused packagesIf a vulnerable package isn't actually used, remove it from the image entirely.Same dayRemove git from production image — it's a dev tool, not a runtime dependency.
4. Accept risk (document!)Some CVEs can't be fixed (zero-day, no patch available). Document the risk, set a review date.Document within 24hCVE with no fix in a library used only in admin panel (internal network only). Accept, review in 7 days.

Automation: Your CI pipeline should block deploys with CRITICAL CVEs (step 1 above). Your Renovate/Dependabot should auto-PR base image and dependency updates (steps 1-2). Your platform should alert on images older than 30 days that haven't been rescanned. The goal: zero CRITICAL CVEs in any running container.

5.9 Container Runtimes — containerd, CRI-O, gVisor, Kata

RuntimeTypeIsolationCNCF StatusBest For
containerdHigh-levelProcess (namespaces + cgroups)🎓 GraduatedDefault K8s runtime. Used by Docker under the hood. Best balance of performance and compatibility.
CRI-OHigh-level (K8s-native)Process🥚 IncubatingOpenShift/OKD. Minimal footprint — only implements what K8s needs via CRI.
gVisorSandboxedUser-space kernel (syscall filtering)— (Google)Multi-tenant platforms where pods run untrusted code. GKE Sandbox, Cloud Run.
Kata ContainersSandboxedLightweight VM (hardware virt)— (OpenInfra)Maximum isolation — each container gets its own micro-VM. Financial services, regulated workloads.

The CRI (Container Runtime Interface): K8s doesn't care which runtime you use — as long as it speaks CRI. This is why Docker was deprecated as a K8s runtime: Docker doesn't implement CRI natively. containerd does. The platform engineering decision tree: default to containerd for trusted internal workloads → upgrade to gVisor/Kata for multi-tenant platforms with untrusted code.

📖 Docker Volumes — Bind Mounts vs Named Volumes vs tmpfs

Containers are ephemeral — data written inside a container DIES with it. Volumes solve this. Understanding Docker volumes is essential because K8s PVCs are the same concept at cluster scale:

TypeWhere Data LivesSurvives Container Delete?Use CaseK8s Equivalent
Bind MountAny path on the HOST filesystem. -v /host/path:/container/path✅ (data is on host disk)Development: mount source code for live reload. Config injection: mount a config file from the host.K8s hostPath volume — use sparingly, ties pod to specific node
Named VolumeDocker-managed directory (/var/lib/docker/volumes/). -v myvolume:/container/path✅ (managed by Docker, portable)Production data: databases, uploaded files, any persistent state. Can be backed up.K8s PersistentVolume + PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)
tmpfsRAM (memory). --tmpfs /container/path❌ (dies with container or reboot)Temporary data: caches, session data, secrets that should never touch disk.K8s emptyDir with medium: Memory

anihpj volume strategy: PostgreSQL data → Named Volume (persistent, backed up). Redis AOF/RDB → Named Volume (persistent, rebuildable). Static files → Built into the IMAGE (no volume needed). Uploaded media → Named Volume OR S3 (depends on scale). Code → In the IMAGE, not a mounted volume (immutable!).

💡 Multi-Architecture Builds — ARM64 + AMD64 from One Dockerfile

Apple Silicon Macs (ARM64) and cloud servers (AMD64) use different CPU architectures. A Docker image built on a Mac won't run on an AMD64 cloud server unless you build for the target architecture. docker buildx solves this:

# Create a multi-architecture builder (one-time setup)
docker buildx create --name multiarch --use

# Build for BOTH ARM64 and AMD64 simultaneously
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  -t registry.example.com/anihpj:v1.0.0 --push .

# What happens:
# 1. Buildx spins up TWO builders (ARM64 + AMD64 emulation)
# 2. Both builders run the same Dockerfile in parallel
# 3. Both images are pushed as a "manifest list" (one tag, two architectures)
# 4. When a user pulls: Docker auto-selects the right architecture

# Verify the manifest
docker buildx imagetools inspect registry.example.com/anihpj:v1.0.0
# Shows: linux/amd64, linux/arm64 — both under the same tag

When multi-arch matters: (1) Your team uses MacBooks for development but deploys to AMD64 cloud servers. (2) You're using ARM-based cloud instances (AWS Graviton) for cost savings. (3) You publish public images that anyone should be able to pull. The CNPE exam doesn't test buildx specifically, but it tests the principle: images should be built for the target platform.

🏋️ Chapter 5 — Hands-On Practice Drills (10 Exercises)

The CNPE is a performance-based exam — you solve tasks in a live Linux terminal. Practice these drills in your lab environment until you can complete each within the target time.

⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 5.1 — Build and Inspect the anihpj Image Layers

Build the anihpj image and analyze its layers.

  1. Build the image: docker build -t anihpj:latest .
  2. Check image size: docker images anihpj
  3. Inspect all layers: docker history anihpj:latest
  4. Rebuild without changing anything — verify ALL layers say "CACHED"
  5. Change one line in views.py and rebuild — which layers are now "CACHED" vs rebuilt?
💡 Hint: docker build, docker images, docker history. The first rebuild should show all CACHED.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Build
docker build -t anihpj:latest .
# Watch the output — layers 1-7 as defined in the Dockerfile

# Step 2: Size
docker images anihpj
# REPOSITORY   TAG       SIZE
# anihpj       latest    200MB

# Step 3: Layers
docker history anihpj:latest
# IMAGE          CREATED         SIZE    COMMENT
# <sha>          5 min ago       5MB     COPY . .  (app code)
# <sha>          5 min ago       120MB   RUN pip install
# <sha>          5 min ago       28MB    FROM python:3.12-slim

# Step 4: Rebuild (no changes)
docker build -t anihpj:latest .
# → Using cache for every layer. Build completes in <5 seconds.

# Step 5: Change code, rebuild
echo "# comment" >> jobpost/views.py
docker build -t anihpj:latest .
# → CACHED: FROM python, RUN apt-get, COPY requirements, RUN pip install
# → REBUILT: COPY . . (because views.py changed!)
# Only the LAST layer rebuilds. Everything else is cached.
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 5.2 — Run anihpj Locally and Verify It Works

Start the anihpj container and test the application.

  1. Run: docker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name anihpj-test anihpj:latest
  2. Check logs: docker logs anihpj-test
  3. Test: curl http://localhost:8000/healthz (should return "healthy")
  4. Enter the container: docker exec -it anihpj-test /bin/bash and verify Gunicorn is running as non-root
💡 Hint: docker run -d -p, docker logs, curl, docker exec -it
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Run
docker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name anihpj-test anihpj:latest

# Step 2: Logs
docker logs anihpj-test
# [INFO] Starting gunicorn 21.2.0
# [INFO] Listening at: http://0.0.0.0:8000
# [INFO] Using worker: sync
# [INFO] Booting worker with pid: 7

# Step 3: Test
curl http://localhost:8000/healthz
# healthy

# Step 4: Verify non-root
docker exec -it anihpj-test whoami
# anihpj  ← NOT root!
docker exec -it anihpj-test ps aux
# USER       PID  COMMAND
# anihpj       1  gunicorn --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 ...
# anihpj       7  gunicorn worker
# anihpj       8  gunicorn worker
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 5.3 — Tag and Push to a Local Registry

Push the anihpj image to a local Docker registry.

  1. Start a local registry: docker run -d -p 5000:5000 --name registry registry:2
  2. Tag the image: docker tag anihpj:latest localhost:5000/anihpj:v1.0.0
  3. Also tag with git SHA: docker tag anihpj:latest localhost:5000/anihpj:$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
  4. Push both tags: docker push localhost:5000/anihpj:v1.0.0
  5. Verify: curl http://localhost:5000/v2/anihpj/tags/list
💡 Hint: docker tag, docker push. Registry API: /v2/<name>/tags/list
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Start registry
docker run -d -p 5000:5000 --name registry registry:2

# Step 2-3: Tag with version and git SHA
docker tag anihpj:latest localhost:5000/anihpj:v1.0.0
SHA=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
docker tag anihpj:latest localhost:5000/anihpj:$SHA

# Step 4: Push
docker push localhost:5000/anihpj:v1.0.0
docker push localhost:5000/anihpj:$SHA

# Step 5: Verify
curl http://localhost:5000/v2/anihpj/tags/list
# {"name":"anihpj","tags":["v1.0.0","abc1234"]}
# This is what Argo CD/K8s will pull from
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 5.4 — Scan the anihpj Image with Trivy

Install Trivy and scan the anihpj image for vulnerabilities.

  1. Install Trivy (if not installed): follow instructions at aquasecurity.github.io/trivy
  2. Scan: trivy image anihpj:latest
  3. Scan for CRITICAL only: trivy image --severity CRITICAL anihpj:latest
  4. Scan and fail if CRITICAL found: trivy image --severity CRITICAL --exit-code 1 anihpj:latest
  5. Save report as JSON: trivy image -f json -o trivy-report.json anihpj:latest
💡 Hint: Trivy scans OS packages (apt) AND Python packages (pip). Most CVEs are in the base OS image.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Install Trivy
curl -sfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aquasecurity/trivy/main/contrib/install.sh | sh

# Step 2: Full scan
trivy image anihpj:latest
# Shows all vulnerabilities with severity, package name, and CVE ID

# Step 3: CRITICAL only
trivy image --severity CRITICAL anihpj:latest
# If output is empty → no CRITICAL CVEs! (good)
# If output shows CVEs → need to update base image or packages

# Step 4: CI pipeline integration
trivy image --severity CRITICAL --exit-code 1 anihpj:latest
echo $?  # 0 = no CRITICAL, 1 = CRITICAL found (CI should fail)

# Step 5: Save report
trivy image -f json -o trivy-report.json anihpj:latest
cat trivy-report.json | jq '.Results[].Vulnerabilities[] | {Severity, PkgName, VulnerabilityID}'
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 5.5 — Run a Container with Resource Limits

Start anihpj with CPU and memory limits — simulating K8s resource constraints.

  1. Run with limits: docker run -d --memory=256m --cpus=0.5 --name anihpj-limited anihpj:latest
  2. Check resource usage: docker stats anihpj-limited --no-stream
  3. Try running with NO memory limit and compare stats
  4. Read-only root filesystem: docker run -d --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --name anihpj-ro anihpj:latest
💡 Hint: --memory=256m, --cpus=0.5, --read-only, docker stats
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Run with limits
docker run -d --memory=256m --cpus=0.5 --name anihpj-limited -p 8001:8000 anihpj:latest

# Step 2: Stats
docker stats anihpj-limited --no-stream
# CONTAINER         CPU %     MEM USAGE / LIMIT   MEM %
# anihpj-limited    0.10%     180MiB / 256MiB     70.3%

# Step 3: Compare without limits
docker run -d --name anihpj-nolimit -p 8002:8000 anihpj:latest
docker stats anihpj-nolimit --no-stream
# MEM USAGE / LIMIT shows the container can use ALL host memory

# Step 4: Read-only filesystem
docker run -d --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --name anihpj-ro -p 8003:8000 anihpj:latest
docker exec anihpj-ro touch /test.txt
# touch: cannot touch '/test.txt': Read-only file system
# This is a security best practice — prevents attackers from writing files
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 5.6 — Inspect Environment Variables and Secrets

Pass configuration via environment variables — the 12-Factor way.

  1. Run with env vars: docker run -d -e DEBUG=true -e DB_HOST=postgres -e DB_PASSWORD=secret123 --name anihpj-env anihpj:latest
  2. Verify env vars inside the container: docker exec anihpj-env env | grep -E 'DEBUG|DB_'
  3. Run with an env file: docker run -d --env-file .env.prod --name anihpj-envfile anihpj:latest
  4. Explain why DB_PASSWORD should NEVER be in the Dockerfile (use env vars/secrets instead)
💡 Hint: docker run -e, docker exec env, --env-file
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Run with env vars
docker run -d -e DEBUG=true -e DB_HOST=postgres -e DB_PASSWORD=secret123 --name anihpj-env -p 8004:8000 anihpj:latest

# Step 2: Verify
docker exec anihpj-env env | grep -E 'DEBUG|DB_'
# DEBUG=true
# DB_HOST=postgres
# DB_PASSWORD=secret123

# Step 3: Env file
echo "DEBUG=false" > .env.prod
echo "DB_HOST=prod-db.anihpj.com" >> .env.prod
docker run -d --env-file .env.prod --name anihpj-envfile -p 8005:8000 anihpj:latest

# Step 4: NEVER in Dockerfile
# WRONG: ENV DB_PASSWORD=secret123  ← visible in docker history!
# RIGHT: Pass at runtime via -e or K8s Secret
# docker history will show ALL ENV values — secrets in ENV = exposed
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 5.7 — Compare Single-Stage vs Multi-Stage Image Size

Build both versions and compare the size difference.

  1. Create a single-stage Dockerfile (same steps, no multi-stage)
  2. Build it: docker build -t anihpj:single -f Dockerfile.single .
  3. Compare sizes: docker images | grep anihpj
  4. Check what's in the single-stage image that shouldn't be: docker run --rm anihpj:single which gcc
  5. Explain: what extra tools exist in the single-stage image that are absent from multi-stage?
💡 Hint: Single-stage keeps gcc, build-essential, and build artifacts. Multi-stage discards the builder stage entirely.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1-2: Build single-stage
cat > Dockerfile.single << 'EOF'
FROM python:3.12
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y gcc libpq-dev
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "anihpj.wsgi:application"]
EOF
docker build -t anihpj:single -f Dockerfile.single .

# Step 3: Compare
docker images | grep anihpj
# anihpj   latest   200MB   ← multi-stage
# anihpj   single   1.2GB   ← single-stage (6x larger!)

# Step 4: What shouldn't be there?
docker run --rm anihpj:single which gcc
# /usr/bin/gcc  ← COMPILER is in the image!
docker run --rm anihpj:single dpkg -l | wc -l
# hundreds of build-time packages
docker run --rm anihpj:latest which gcc
# (empty — gcc is NOT in multi-stage image)

# Step 5: Explanation
# Single-stage includes: gcc, build-essential, headers, pip cache,
# intermediate build artifacts — ALL attack vectors.
# Multi-stage: only runtime libs + app code. No build tools.
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 5.8 — Debug a Failing Container

A container exits immediately. Debug why.

  1. Run a broken container: docker run -d --name broken anihpj:latest sleep 1 (exits after 1s)
  2. Check status: docker ps -a | grep broken — STATUS: Exited
  3. View logs: docker logs broken
  4. Inspect exit code: docker inspect broken | jq '.[0].State.ExitCode'
  5. Override CMD to debug: docker run -it --entrypoint /bin/bash anihpj:latest
💡 Hint: docker ps -a shows exited containers. docker inspect shows detailed state. Override with --entrypoint.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1-2: Run broken, check status
docker run -d --name broken anihpj:latest sleep 1
docker ps -a | grep broken
# broken   Exited (0) 5 seconds ago

# Step 3: Logs
docker logs broken
# (empty — sleep produces no output)

# Step 4: Exit code
docker inspect broken | jq '.[0].State.ExitCode'
# 0 (success exit — sleep finished normally)

# Step 5: Override for debugging
docker run -it --entrypoint /bin/bash anihpj:latest
# Now you're inside the container. You can:
# - Check if files exist: ls /app
# - Check env vars: env
# - Try running manually: gunicorn --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 anihpj.wsgi:application
# This is how you debug "why won't my container start?"
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 5.9 — Clean Up Docker Resources

Docker accumulates unused images, containers, and volumes. Clean them up systematically.

  1. Check disk usage: docker system df
  2. Remove all stopped containers: docker container prune -f
  3. Remove unused images: docker image prune -a -f
  4. Remove everything unused: docker system prune -a -f --volumes
  5. Verify: docker system df — should show much less usage
💡 Hint: docker system df shows disk usage. docker system prune -a is the nuclear option — use in CI cleanup.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Check disk
docker system df
# TYPE           TOTAL     ACTIVE    SIZE      RECLAIMABLE
# Images         12        3         3.5GB     2.1GB (60%)
# Containers     8         2         500MB     300MB (60%)
# Local Volumes  3         1         200MB     100MB (50%)

# Step 2: Remove stopped containers
docker container prune -f
# Deleted Containers: 6

# Step 3: Remove unused images
docker image prune -a -f
# Deleted Images: 9

# Step 4: Nuclear option
docker system prune -a -f --volumes
# WARNING: This removes EVERYTHING not currently running
# Use this in CI pipeline cleanup steps to free disk space

# Step 5: Verify
docker system df
# TYPE           TOTAL     ACTIVE    SIZE      RECLAIMABLE
# Images         1         1         200MB     0B (0%)
# Containers     0         0         0B        0B
⏱️ Target: 6 minutes
Drill 5.10 — Build a Custom Docker Bridge Network and Connect Containers

Containers on the same Docker network can communicate by container name — this is how docker-compose networking works.

  1. Create a network: docker network create anihpj-net
  2. Run postgres on the network: docker run -d --net anihpj-net --name db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres:15
  3. Run anihpj on the network: docker run -d --net anihpj-net --name web -e DB_HOST=db -e DB_PASSWORD=secret -p 8000:8000 anihpj:latest
  4. Verify connectivity: docker exec web ping db — should resolve by container name
  5. Explain how this maps to K8s: Docker network → K8s CNI, container name DNS → K8s Service DNS
💡 Hint: docker network create, docker run --net. Container names become DNS names on user-defined networks.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Create network
docker network create anihpj-net

# Step 2: Run DB
docker run -d --net anihpj-net --name db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret postgres:15

# Step 3: Run app
docker run -d --net anihpj-net --name web \
  -e DB_HOST=db -e DB_PASSWORD=secret \
  -p 8000:8000 anihpj:latest

# Step 4: Verify connectivity
docker exec web ping -c 2 db
# PING db (172.18.0.2): 56 data bytes
# 64 bytes from 172.18.0.2: icmp_seq=0 ttl=64 time=0.1ms
# Container "web" can reach "db" by NAME!

# Step 5: Map to K8s
# Docker network         → K8s CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium, Flannel)
# Container name (db)    → K8s Service name (postgres.anihpj.svc)
# --net anihpj-net       → K8s Namespace
# Docker DNS resolution  → K8s CoreDNS
# In K8s: anihpj-web connects to postgres via postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
# Same pattern, different implementation

📖 Chapter 5 Summary: Docker is the universal packaging format for cloud native applications. Multi-stage builds keep images small (200MB vs 1.2GB), non-root users keep them secure, and layer caching keeps builds fast (30s vs 5 min). As a platform engineer, you'll build Dockerfiles like the anihpj example, push images to registries like ECR/Harbor, scan them with Trivy in CI/CD, and choose runtimes like containerd or gVisor based on security requirements. These containers are the BUILDING BLOCKS that Kubernetes orchestrates — which we'll dive into next.

Chapter 6: Kubernetes Architecture for Platform Engineers

Cluster architecture, control plane components, worker node components, the pod creation journey, networking model, etcd deep dive, and static pods. Understand the engine that powers every cloud native platform.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~3 hours☸️ K8s Arch

📖 Chapter Overview: Kubernetes is the orchestration engine every cloud native platform runs on. This chapter covers the full cluster architecture: control plane components (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager), worker node components (kubelet, kube-proxy, container runtime), the pod creation journey, the networking model, etcd as the cluster's "brain," and static pods. Understanding this architecture is CRITICAL — 15% of the CNPE exam tests platform architecture (Domain 1).

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • Diagram the full Kubernetes cluster architecture from memory
  • Explain the role of each control plane and worker node component
  • Trace a pod creation from kubectl to running container — every step
  • Understand etcd's Raft consensus and why quorum matters
  • Back up and restore etcd — a tested CNPE exam skill
  • Explain how static pods manage the control plane itself
📋 CNPE Domain Mapping: Domain 1 (Platform Architecture — 15%). This chapter is the foundation for cluster design decisions, etcd management, and troubleshooting control plane failures — all directly tested on the CNPE exam.

6.1 Cluster Architecture Overview — Control Plane + Worker Nodes

📖 The API Server — Authentication → Authorization → Admission (AAA)

Every request to the API server goes through a 3-stage pipeline:

1. Authentication (Who are you?): X.509 client certificates (kubelet, scheduler), bearer tokens (ServiceAccounts), OIDC (human users via kubectl). If auth fails → 401 Unauthorized immediately.

2. Authorization (What can you do?): RBAC checks if the authenticated identity has the right RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding for this verb on this resource. Modes: Node, ABAC, RBAC, Webhook. If denied → 403 Forbidden.

3. Admission (Should we allow this?): Mutating webhooks modify the request (inject sidecars, set defaults). Validating webhooks accept/reject the request (Kyverno/OPA policies, resource limits). If rejected → request is denied with a reason.

ComponentPort(s)ProtocolHealth EndpointNotes
kube-apiserver6443HTTPS/healthz, /livezThe ONLY port external clients use. Always TLS.
etcd (client)2379HTTPS/healthAPI server connects here. Use etcdctl endpoint health.
etcd (peer)2380HTTPS—etcd-to-etcd Raft communication. Never expose publicly.
kube-scheduler10259HTTPS/healthzOnly leader scheduler is active (elected via etcd).
controller-manager10257HTTPS/healthzOnly leader controller-manager is active.
kubelet10250HTTPS/healthzAPI server talks to kubelet on this port. Also where kubectl logs/exec go.
kubelet (read-only)10255HTTP/healthzDisabled by default in newer versions (security).
NodePort range30000–32767TCP/UDP—Every node opens these. Avoid conflicts with other services.
⚠️ What Happens When Each Component Fails — The Platform Engineer's Playbook

API Server down: kubectl stops working. No new resources can be created. But existing pods CONTINUE RUNNING (kubelet doesn't need API server to keep containers alive). Calm down — the cluster is NOT on fire.

etcd quorum lost: Cluster is READ-ONLY. Reading works, writing fails. This is catastrophic — no healing can happen. Restore from backup if quorum can't be reestablished.

Scheduler down: New pods stay Pending. Existing pods unaffected. Workloads that are already running are FINE. You have hours to fix it.

Controller-manager down: Deployments stop reconciling. Nodes that die won't have their pods rescheduled. The cluster slowly degrades. Single point of control (only one leader at a time).

kubelet down (1 node): After ~40s, node marked NotReady. After 5 minutes, controller-manager evicts pods and reschedules them on healthy nodes. Kubernetes self-heals.

kube-proxy down (1 node): Pods on this node can't reach Services (no iptables rules). Pods on other nodes are fine. Service IP still works from other nodes.

6.2 Control Plane Components — Deep Dive

📖 The API Server Watch Mechanism — How Controllers React in Sub-Second Time

The API server is NOT a polling-based REST API. It uses watches — clients open a long-lived HTTP connection and the server STREAMS changes as they happen (ADDED, MODIFIED, DELETED events). This is how the scheduler knows about new pods instantly. When you run kubectl get pods -w, the -w flag opens a watch. Every K8s controller (scheduler, controller-manager, kubelet) uses watches — not polling. Understanding this is essential for building your own Operators in Domain 3.

ComponentRoleFailure ImpactScaling
kube-apiserverThe "front door." REST API that ALL components use. Validates and persists API objects. Only component that talks to etcd.No new commands work (kubectl fails). Existing pods keep running. Can't deploy, scale, or update.Horizontal: run multiple API servers behind a load balancer. Stateless.
etcdThe "memory." Distributed key-value store holding ALL cluster state. Uses Raft consensus for consistency.Lose quorum = cluster is READ-ONLY. Lose all etcd data = cluster is GONE. BACK IT UP.3, 5, or 7 nodes. Odd numbers only (Raft quorum). 3-node tolerates 1 failure.
kube-schedulerThe "placement engine." Watches for unassigned pods and decides which node runs them based on resources, affinity, taints.New pods stay Pending forever. Existing pods unaffected. No auto-healing of scheduling.Multiple schedulers possible (with different rules). Default: one per cluster.
controller-managerThe "reconciliation engine." Runs controller loops: Node controller, Replication controller, Endpoints, ServiceAccount. Each watches state and drives toward desired state.Controllers stop reconciling. Deployments won't scale. Endpoints won't update. Nodes won't be marked NotReady.Leader election: only ONE controller-manager is active at a time. Others are standby.
API REQUEST LIFECYCLE — From kubectl to etcd and Back

  │  kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml → What ACTUALLY Happens                │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────┐
  │ kubectl  │  Reads ~/.kube/config → connects to https://MASTER:6443
  │ apply -f │  Sends HTTP POST with Deployment YAML in body
  └────┬─────┘

       ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  API SERVER (:6443) — 6-stage pipeline                                   │
  │                                                                         │
  │  1. AUTHENTICATION → 2. AUTHORIZATION → 3. MUTATING ADMISSION           │
  │       (Who?)              (Can they?)       (Modify request)             │
  │            │                    │                    │                   │
  │            ▼                    ▼                    ▼                   │

  │                                                                         │

  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  STEP 6 IS CRITICAL: etcd must ACK the write before API server returns 201.

6.3 Worker Node Components — Deep Dive

ComponentRoleFailure Impact
kubeletThe "node agent." Registers node with API server. Watches for PodSpecs assigned to its node. Tells container runtime to run containers. Reports pod/node status back to API server.Pods on that node show Unknown/NotReady. After 5 minutes (default), controller-manager marks node NotReady and evicts pods. Scheduler stops assigning new pods to that node.
kube-proxyThe "network proxy." Implements Service abstraction by maintaining iptables/IPVS rules on each node. Routes traffic to correct pod IPs based on Service selectors.Service IP still works (kube-proxy on OTHER nodes handles it). But pods on THIS node can't reach Services via ClusterIP.
Container RuntimeThe "engine." Actually pulls images, creates containers, starts/stops them. Communicates with kubelet via CRI (Container Runtime Interface).kubelet can't start new pods on this node. Existing containers keep running (they're Linux processes). Node eventually marked NotReady.
📖 kube-proxy Modes — iptables vs IPVS

iptables (default): Writes iptables rules with random backend selection. Good up to ~5000 Services. IPVS: In-kernel L4 load balancer with O(1) hash table lookup. Scales to 10,000+ Services. Enable with --proxy-mode=ipvs. Userspace (legacy): kube-proxy proxies every packet through user space. Slowest — not for production.

📖 Container Runtimes Deep Dive — CRI, OCI, and the Runtime Landscape

Kubernetes doesn't run containers directly. It talks to a Container Runtime via CRI (Container Runtime Interface) — a gRPC API that standardizes how kubelet communicates with ANY runtime. The runtime then uses OCI (Open Container Initiative) standards to actually create and run containers.

The Evolution: Pre-1.24, Docker was supported via dockershim (a CRI adapter inside kubelet). Since 1.24, dockershim is REMOVED. You MUST use a CRI-compliant runtime. Docker images still work — they're OCI-compatible. You just can't use the Docker daemon directly.

RuntimeTypeFootprintBest ForCRI Socket
containerdHigh-level CRI~50MBDefault for most K8s distros. Stable, well-tested.unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock
CRI-OHigh-level CRI~40MBPurpose-built for K8s. No Docker compatibility layer. Red Hat's default.unix:///var/run/crio/crio.sock
gVisorSandbox (runsc)~100MBUser-space kernel. Each container gets its OWN kernel. High security for untrusted workloads.Via containerd (RuntimeClass)
Kata ContainersSandbox (VM)~150MBEach pod runs in a lightweight VM. Strongest isolation. Hardware virtualization required.Via containerd/CRI-O (RuntimeClass)

How it works: kubelet → CRI gRPC call (RunPodSandbox, CreateContainer) → containerd → OCI runtime (runc) → Linux namespaces + cgroups → your process. When you run kubectl logs, kubelet makes a CRI call to get stdout/stderr from the container runtime. Everything goes through CRI.

RuntimeClass example — run untrusted workload in gVisor:

apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: gvisor
handler: runsc
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: untrusted-pod
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor  # This pod gets its own user-space kernel
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx

As a platform engineer, you configure which runtimes are available per node and enforce RuntimeClass via admission policies. Finance pods might require Kata for compliance; dev pods use containerd.

6.5 Cluster Networking Model — Pod-to-Pod, Pod-to-Service, External

Kubernetes mandates a flat networking model: every pod gets its own IP address. All pods can communicate with all other pods without NAT. CNI plugins implement this.

CommunicationHow It WorksExample
Pod-to-Pod (same node)Direct via local bridge/veth pair. No network hop.Pod A (10.0.1.5) → Pod B (10.0.1.6) on same worker. <0.1ms latency.
Pod-to-Pod (different nodes)CNI plugin encapsulates packet (VXLAN/Geneve) or routes directly (BGP). Cross-node hop.Pod A (10.0.1.5) on worker-1 → Pod C (10.0.2.8) on worker-2. ~0.5ms latency.
Pod-to-ServiceDNS resolves Service name → ClusterIP. kube-proxy iptables/IPVS rules route to a random backend pod IP.anihpj-web connects to postgres.anihpj.svc → ClusterIP 10.96.0.5 → iptables → backend pod 10.0.1.10:5432.
External-to-PodNodePort (30000-32767), LoadBalancer (cloud LB), or Ingress (L7 routing). Traffic enters the cluster through these.User visits anihpj.com → Cloud LB → NodePort 30080 → kube-proxy → pod 10.0.1.5:8000.

🎉 Real-World CNI Decision — anihpj Platform (3 Clusters)
  • ✅ Dev cluster: Flannel — simple, no policies needed, fast setup for developers.
  • ✅ Staging cluster: Calico (VXLAN mode) — NetworkPolicies to simulate production security. Moderate performance acceptable.
  • ✅ Production cluster: Cilium (eBPF mode) — maximum performance, Hubble observability, L7 NetworkPolicies for PCI compliance (blocking SQL injection at kernel level!).
  • ✅ Platform engineer's job: Not just picking one CNI — managing DIFFERENT CNIs per cluster based on requirements. The CNPE exam expects you to justify these choices.

6.6 etcd — The Cluster Database

⚠️ etcd is the MOST CRITICAL component. If you lose etcd data, you lose the ENTIRE cluster.

Every Kubernetes object — pods, services, deployments, secrets, RBAC rules — is stored in etcd. The API server is the ONLY component that reads/writes etcd. Back up etcd REGULARLY.

Raft Consensus: etcd uses Raft for consistency. A write succeeds only if a MAJORITY (quorum) of etcd members agree. 3-node cluster: quorum = 2, tolerates 1 failure. 5-node: quorum = 3, tolerates 2 failures. Always use ODD numbers.

RAFT CONSENSUS — How etcd Keeps 3 Nodes in Sync

  │                    3-NODE ETCD CLUSTER — RAFT CONSENSUS                  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────────┐
  │  ETCD NODE A          │   │  ETCD NODE B          │   │  ETCD NODE C          │
  │  ROLE: LEADER 👑      │   │  ROLE: FOLLOWER       │   │  ROLE: FOLLOWER       │
  │                       │   │                       │   │                       │
  │  ① Receives write     │   │  Receives heartbeat   │   │  Receives heartbeat   │
  │     from API server   │   │  from Leader every    │   │  from Leader every    │
  │                       │   │  100ms                │   │  100ms                │
  │  ② Appends to its     │   │                       │   │                       │
  │     own log           │   │  ③ Leader sends       │   │  ③ Leader sends       │
  │                       │   │     AppendEntries     │   │     AppendEntries     │
  │  ④ Waits for majority │◄──│  ④ B writes to log   │◄──│  ④ C writes to log   │
  │     (A + B = 2/3)     │──►│     (ACK)             │──►│     (ACK)             │
  │                       │   │                       │   │                       │

  │     to API server      │   │                       │   │                       │
  └───────────────────────┘   └───────────────────────┘   └───────────────────────┘

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

  │                                                                         │
  │  ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐                         │
  │  │ A: CRASH │     │ B: FOLLOWER    │ C: FOLLOWER                        │
  │  │ 💀       │     │                │                                     │
  │  └──────────┘     └─────┬──────────┘     └─────┬──────────┘             │
  │                         │ election timeout    │ election timeout         │
  │                         │ (150-300ms no       │ (150-300ms no            │
  │                         │  heartbeat)         │  heartbeat)              │
  │                         ▼                     ▼                          │
  │                   ┌──────────┐          ┌──────────┐                     │
  │                   │ CANDIDATE│          │ CANDIDATE│                     │
  │                   │ votes for│◄────────►│ votes for│                     │
  │                   │ self     │  race!    │ self     │                     │
  │                   └────┬─────┘          └────┬─────┘                     │
  │                        │ B wins (2/3 votes)  │ C loses                   │
  │                        ▼                     ▼                           │
  │                   ┌──────────┐          ┌──────────┐                     │
  │                   │ B: LEADER│          │ FOLLOWER │                     │
  │                   │ 👑       │          │          │                     │
  │                   └──────────┘          └──────────┘                     │
  │  Election takes ~1 second. During election: writes UNAVAILABLE.           │
  │  Reads still work.                                                       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  QUORUM MATH:  3 nodes → quorum=2 → tolerate 1 failure
                5 nodes → quorum=3 → tolerate 2 failures (BUT more overhead)
                2 nodes → quorum=2 → tolerate 0 failures (NEVER use 2 nodes!)
  Why odd? 3-node and 4-node BOTH tolerate only 1 failure, but 4-node costs
  more. Always use odd numbers. For production: 3 or 5 nodes.
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Raft Leader Election — The Heartbeat That Keeps etcd Alive: In a 3-node etcd cluster, one node is the LEADER (handles all writes), and two are FOLLOWERS. The leader sends heartbeats every 100ms. If followers don't hear a heartbeat for 150-300ms (election timeout), they become CANDIDATES and start an election. The first candidate to get votes from a majority becomes the new leader. During an election (~1-2 seconds), etcd is UNAVAILABLE for writes (but reads still work). This is why you need ODD numbers — a 2-node cluster can NEVER reach majority (quorum = 2, but with 1 failure, only 1 node remains → no quorum). Always 3, 5, or 7 nodes.

Critical commands:

  • ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd-snapshot.db — saves entire cluster state
  • ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot restore /backup/etcd-snapshot.db — recovers from backup
  • ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl member list — see all etcd members and their status
🧠 CNPE Exam: Expect a task to backup and restore etcd. Know the exact flags: --endpoints, --cacert, --cert, --key. These are in /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/. The restore command creates a NEW data directory — you must update the etcd manifest to point to it.
📖 etcd Internals — MVCC, Compaction, and Why etcd Grows Forever

etcd stores data using MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control). Every key has a revision number — a monotonically increasing counter across the entire cluster. When you update a key, the OLD version is NOT deleted. It's retained with its old revision. This is how watches work: a controller can say "give me all changes since revision 15432" and etcd replays them.

The problem: Old revisions accumulate FOREVER. Every Deployment update, every Pod status change, every heartbeat — all stored permanently. An etcd database starting at 100MB can grow to 8GB+. This is database bloat.

The fix — Compaction + Defrag: Compaction discards old revisions. Defrag reclaims disk space (the DB file actually shrinks).

# Check current etcd size
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint status --write-out=table
# DB SIZE: 2.1 GB  → problem!

# Compact (delete old revisions)
REV=$(ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint status --write-out=json | jq '.[0].Status.header.revision')
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl compact $REV

# Defragment (reclaim disk)
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl defrag

# Check again → DB SIZE: 350 MB (down from 2.1 GB!)

Platform responsibility: Schedule automatic compaction (API server does it hourly) + defrag (manual, run weekly). Monitor etcd_mvcc_db_total_size_in_bytes via Prometheus. A bloated etcd causes: slow API responses, snapshot timeouts, and crashes at 8GB quota.

📖 etcd Backup Automation — CronJob for Daily Snapshots

Never manually run backups. Schedule them with a K8s CronJob that mounts the etcd certs from the host and writes snapshots to a persistent location. Restore drill for the exam: (1) Move kube-apiserver.yaml out of manifests/. (2) etcdctl snapshot restore snapshot.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restore. (3) Edit etcd.yaml to point --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restore. (4) Kubelet restarts etcd. (5) Return kube-apiserver.yaml. (6) Verify with kubectl get pods -A.

6.7 Static Pods and Control Plane Management

Static Pods are pods managed directly by kubelet, NOT by the API server. Kubelet watches /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ — any YAML file there becomes a static pod. The control plane components (api-server, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager) run as static pods in kubeadm clusters.

Key facts: (1) If you edit a manifest file, kubelet restarts the pod automatically. No kubectl apply needed. (2) If you DELETE a manifest file, kubelet stops the pod. (3) Static pods appear in kubectl get pods -n kube-system with a mirror pod on the API server — but the API server CANNOT delete them. Only kubelet can.

💡 Static Pod Lifecycle — How kubeadm Bootstraps the Control Plane

kubeadm writes 4 YAML files to /etc/kubernetes/manifests/. kubelet detects them and starts each as a static pod. Each creates a mirror pod visible in kube-system. If you kubectl delete pod a control plane component, kubelet RESTARTS it — mirror pods are reflections, control is at the kubelet level. To PERMANENTLY stop a component: MOVE its manifest out of the directory. Move it back → pod restarts. This is how you "pause" a control plane component for maintenance.

📖 Scheduler Scoring — How K8s Picks the Best Node

The scheduler uses 2 phases: Filtering (eliminate nodes that can't run the pod — insufficient resources, taint mismatch, port conflicts) and Scoring (rank survivors by preference). Key scoring plugins: NodeResourcesFit (prefers less-loaded nodes), ImageLocality (prefers nodes that already have the image cached), PodTopologySpread (spreads pods across zones for HA). Highest total score wins. Tie → random pick.

SCHEDULER SCORING — How a Node Wins the Pod

  PHASE 2: SCORING (rank the survivors)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Plugin              │ Worker-1 Score │ Worker-2 Score │ Weight        │
  ├──────────────────────┼────────────────┼────────────────┼───────────────┤
  │ NodeResourcesFit     │ 8 (more free)  │ 3 (nearly full)│ 1 (default)   │
  │ ImageLocality        │ 10 (cached!)   │ 0 (needs pull) │ 1             │
  │ PodTopologySpread    │ 5 (1a has pod) │ 8 (1b, fewer)  │ 2             │
  │ NodeAffinity         │ 10 (matched)   │ 10 (matched)   │ 1             │
  ├──────────────────────┼────────────────┼────────────────┼───────────────┤
  │ TOTAL WEIGHTED SCORE │ 8+10+10+10=38  │ 3+0+16+10=29   │               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  🏆 WINNER: Worker-1 (score 38 vs 29)
  Scheduler updates Pod.spec.nodeName = "worker-1" → kubelet takes over
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
💡 kubeadm Bootstrap Walkthrough — How the Control Plane Comes Alive

When you run kubeadm init, here's exactly what happens step-by-step:

# 1. Preflight checks — are we ready?
kubeadm init phase preflight
# [preflight] Running pre-flight checks
# [preflight] Pulling images required for setting up a Kubernetes cluster

# 2. Generate self-signed CA certificate (valid 10 years)
kubeadm init phase certs all
# [certs] Generated ca certificate and key
# [certs] Generated apiserver certificate and key
# [certs] apiserver serving cert is signed for DNS names [kubernetes, ...]
# [certs] Generated etcd/ca certificate and key

# 3. Write kubeconfig files for controller-manager, scheduler, kubelet, admin
kubeadm init phase kubeconfig all
# [kubeconfig] Wrote "admin.conf" — THIS IS YOUR ~/.kube/config

# 4. Generate static pod manifests (written to /etc/kubernetes/manifests/)
kubeadm init phase control-plane all
# [control-plane] Wrote static Pod manifest for kube-apiserver
# [control-plane] Wrote static Pod manifest for kube-controller-manager
# [control-plane] Wrote static Pod manifest for kube-scheduler

# 5. Start local etcd (static pod)
kubeadm init phase etcd local
# [etcd] Wrote static Pod manifest for local etcd

# 6. Wait for control plane to be healthy
# kubelet watches /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ → starts all 4 pods
# After ~30 seconds: kubectl get pods -n kube-system shows control plane

# 7. Upload kubeadm/kubelet config to cluster as ConfigMaps
kubeadm init phase upload-config all

# 8. Mark the node as control-plane + add taints
kubeadm init phase mark-control-plane

# 9. Generate bootstrap token for joining workers
kubeadm init phase bootstrap-token

# 10. Install CoreDNS and kube-proxy as addons
kubeadm init phase addon all

After init: kubelet runs as a systemd service. Control plane runs as static pods. You join workers with kubeadm join <IP>:6443 --token <token> --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<hash>. Understanding this flow means you can troubleshoot ANY kubeadm cluster issue — from certificate expiration to manifest corruption.

😰 Control Plane Upgrade Gone Wrong — A Real Platform Engineer Story
  • 🔴 Scenario: You run kubeadm upgrade apply v1.29.0. The new kube-apiserver won't start. kubectl is dead. What now?
  • 🔴 Diagnosis: SSH to the control plane node. Check crictl ps | grep kube-apiserver — no container. Check journalctl -u kubelet -f — kubelet says "manifest parsing error: unknown field 'encryptionAlgorithm'." The new API server manifest has a field the old kubelet doesn't understand.
  • 🔴 Fix: Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml, remove the unknown field. Kubelet detects the change, restarts the API server. Within 30 seconds, kubectl works again. This is why you ALWAYS have SSH access to control plane nodes.
  • 🟡 Lesson: kubectl relies on the API server. When the API server is down, you need node-level access. Always maintain both paths: API access (kubectl) AND node access (SSH/journalctl/crictl).

🏋️ Chapter 6 — Hands-On Practice Drills (10 Exercises)

The CNPE is a performance-based exam — you solve tasks in a live Linux terminal. Practice these drills in your lab environment until you can complete each within the target time.

⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 6.1 — Inspect Control Plane Components

Identify and verify all control plane components are healthy.

  1. List all pods in kube-system: kubectl get pods -n kube-system
  2. Filter for control plane: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'etcd|apiserver|scheduler|controller'
  3. Check component statuses: kubectl get componentstatuses
  4. Describe the API server pod: kubectl describe pod -n kube-system -l component=kube-apiserver
💡 Hint: Control plane pods run as static pods. Their names include the node name. Use kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'etcd|apiserver|scheduler|controller'
kubectl get componentstatuses
kubectl describe pod -n kube-system -l component=kube-apiserver
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 6.2 — Backup and Restore etcd

Take an etcd snapshot and verify it.

  1. SSH into the control plane node
  2. Run: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key snapshot save /tmp/etcd-backup.db
  3. Verify: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /tmp/etcd-backup.db
💡 Hint: Cert paths are standard for kubeadm. snapshot status shows hash, revision, total keys.
📝 View Solution 
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /tmp/etcd-backup.db
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /tmp/etcd-backup.db
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 6.3 — Trace a Failed Pod Scheduling

Create a pod with impossible resource requests and debug it.

  1. Create a pod requesting 100 CPUs (impossible): kubectl run greedy --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml → edit resources
  2. Check status: kubectl get pods — it should show Pending
  3. Describe: kubectl describe pod greedy — find the Events section
  4. Check scheduler logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l component=kube-scheduler --tail=20
💡 Hint: The Events section tells you WHY scheduling failed. Scheduler logs show the filtering/scoring process.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl run greedy --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > greedy.yaml
# Edit: resources.requests.cpu: "100"
kubectl apply -f greedy.yaml
kubectl get pods  # STATUS: Pending
kubectl describe pod greedy | grep -A10 Events
# Events: 0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu.
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 6.4 — Locate and Inspect Static Pod Manifests

Find the static pod manifests that define the control plane.

  1. SSH to a control plane node
  2. List manifests: ls -la /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
  3. Read one: cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
  4. Count how many static pods are running: check kube-system
💡 Hint: 4 manifests: etcd.yaml, kube-apiserver.yaml, kube-controller-manager.yaml, kube-scheduler.yaml.
📝 View Solution 
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | head -30
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide | grep $(hostname)
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 6.5 — Check etcd Cluster Health

Verify your etcd cluster is healthy and has quorum.

  1. SSH to control plane node
  2. Check member list: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl member list
  3. Check endpoint health: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint health
  4. Explain: what happens if 2 out of 3 etcd members go down?
💡 Hint: endpoint health shows each member's status. Quorum = (total/2) + 1. 3 members → quorum=2.
📝 View Solution 
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  member list --write-out=table
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint health
# 2/3 down → no quorum → cluster READ-ONLY
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 6.6 — View Controller Manager and Scheduler Logs

The control plane logs tell you what's happening behind the scenes.

  1. View scheduler logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l component=kube-scheduler --tail=30
  2. View controller-manager logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l component=kube-controller-manager --tail=30
  3. Watch logs in real-time as you create a Deployment: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l component=kube-controller-manager -f (in one terminal) while running kubectl create deployment test --image=nginx (in another)
💡 Hint: Controller-manager logs show the reconciliation loop in action.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l component=kube-scheduler --tail=30
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l component=kube-controller-manager --tail=30
# In terminal 1: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l component=kube-controller-manager -f
# In terminal 2: kubectl create deployment test --image=nginx
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 6.7 — Verify CNI and Node Networking

Check the CNI plugin and pod network configuration.

  1. List CNI pods: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'calico|cilium|flannel|weave'
  2. Check node pod CIDRs: kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.podCIDR}'
  3. Get a pod IP and verify you can ping it from another pod
💡 Hint: Each node gets a /24 CIDR range for pod IPs. All pods on a node get IPs from that range.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'calico|cilium|flannel|weave'
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.podCIDR}'
POD_IP=$(kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.podIP}')
kubectl run pingtest --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -- ping -c2 $POD_IP
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 6.8 — Identify Which Node a Pod is Running On

Trace pod placement and understand how the scheduler made its decision.

  1. Create 3 pods: kubectl create deployment spread --image=nginx --replicas=3
  2. Check which node each pod is on: kubectl get pods -o wide
  3. Describe one pod to see scheduler events: kubectl describe pod <name> | grep -A5 Events
  4. Explain: why did the scheduler choose those specific nodes?
💡 Hint: -o wide shows NODE column. Scheduler spreads pods across nodes by default (anti-affinity scoring).
📝 View Solution 
kubectl create deployment spread --image=nginx --replicas=3
kubectl get pods -o wide
POD=$(kubectl get pods -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl describe pod $POD | grep -A5 Events
# Events: Successfully assigned default/spread-xxx to worker-1
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 6.9 — Simulate a Node Failure

Cordon and drain a node, then watch pods reschedule.

  1. Cordon a worker node: kubectl cordon <node>
  2. Watch pods: kubectl get pods -o wide -w (in a separate terminal)
  3. Drain the node: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
  4. Uncordon: kubectl uncordon <node>
💡 Hint: cordon = no new pods. drain = evict existing pods. uncordon = allow pods again.
📝 View Solution 
NODE=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[1].metadata.name}')
kubectl cordon $NODE
kubectl drain $NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
kubectl get pods -o wide
kubectl uncordon $NODE
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 6.10 — Draw the Cluster Architecture from Memory

Recreate the architecture diagram without looking at references.

  1. Draw the control plane (4 components) and their connections
  2. Draw worker nodes (3 components) and their connections
  3. Label each arrow with the protocol/port
  4. Identify which component is the single point of failure in each plane
💡 Hint: API server:6443, etcd:2379, kubelet:10250. API server is stateless (HA possible). etcd is the critical SPOF.
📝 View Solution 
# Draw on paper or whiteboard:
# Control Plane:
#   kube-apiserver (port 6443) ← ALL components talk here
#   etcd (port 2379) ← ONLY apiserver talks to etcd
#   scheduler (port 10251) ← watches apiserver for unbound pods
#   controller-manager (port 10252) ← watches apiserver
#
# Worker Nodes:
#   kubelet (port 10250) ← registers with apiserver
#   kube-proxy ← watches apiserver for Service/Endpoint changes
#   Container Runtime ← controlled by kubelet via CRI
#
# SPOF: etcd — if etcd loses quorum, cluster is read-only

📖 Chapter 6 Summary: The Kubernetes control plane (API server + etcd + scheduler + controller manager) is the brain. Worker nodes (kubelet + kube-proxy + container runtime) are the muscle. etcd is the most critical component — lose etcd, lose the cluster. As a platform engineer, you design, deploy, and maintain the control plane itself. The CNPE exam tests cluster architecture decisions, etcd backup/restore, and troubleshooting control plane failures.
