Chapter 7: Core Kubernetes Objects — Platform Engineer's Toolkit

Pods, ReplicaSets, Deployments, Services, Namespaces, ConfigMaps, Secrets, and Labels/Selectors. The building blocks every platform engineer uses daily.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~2 hours📦 Objects

📖 Chapter Overview: Every Kubernetes platform is built from the same set of core objects. Pods are the smallest unit, ReplicaSets maintain count, Deployments manage lifecycle, Services provide stable networking, Namespaces partition resources, ConfigMaps and Secrets inject configuration, and Labels connect everything. Master these — they're the building blocks for everything that follows.

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • Create and manage Pods, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, and Secrets
  • Understand the Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod ownership chain
  • Explain how Services provide stable DNS despite ephemeral pod IPs
  • Design a label strategy for multi-environment, multi-team platforms
  • Use Namespaces for multi-tenancy with resource quotas
📋 CNPE Domain Mapping: All 5 CNPE domains build on these core objects. Domain 1 (Architecture) uses Namespaces for multi-tenancy. Domain 2 (GitOps) deploys Deployments via Argo CD. Domain 3 (Platform APIs) extends these with CRDs. Domain 4 (Observability) monitors them. Domain 5 (Security) protects them with NetworkPolicies and admission control.

7.1 Pods — The Smallest Deployable Unit

A Pod is a group of one or more containers that share network namespace, IPC namespace, and volumes. Every pod gets its own IP. Containers inside a pod communicate via localhost. Pods are EPHEMERAL — they can be killed and replaced at any time.

📖 Pod Lifecycle — Pending → Running → Succeeded/Failed

Pending: Pod accepted, scheduler finding node, pulling images. Running: At least one container started. Succeeded: All containers exited with code 0 (Jobs/CronJobs). Failed: Container exited with error. Unknown: Node unreachable — kubelet stopped reporting. Check with: kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}'.

💡 QoS Classes — Who Gets OOM-Killed First

K8s assigns OOM scores: BestEffort (no requests/limits, score 1000) killed FIRST. Burstable (requests set, limits higher, score based on ratio) killed SECOND. Guaranteed (requests == limits, score -998) killed LAST. This is why Kyverno policies should block BestEffort in production — a BestEffort pod is the first victim when memory runs low.

anihpj-web Pod: Contains 2 containers — Nginx (reverse proxy, port 80) + Gunicorn/Django (app, port 8000). They share the pod IP and can communicate via localhost. Nginx proxies to http://127.0.0.1:8000.

📖 Multi-Container Pod Design Patterns — Sidecar, Ambassador, Adapter

When should you put multiple containers in ONE pod vs separate pods? The rule: same pod = same lifecycle. Containers in a pod are scheduled together, scaled together, and die together. They share network (localhost), IPC, and volumes.

PatternWhat It Doesanihpj ExampleOther Examples
SIDECAREnhances the main container without changing it. Runs alongside, shares resources.Nginx sidecar: Reverse proxies to Gunicorn. Handles TLS termination, static files, rate limiting. Gunicorn doesn't know Nginx exists — it just listens on localhost:8000.Istio Envoy proxy, logging sidecar (Fluentd), Cloud SQL Auth proxy
AMBASSADORProxies external connections. Main container talks to localhost, ambassador handles external complexity.Redis Ambassador: If Redis was external (AWS ElastiCache), an ambassador container handles TLS + auth. Django talks to localhost:6379 — ambassador proxies to external Redis.Twemproxy for sharded Redis, any external DB proxy
ADAPTERTransforms output. Main container emits in one format, adapter converts to standard format.Metrics adapter: Django emits custom metrics on :9090. Adapter container scrapes them, converts to Prometheus format on :9091. Prometheus scrapes :9091.Prometheus exporters (Redis, Postgres), log format normalizers

When NOT to use multi-container pods: If containers have independent lifecycles (different scaling needs, different update cadences), use separate Deployments + Services. Only group containers that MUST share fate.

💡 Init Containers — Run Setup Before Your Main App Starts

Init containers run BEFORE app containers and must complete successfully before the app starts. They're perfect for: waiting for a database to be ready, running migrations, setting up permissions. Unlike app containers, init containers run SEQUENTIALLY (A finishes → B starts → C starts → then app containers). If an init container fails, the pod restarts (depending on restartPolicy). anihpj example: an init container runs python manage.py migrate before Gunicorn starts — ensuring the database schema is up to date before any requests arrive.

📖 Probes Deep Dive — Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes

Probes are K8s' health-check system. They determine whether your container is alive, ready for traffic, or still starting up. Misconfigured probes are the #1 cause of unnecessary pod restarts in production.

ProbeWhat It ChecksOn FailureOn SuccessUse Case
livenessProbe"Is the app alive or deadlocked?"Container is KILLED and restarted (crash loop).Nothing — container keeps running.Detect deadlocks, infinite loops, memory corruption. DO NOT check external dependencies here!
readinessProbe"Can this pod serve traffic RIGHT NOW?"Pod removed from Service endpoints. No traffic sent.Pod added to Service endpoints.Wait for DB connection, cache warmup, or heavy computation. Route traffic only when ready.
startupProbe"Has the application finished starting?"Container is KILLED (same as liveness).Liveness and readiness probes take over.Slow-starting apps (JVM, ML models). Disables liveness/readiness until startup completes.

Probe types — how K8s performs the check:

  • HTTP GET: Kubelet sends GET to container on specified port/path. 200-399 = success. Anything else = failure. GET /healthz → 200 OK.
  • TCP Socket: Kubelet tries to open TCP connection. Connection established = success. Refused/timeout = failure. Good for databases (PostgreSQL on :5432).
  • Exec: Kubelet runs a command INSIDE the container. Exit code 0 = success. Non-zero = failure. cat /tmp/healthy — if file exists, healthy.
  • gRPC: (K8s 1.24+) Kubelet makes a gRPC health check call. Requires the app to implement gRPC health protocol.

anihpj probe configuration — with explanation:

livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz          # Django health endpoint
    port: 8000
  initialDelaySeconds: 30   # Wait 30s after start before first check
  periodSeconds: 10         # Check every 10 seconds
  timeoutSeconds: 3         # Timeout after 3s → count as failure
  failureThreshold: 3       # Fail 3 times in a row → KILL container
  # Total: 30 + (10+3)*3 = 69 seconds before restart

readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz?ready=1  # Separate endpoint that checks DB connectivity
    port: 8000
  initialDelaySeconds: 5    # Check almost immediately
  periodSeconds: 5           # Check frequently (traffic routing is critical)
  failureThreshold: 1        # One failure = remove from Service immediately

startupProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8000
  failureThreshold: 30       # Allow 30 failures (30 × 10s = 5 min startup time)
  periodSeconds: 10
  # Gives Django migrations 5 minutes to complete before livenessProbe activates

Common probe mistakes platform engineers must block:

  • 🔴 Liveness probe checks the database: DB is slow → liveness fails → K8s restarts pod → new pod also can't reach DB → restart loop. Liveness should ONLY check if the app process is alive, not its dependencies.
  • 🔴 No startup probe for slow apps: Django migrations take 2 minutes. Liveness probe fires after 30s → K8s kills the pod mid-migration → corrupted database. Add a startup probe with high failureThreshold.
  • 🔴 Readiness probe too aggressive: failureThreshold: 1, periodSeconds: 1 — a single hiccup removes pod from Service. Use at least failureThreshold: 3 to tolerate transient errors.

7.2 ReplicaSets — Maintaining Pod Count

A ReplicaSet ensures a specified number of identical pod replicas are running. If a pod crashes or is deleted, the ReplicaSet creates a replacement. It uses label selectors to identify its pods. You rarely create ReplicaSets directly — Deployments manage them for you.

HOW A REPLICASET WORKS — The Label Selector Pattern
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  REPLICASET: anihpj-web-7f3a2b  (desired: 3)                            │
  │  selector: matchLabels { app: anihpj-web, tier: frontend }              │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                    │
            ┌───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┐
            ▼                       ▼                       ▼
  ┌─────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────┐
  │ POD abcde       │    │ POD fghij       │    │ POD klmno       │
  │ labels:         │    │ labels:         │    │ labels:         │
  │ app: anihpj-web │    │ app: anihpj-web │    │ app: anihpj-web │
  │ tier: frontend  │    │ tier: frontend  │    │ tier: frontend  │
  │ IP: 10.0.1.5    │    │ IP: 10.0.1.6    │    │ IP: 10.0.1.7    │
  │ STATUS: Running  │    │ STATUS: Running  │    │ STATUS: Running  │
  └─────────────────┘    └─────────────────┘    └─────────────────┘
           ▲                      ▲                      ▲
           └──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘
           ALL match the selector → ReplicaSet "owns" them
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  If Pod fghij crashes → ReplicaSet counts: 2 Running, desired=3 → CREATE pod
  If someone creates a pod WITH matching labels → ReplicaSet owns it AND
  deletes it (because count would be 4, exceeding desired: 3)
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

How ReplicaSet watches its Pods: Every second, the Replicaset controller queries the API server: "Give me all pods with labels app=anihpj-web, tier=frontend." If the count ≠ desired replicas, it creates/deletes pods. This is the same reconciliation loop every K8s controller uses. The label selector is the OWNERSHIP LINK — pods with matching labels belong to this ReplicaSet.

😰 ReplicaSet Anti-Pattern — Two ReplicaSets Fighting Over Pods
  • 🔴 ReplicaSet-A: desired=3, selector: app=web. ReplicaSet-B: desired=2, selector: app=web.
  • 🔴 Each ReplicaSet sees 5 pods with app=web. A thinks "too many! delete 2." B thinks "too many! delete 3." They FIGHT — pods are created and deleted in an infinite loop.
  • 🔴 Solution: Unique selectors (app=web, component=api vs app=web, component=worker) or let Deployments handle ReplicaSets (they add pod-template-hash automatically).
💡 ReplicaSet YAML — The Key Fields
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: ReplicaSet
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  labels:
    app: anihpj-web
spec:
  replicas: 3                     # How many pods I want
  selector:
    matchLabels:                  # WHICH pods are mine
      app: anihpj-web
  template:                       # Blueprint for new pods
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web           # MUST match selector!
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: anihpj-web:latest

Critical rule: template.metadata.labels MUST include ALL labels in selector.matchLabels. If they don't match, the API server rejects the ReplicaSet with "selector does not match template labels".

7.3 Deployments — Managing Application Lifecycle

A Deployment provides declarative updates for Pods and ReplicaSets. It manages rolling updates (gradually replace old pods), rollbacks (kubectl rollout undo), scaling, and pausing. The anihpj-web Deployment: 3 replicas, rolling update with maxSurge: 1 and maxUnavailable: 0.

💡 Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod Chain

Deployment creates ReplicaSet, ReplicaSet creates Pods. When you update a Deployment (new image), it creates a NEW ReplicaSet and scales down the old one. kubectl rollout history deployment/anihpj-web shows all revisions — each is a ReplicaSet.

📖 The Controller Reconciliation Loop — Observe → Diff → Act

Every K8s controller runs an infinite loop: Observe current state (via API server watch), Diff against desired state (from spec), Act to reconcile. The Deployment controller watches Deployments, ReplicaSets, and Pods. Every second: "Does reality match spec.replicas: 3?" If 2 pods exist → create one. If 4 exist → delete one. You never tell K8s to "create a pod" — you declare "I want 3" and the controller figures it out. This same pattern powers Argo CD, Crossplane, and every Operator you'll build.

ROLLING UPDATE — How Deployments Replace Pods With Zero Downtime
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  DEPLOYMENT: anihpj-web  (replicas: 3, update: RollingUpdate)           │
  │  maxSurge: 1 (allow +1 extra pod during update)                         │
  │  maxUnavailable: 1 (allow at most 1 pod to be down)                     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  BEFORE UPDATE — All pods running v1.0.0
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ReplicaSet 1 (v1.0.0):  3/3 Ready                                    │
  │  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐                                        │
  │  │ P1   │  │ P2   │  │ P3   │    All 3 serving traffic               │
  │  │ v1.0 │  │ v1.0 │  │ v1.0 │                                        │
  │  └──────┘  └──────┘  └──────┘                                        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  STEP 1 — Create new ReplicaSet, scale UP by maxSurge (1)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ReplicaSet 1 (v1.0.0):  3/3 Ready    ReplicaSet 2 (v2.0.0):  1/1    │
  │  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐         ┌──────┐                       │
  │  │ P1   │  │ P2   │  │ P3   │         │ P4   │  ← NEW pod v2.0       │
  │  │ v1.0 │  │ v1.0 │  │ v1.0 │         │ v2.0 │                       │
  │  └──────┘  └──────┘  └──────┘         └──────┘                       │
  │  4 total pods (3 v1 + 1 v2) — maxSurge=1 allows 4                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  STEP 2 — Scale DOWN old by 1, scale UP new by 1
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ReplicaSet 1 (v1.0.0):  2/2 Ready    ReplicaSet 2 (v2.0.0):  2/2    │
  │  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐                   ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐              │
  │  │ P1   │  │ P2   │                   │ P4   │  │ P5   │              │
  │  │ v1.0 │  │ v1.0 │                   │ v2.0 │  │ v2.0 │              │
  │  └──────┘  └──────┘                   └──────┘  └──────┘              │
  │  P3 terminated gracefully (SIGTERM → 30s → SIGKILL)                    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  STEP 3 — Continue until old ReplicaSet = 0, new ReplicaSet = 3
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ReplicaSet 1 (v1.0.0):  0/0 (kept for rollback!)                    │
  │  ReplicaSet 2 (v2.0.0):  3/3 Ready                                    │
  │  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐                                        │
  │  │ P4   │  │ P5   │  │ P6   │    All 3 now v2.0                      │
  │  │ v2.0 │  │ v2.0 │  │ v2.0 │    Zero downtime!                      │
  │  └──────┘  └──────┘  └──────┘                                        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  IF v2.0 crashes → kubectl rollout undo → ReplicaSet 1 scales back to 3
  OLD ReplicaSets are NEVER deleted automatically → kubectl rollout history
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
⚠️ Rolling Update Strategy — maxSurge and maxUnavailable

maxSurge: Maximum number of EXTRA pods allowed during update (over desired count). Default: 25% (1 extra per 4 desired). maxUnavailable: Maximum number of pods that can be UNAVAILABLE during update. Default: 25%.

Production values for anihpj (3 replicas): maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 — creates 1 new pod before killing old one, never loses capacity. Development: maxSurge: 0, maxUnavailable: 1 — kills old pod first (saves resources, tolerates brief downtime).

📖 Deployment Strategies — Recreate vs RollingUpdate vs Blue/Green vs Canary

Kubernetes Deployments natively support two strategies. For advanced strategies (Blue/Green, Canary), you need additional tools like Argo Rollouts or service meshes. Here's the full comparison:

StrategyHow It WorksDowntimeResourcesRollbackBest For
RecreateKill ALL old pods → create ALL new pods. Simple, brutal.⚠️ YES — full downtime during pod replacementMinimal (no overlap)Instant (just old version)Batch jobs, dev environments, stateful apps that can't have 2 instances
RollingUpdateReplace pods one-by-one. Old + new coexist during update.✅ ZERO (if configured right)+1 extra pod during update (maxSurge)kubectl rollout undoMost production workloads. Default K8s strategy.
Blue/GreenDeploy entire new stack (green) alongside old (blue). Switch traffic via Service selector change.✅ ZERO2× full capacity (both stacks running)Instant (switch selector back)Critical workloads needing instant rollback. Requires Argo Rollouts or manual Service update.
CanaryRoute small % of traffic to new version. Gradually increase. Monitor for errors.✅ ZERO+X% extra (canary pods)Instant (shift traffic back)High-risk changes. Requires Argo Rollouts, Flagger, or service mesh (Istio/Linkerd).

anihpj strategy: RollingUpdate for web (stateless, 3 replicas, no downtime). Blue/Green for database schema changes (migrate → verify → switch). Canary for major Django version upgrades (route 5% traffic → check error rate → ramp to 100%). The CNPE exam asks you to CHOOSE the right strategy — not just implement it.

7.4 Services — Stable Network Endpoints

Pod IPs change when pods are replaced. A Service provides a STABLE IP (ClusterIP) and DNS name that doesn't change. It load-balances traffic to healthy pods matching its label selector.

TypeAccessUse Case
ClusterIPInternal onlyanihpj-web → postgres via postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
NodePortExternal via <NodeIP>:30000-32767Quick testing. NOT for production (bypasses load balancer)
LoadBalancerExternal via cloud LBProduction. Provisions AWS NLB/ALB automatically
😰 Without Services — The Hardcoded IP Nightmare
  • 🔴 anihpj-web pod gets IP 10.0.1.5. You hardcode it in Django settings. Pod crashes → replacement gets IP 10.0.1.9. Django still tries 10.0.1.5 → connection refused.
  • 🔴 You update the Deployment. Old pods terminate, new pods start with NEW random IPs. Every hardcoded IP connection breaks.
  • 🔴 Scale from 3→5 pods. How do you add 2 new IPs to nginx config? Every scale event becomes a manual ops task.
🎉 With Services — Stable DNS and Auto-Discovery
  • ✅ Django connects to postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local — this DNS name NEVER changes, regardless of pod recreation.
  • ✅ Service selector app: anihpj-web auto-discovers new pods. Scale 3→5 → Service immediately includes all 5. Zero config.
  • ✅ kube-proxy updates iptables rules within seconds. Failed pods auto-removed from backend. Healthy pods auto-added.
SERVICE TRAFFIC FLOW — DNS → ClusterIP → kube-proxy → Backend Pod
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  HOW A SERVICE ROUTES TRAFFIC — End-to-End Flow                          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────┐
  │  anihpj-web  │  Pod wants to reach postgres
  │  Pod         │  DNS query: "postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"
  │  IP:10.0.1.5 │
  └──────┬───────┘
         │ ① DNS Lookup
         ▼
  ┌──────────────┐
  │  CoreDNS     │  Returns: postgres.anihpj.svc = 10.96.0.5 (ClusterIP)
  │  (kube-dns)  │  This ClusterIP NEVER changes!
  └──────┬───────┘
         │ ② Returns 10.96.0.5
         ▼
  ┌──────────────┐
  │  kube-proxy  │  Looks up Service "postgres" → 2 healthy endpoints:
  │  (iptables)  │  10.0.1.10:5432 (READY) and 10.0.1.11:5432 (READY)
  │              │  Randomly picks one → rewrites packet destination
  └──────┬───────┘
         │ ③ Packet routed to chosen backend
         ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  BACKEND PODS (selected by label app=postgres)                       │
  │  ┌─────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────┐                     │
  │  │ Postgres Pod 1  │         │ Postgres Pod 2  │                     │
  │  │ IP: 10.0.1.10   │         │ IP: 10.0.1.11   │                     │
  │  │ STATUS: Ready ✓  │         │ STATUS: Ready ✓  │                     │
  │  └─────────────────┘         └─────────────────┘                     │
  │  kube-proxy picks one → rewrites 10.96.0.5:5432 → 10.0.1.10:5432    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  KEY: DNS resolves Service NAME → ClusterIP (virtual, no interface).
  kube-proxy translates ClusterIP → real Pod IP. This is a 2-step process.
  If the chosen pod goes down → kube-proxy removes it from the iptables rules
  within ~5 seconds (endpoint controller sync period).
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

7.5 Namespaces — Virtual Clusters for Multi-Tenancy

Namespaces partition a physical cluster into virtual clusters. Each team gets their own namespace with resource quotas, RBAC, and NetworkPolicies. Platform engineering pattern: Namespace-as-a-Service — developers request a namespace via a self-service portal and get it pre-configured.

NAMESPACE-AS-A-SERVICE — Platform Engineering Pattern
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    PHYSICAL KUBERNETES CLUSTER                           │
  │                                                                         │
  │  ┌───────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────┐   │
  │  │ NAMESPACE: team-a │  │ NAMESPACE: team-b │  │ NAMESPACE: team-c │   │
  │  │                   │  │                   │  │                   │   │
  │  │ Quota: 10 pods    │  │ Quota: 20 pods    │  │ Quota: 5 pods     │   │
  │  │ CPU: 4 cores      │  │ CPU: 8 cores      │  │ CPU: 2 cores      │   │
  │  │ Mem: 8Gi          │  │ Mem: 16Gi         │  │ Mem: 4Gi          │   │
  │  │                   │  │                   │  │                   │   │
  │  │ RBAC: team-a-edit │  │ RBAC: team-b-edit │  │ RBAC: team-c-view │   │
  │  │ NetPol: allow     │  │ NetPol: allow     │  │ NetPol: deny-all  │   │
  │  │   from team-b     │  │   from team-a     │  │                   │   │
  │  │                   │  │                   │  │                   │   │
  │  │ ┌───┐ ┌───┐ ┌───┐ │  │ ┌───┐ ┌───┐ ┌───┐ │  │ ┌───┐             │   │
  │  │ │ P │ │ P │ │ P │ │  │ │ P │ │ P │ │ P │ │  │ │ P │             │   │
  │  │ └───┘ └───┘ └───┘ │  │ └───┘ └───┘ └───┘ │  │ └───┘             │   │
  │  └───────────────────┘  └───────────────────┘  └───────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                         │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ SYSTEM NAMESPACES (never touch unless you know what you're doing)│   │
  │  │ kube-system  │  kube-public  │  kube-node-lease  │  default      │   │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  Each namespace = isolated boundary with its OWN: ResourceQuota, RBAC,
  NetworkPolicy, LimitRange. Teams can't see/access each other's resources.
  But they SHARE: physical nodes, CNI network, cluster DNS (CoreDNS).
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ResourceQuota: A namespace-wide limit on total resources. Prevents one team from monopolizing the cluster. LimitRange: Sets default requests/limits for pods that don't specify them. Together they enforce fair sharing and prevent untracked resource consumption.

💡 ResourceQuota + LimitRange — The Platform Engineer's Guardrails
# ResourceQuota: Hard limits for the namespace
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: team-a-quota
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  hard:
    pods: "10"            # Max 10 pods
    requests.cpu: "4"     # Total CPU requested ≤ 4 cores
    requests.memory: "8Gi"
    limits.cpu: "8"       # Total CPU limits ≤ 8 cores
    limits.memory: "16Gi"
    persistentvolumeclaims: "5"
---
# LimitRange: Default values for pods without explicit requests
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: team-a-limits
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    default:              # If no limits set
      cpu: "500m"
      memory: "512Mi"
    defaultRequest:       # If no requests set
      cpu: "250m"
      memory: "256Mi"
    max:                  # Hard upper bound
      cpu: "2"
      memory: "2Gi"

Why this matters: A pod without requests/limits can consume ALL CPU on a node. LimitRange ensures every pod gets sensible defaults. ResourceQuota prevents namespace explosion. Together they're the platform engineer's multi-tenancy guardrails.

🎉 Namespace-as-a-Service — Self-Service Platform Pattern
  • ✅ Developer opens Backstage portal → clicks "Create Namespace" → enters team name, requested CPU/memory → submits.
  • ✅ Backstage triggers a pipeline that creates: Namespace + ResourceQuota + LimitRange + RBAC (RoleBinding to team's AD group) + NetworkPolicy (default-deny) + ServiceAccount.
  • ✅ Developer gets a fully provisioned namespace with all guardrails in ~30 seconds. No platform engineer involved.
  • ✅ This is the "Golden Path" — self-service with baked-in security. The CNPE exam tests your ability to DESIGN this, not just configure it.
📖 Namespace Naming Convention — The Platform Engineer's Standard

Good naming prevents chaos across hundreds of namespaces:

  • <team>-<environment>: team-a-dev, team-b-prod
  • <app>-<stage>: anihpj-staging, anihpj-production
  • Avoid: test1, johns-namespace, temp123. These tell you nothing.
  • Label namespaces: kubectl label ns team-a-dev environment=dev team=team-a cost-center=1234 — labels enable queries like "show me all production namespaces."

7.6 Labels, Selectors, and Annotations

Labels are key-value pairs that organize objects. Selectors query objects by labels. Services use selectors to find their backend pods. Annotations store non-identifying metadata (git commit, build timestamp). Labels are the GLUE of Kubernetes. Example: app: anihpj-web, tier: frontend, environment: production.

FeatureLabelsAnnotations
PurposeIdentify and select objectsStore non-identifying metadata
QueryableYes — kubectl get pods -l app=webNo — not queryable by selector
Used byServices, Deployments, ReplicaSets (selectors)Tools: kubectl, monitoring, GitOps
Size limit63 chars for key, 63 chars for valueNo size limit (but etcd has 1.5MB total per object)
Examplesapp: anihpj-web
tier: frontend		git-commit: a1b2c3d
deployed-at: 2024-01-15
💡 Kubernetes Recommended Labels — The app.kubernetes.io Standard

Every resource SHOULD have these 6 labels. Argo CD, Helm, and kubectl all understand them:

LabelExampleMeaning
app.kubernetes.io/nameanihpjThe application name
app.kubernetes.io/instanceanihpj-prodUnique instance of the app
app.kubernetes.io/version1.2.0The current version
app.kubernetes.io/componentwebThe component within the architecture
app.kubernetes.io/part-ofanihpjThe higher-level application this belongs to
app.kubernetes.io/managed-byhelmThe tool managing this resource

Why this matters: Argo CD uses these labels to group resources in the UI. Helm adds app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: Helm automatically. If you use these labels consistently, every tool in the ecosystem understands your deployments.

📖 Selector Types — Equality vs Set-Based

Equality-based: environment = production, tier != frontend. Used by Services and ReplicaSets (matchLabels). Simple: matches or doesn't.

Set-based: environment in (production, staging), tier notin (frontend), app (exists), !critical (does not exist). Used by Deployments (matchExpressions), RBAC, and NetworkPolicy. More expressive.

Production example — anihpj staging Service that matches ALL frontend AND backend:

selector:
  matchLabels:
    app: anihpj-web
  matchExpressions:
    - {key: environment, operator: In, values: [staging]}
    - {key: tier, operator: NotIn, values: [batch]}  # exclude batch jobs
🎉 Label Strategy — The Platform Engineer's Auto-Discovery Pattern
  • ✅ Every anihpj resource gets: app.kubernetes.io/part-of: anihpj, app.kubernetes.io/environment: production
  • ✅ Services auto-discover pods by label (app: anihpj-web) — no hardcoded pod IPs.
  • ✅ Prometheus auto-discovers scrape targets by label (prometheus.io/scrape: "true").
  • ✅ NetworkPolicies allow traffic by label (from: podSelector: tier: frontend).
  • ✅ Argo CD groups resources by app.kubernetes.io/part-of in its tree view.
  • ✅ A well-designed label strategy means you NEVER lookup pod IPs — you query by label instead.

7.7 ConfigMaps and Secrets

ConfigMap stores non-sensitive config. Secret stores sensitive data (base64 encoded, NOT encrypted by default). Both can be mounted as environment variables or files. anihpj ConfigMap: DEBUG, ALLOWED_HOSTS, DB_HOST. anihpj Secret: DB_PASSWORD, SECRET_KEY.

🧠 CNPE Exam: Secrets are base64 ENCODED, not encrypted. Anyone with kubectl get secret -o yaml can decode them. Use Sealed Secrets, External Secrets Operator, or Vault for production.
📖 Secret Management Tools — From Basic to Enterprise

Base64-encoded Secrets in etcd are NOT production-ready. Here's the evolution of Secret management — and what platform engineers should deploy at each maturity level:

ToolHow It WorksEncrypted in Git?Auto-Rotate?ComplexityBest For
Encryption at RestAPI server encrypts Secrets before writing to etcd. Built-in. Configure with EncryptionConfiguration.N/A (etcd only)❌ No⭐ LowFirst step. Every production cluster MUST enable this. Prevents etcd compromise = secret exposure.
Sealed SecretsEncrypt Secret with cluster's public key. Only that cluster can decrypt. Encrypted YAML is safe in Git.✅ Yes❌ No (manual)⭐⭐ MediumGitOps workflows. Devs commit encrypted secrets. Controller decrypts in cluster. Simple, effective.
External Secrets OperatorSyncs secrets from external store (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault) INTO K8s Secrets.✅ Yes (in external store)✅ Yes (if external store supports it)⭐⭐⭐ MediumCloud-native. One ExternalSecret CRD → auto-syncs → K8s Secret stays updated. anihpj uses this for DB_PASSWORD from AWS Secrets Manager.
HashiCorp Vault + Vault CSISecrets NEVER touch etcd. Vault CSI provider mounts secrets directly into pod filesystem. App reads from file.✅ Yes (in Vault)✅ Yes (Vault dynamic secrets)⭐⭐⭐⭐ HighEnterprise. Dynamic DB credentials (new user per pod!), audit logging, multi-cloud. Most secure — secret never exists as K8s object.

anihpj secret flow (Production): Developer creates ExternalSecret CRD → ESO fetches DB_PASSWORD from AWS Secrets Manager → creates K8s Secret → Deployment mounts it via env var → Django reads os.environ['DB_PASSWORD']. Rotating the secret: update AWS Secrets Manager → ESO auto-syncs to K8s → trigger rollout restart.

📖 Encryption at Rest — Making Secrets Actually Secret

By default, Secrets in etcd are plain base64 (easily decoded). Enable EncryptionConfiguration on the API server to encrypt them with AES-CBC before writing to etcd. Add --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml to the kube-apiserver static pod manifest. Existing Secrets won't be auto-encrypted — rewrite them with kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -. This is a Domain 5 (Security) tested skill.

💡 ConfigMap Updates — 3 Ways to Reload Without Manual Restarts

ConfigMaps injected as env vars require pod restart. ConfigMaps mounted as files update on disk within ~60s (kubelet sync) but apps may cache old values. Three solutions: (1) Reloader — watches ConfigMap changes, auto-restarts Deployments. (2) Mount + inotify — app watches mounted file for changes. (3) Versioned ConfigMaps — name includes hash (anihpj-config-a1b2c3), update Deployment to reference new name → rolling update naturally.

KUBERNETES OBJECT RELATIONSHIP MAP

🏋️ Chapter 7 — Hands-On Practice Drills (10 Exercises)

The CNPE is a performance-based exam — you solve tasks in a live Linux terminal. Practice these drills in your lab environment until you can complete each within the target time.

⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 7.1 — Create a Deployment with Resource Limits

Create a Deployment for anihpj-web with 3 replicas, resource requests/limits, and health probes.

  1. Write a Deployment YAML for anihpj-web: 3 replicas, image anihpj-web:latest, container port 8000
  2. Add resources: requests (256Mi, 250m), limits (512Mi, 500m)
  3. Add liveness probe: HTTP GET /healthz every 10s, timeout 3s
  4. Add readiness probe: HTTP GET /healthz?ready=1 every 5s
  5. Apply and verify: kubectl get deploy,pods -n anihpj
💡 Hint: kubectl create deployment --dry-run=client -o yaml for a starting template.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl create deployment anihpj-web --image=anihpj-web:latest --replicas=3 \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml -n anihpj > deploy.yaml
# Edit: add resources, livenessProbe, readinessProbe
kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml -n anihpj
kubectl get deploy,pods -n anihpj
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 7.2 — Expose a Deployment with a Service and Test DNS

Create a ClusterIP Service and verify DNS resolution.

  1. Expose the Deployment: kubectl expose deployment anihpj-web --port=8000 --target-port=8000 -n anihpj
  2. Check the Service: kubectl get svc -n anihpj
  3. Test DNS from a debug pod: kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox -n anihpj -- nslookup anihpj-web
💡 Hint: Full DNS name: anihpj-web.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
📝 View Solution 
kubectl expose deployment anihpj-web --port=8000 --target-port=8000 -n anihpj
kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox -n anihpj -- nslookup anihpj-web
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 7.3 — Perform a Rolling Update and Rollback

Update the anihpj-web image and verify the rolling update, then rollback.

  1. Update image: kubectl set image deployment/anihpj-web anihpj-web=anihpj-web:v2.0.0 -n anihpj
  2. Watch: kubectl rollout status deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj
  3. Check history: kubectl rollout history deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj
  4. Rollback: kubectl rollout undo deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj
💡 Hint: rollout undo reverts to the previous revision. --to-revision=1 goes to a specific one.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl set image deployment/anihpj-web anihpj-web=anihpj-web:v2.0.0 -n anihpj
kubectl rollout status deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj
kubectl rollout undo deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 7.4 — Create ConfigMap and Secret, Mount in Pod

Inject configuration into pods the proper way.

  1. Create ConfigMap: kubectl create configmap anihpj-config --from-literal=DEBUG=false --from-literal=DB_HOST=postgres -n anihpj
  2. Create Secret: kubectl create secret generic anihpj-secret --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=s3cret123 -n anihpj
  3. Update Deployment to mount both as env vars using envFrom
  4. Verify: kubectl exec <pod> -n anihpj -- env | grep -E 'DEBUG|DB_'
💡 Hint: Use envFrom.configMapRef and envFrom.secretRef in the Deployment spec.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl create configmap anihpj-config --from-literal=DEBUG=false -n anihpj
kubectl create secret generic anihpj-secret --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=s3cret123 -n anihpj
# Edit deployment: add envFrom to container spec
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl exec $POD -n anihpj -- env | grep -E 'DEBUG|DB_'
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 7.5 — Create Namespace with Resource Quota

Set up multi-tenancy with ResourceQuota.

  1. Create namespace: kubectl create ns team-blue
  2. Apply ResourceQuota: max 10 pods, max 4 CPUs, max 8Gi memory
  3. Try creating 11 pods — the 11th should be rejected
💡 Hint: kubectl create quota or write a ResourceQuota YAML.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl create ns team-blue
kubectl create quota team-blue-quota --hard=pods=10,cpu=4,memory=8Gi -n team-blue
# Create 11 pods — the 11th fails with "exceeded quota"
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 7.6 — Query Objects with Label Selectors

Use labels to filter and find specific resources.

  1. List pods with label app=anihpj-web
  2. List pods across ALL namespaces with tier=frontend
  3. Show labels on all deployments: kubectl get deploy -n anihpj --show-labels
💡 Hint: kubectl get pods -l app=anihpj-web, kubectl get pods -A -l tier=frontend
📝 View Solution 
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web
kubectl get pods -A -l tier=frontend
kubectl get deploy -n anihpj --show-labels
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 7.7 — Scale a Deployment Manually and with Autoscaling

Scale up and down, then set up HPA.

  1. Scale up: kubectl scale deployment anihpj-web --replicas=5 -n anihpj
  2. Verify 5 pods are running
  3. Scale down to 2 and verify
  4. Set up HPA: kubectl autoscale deployment anihpj-web --min=2 --max=10 --cpu-percent=80 -n anihpj
💡 Hint: kubectl scale for manual. kubectl autoscale for HPA.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl scale deployment anihpj-web --replicas=5 -n anihpj
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web
kubectl scale deployment anihpj-web --replicas=2 -n anihpj
kubectl autoscale deployment anihpj-web --min=2 --max=10 --cpu-percent=80 -n anihpj
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 7.8 — Debug a CrashLoopBackOff Pod

A pod keeps crashing. Debug and fix it.

  1. Create a pod with a bad command: kubectl run crash --image=nginx --command -- /bin/false -n anihpj
  2. Check status: should show CrashLoopBackOff
  3. Describe: kubectl describe pod crash -n anihpj — note exit code
  4. Check logs of previous instance: kubectl logs crash -n anihpj --previous
💡 Hint: --previous shows logs from the LAST crashed container.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl run crash --image=nginx --command -- /bin/false -n anihpj
kubectl get pods -n anihpj  # STATUS: CrashLoopBackOff
kubectl describe pod crash -n anihpj | grep -E 'State|Exit Code'
kubectl logs crash -n anihpj --previous
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 7.9 — Create a NodePort Service and Access It Externally

Expose anihpj-web externally via NodePort.

  1. Create NodePort service: kubectl expose deployment anihpj-web --type=NodePort --port=8000 -n anihpj
  2. Get the assigned port: kubectl get svc -n anihpj
  3. Access externally: curl http://<NODE_IP>:<NODEPORT>/healthz
💡 Hint: NodePort range is 30000-32767. Get node IP: kubectl get nodes -o wide.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl expose deployment anihpj-web --type=NodePort --port=8000 -n anihpj
kubectl get svc -n anihpj
NODE_IP=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.addresses[0].address}')
NODEPORT=$(kubectl get svc anihpj-web -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[0].nodePort}')
curl http://$NODE_IP:$NODEPORT/healthz
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 7.10 — Design a Complete Label Strategy

Apply a comprehensive label strategy to all anihpj resources.

  1. Define labels: app.kubernetes.io/name, app.kubernetes.io/part-of, app.kubernetes.io/environment
  2. Label the namespace: kubectl label ns anihpj environment=staging team=platform
  3. Verify all pods inherit the right labels via their Deployment template
💡 Hint: app.kubernetes.io/* labels are the Kubernetes recommended standard.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl label ns anihpj app.kubernetes.io/part-of=anihpj app.kubernetes.io/environment=staging
kubectl get pods -n anihpj --show-labels

📖 Chapter 7 Summary: Kubernetes objects form a hierarchy: Namespace contains Deployments → Deployments own ReplicaSets → ReplicaSets own Pods. Services provide stable networking. ConfigMaps and Secrets inject configuration. Labels connect everything. Master these building blocks — they're used in every subsequent chapter.

Chapter 8: Setting Up Your Platform Lab Environment

6-cluster local lab, kubectl, kubeconfig, multi-cluster context switching, deploying anihpj step by step, and verifying everything works.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~2 hours🛠️ Hands-On

📖 Chapter Overview: Theory is useless without practice. This chapter guides you through setting up a 6-cluster local lab where you'll run every example in this guide: kubeadm for production-like scenarios, 3 kind clusters for GitOps multi-cluster workflows, minikube for quick testing, and k3d for security experiments. We'll install kubectl, configure kubeconfig for multiple clusters, deploy anihpj, and verify everything.

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • Set up 6 local Kubernetes clusters with different tools
  • Configure kubectl and kubeconfig for multi-cluster management
  • Safely switch between cluster contexts
  • Deploy the full anihpj stack to your lab cluster
  • Verify deployments with describe, logs, exec, and port-forward

8.1 Choosing Local Kubernetes Tools

ToolTypeBest ForStartup TimeMemory Usage
kubeadmProduction-like (VMs)Full control plane experience. etcd backup/restore, static pods, upgrades. Closest to real CNPE exam.5-10 min~4GB
kindDocker-basedFast create/destroy. Multi-node clusters in Docker. Great for CI/CD and GitOps testing.30 sec~500MB/node
minikubeSingle-node VM/containerEasy local dev with built-in addons (ingress, dashboard, metrics-server).2 min~2GB
k3dK3s in DockerUltra-lightweight. K3s is a certified K8s distribution. Good for policy/security experiments.15 sec~300MB/node
💡 Installation Guide — All 4 Tools on Ubuntu
# === kubeadm (requires 2+ VMs or multipass) ===
# On each VM:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y apt-transport-https ca-certificates curl
curl -fsSL https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.29/deb/Release.key | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/kubernetes-apt-keyring.gpg
echo 'deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/kubernetes-apt-keyring.gpg] https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.29/deb/ /' | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/kubernetes.list
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y kubelet kubeadm kubectl
sudo apt-mark hold kubelet kubeadm kubectl  # prevent auto-updates

# Install container runtime (containerd)
sudo apt install -y containerd
sudo mkdir -p /etc/containerd
containerd config default | sudo tee /etc/containerd/config.toml
sudo systemctl restart containerd

# On control-plane node:
sudo kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16
mkdir -p $HOME/.kube && sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config
sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) $HOME/.kube/config
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/flannel-io/flannel/releases/latest/download/kube-flannel.yml

# On worker nodes (use token from kubeadm init output):
sudo kubeadm join :6443 --token  --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# === kind (requires Docker) ===
# On Ubuntu/Debian:
[ $(uname -m) = x86_64 ] && curl -Lo ./kind https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/dl/v0.22.0/kind-linux-amd64
chmod +x ./kind && sudo mv ./kind /usr/local/bin/kind

# Create 3 clusters:
kind create cluster --name dev
kind create cluster --name staging
kind create cluster --name prod

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# === minikube ===
curl -LO https://storage.googleapis.com/minikube/releases/latest/minikube-linux-amd64
sudo install minikube-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/minikube
minikube start --driver=docker --cpus=2 --memory=4096

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# === k3d (requires Docker) ===
curl -s https://raw.githubusercontent.com/k3d-io/k3d/main/install.sh | bash
k3d cluster create security --servers 1 --agents 2

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# Verify all clusters are accessible:
kubectl config get-contexts
# Should show 6 contexts: cluster1-admin@cluster1, kind-dev, kind-staging,
# kind-prod, minikube, k3d-security
😰 "I destroyed my production cluster!" — A Context Horror Story
  • 🔴 What happened: Platform engineer was debugging an issue. Switched to kind-dev to test a fix. Got distracted by a Slack message. Came back, forgot to switch context. Ran kubectl delete namespace anihpj — but current-context was kind-prod, not kind-dev.
  • 🔴 Result: The ENTIRE production namespace — including the Postgres StatefulSet and PVC — was deleted in 2 seconds. No confirmation prompt. No undo.
  • 🔴 Recovery: Velero backup restored the namespace in ~5 minutes. PVC data was recovered from the backup. Downtime: 8 minutes. Root cause: no context verification before destructive commands.
  • 🟡 Prevention: (1) Context in PS1 prompt. (2) kubectl config current-context before DELETE. (3) Production cluster uses a DIFFERENT kubeconfig file entirely — export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/prod-config only when needed. (4) Enable kubectl delete dry-run: alias kdelete='echo "Are you sure? Use: kubectl delete --dry-run=client ... first"'.

8.2 Installing kubectl and Configuring kubeconfig

kubectl is the CLI for Kubernetes. Install via brew install kubectl (macOS), choco install kubernetes-cli (Windows), or apt install kubectl (Linux).

kubeconfig (~/.kube/config) stores cluster connection info, user credentials, and contexts. A context = cluster + user + namespace. Switch between clusters with kubectl config use-context cluster1.

💡 kubectl Plugins and Krew — Extend kubectl with Custom Commands

kubectl has a plugin system: any executable named kubectl-<name> on your PATH becomes a kubectl <name> command. Krew is the plugin manager (like brew for kubectl). Essential plugins for platform engineers:

  • kubectl ctx (kubectx): Interactive context switcher. kubectl ctx → pick from list. Safer than typing context names manually.
  • kubectl ns (kubens): Interactive namespace switcher. kubectl ns → pick namespace. Sets default namespace for current context.
  • kubectl neat: Removes clutter from kubectl get -o yaml output — strips status, managedFields, and default values. Clean YAML for documentation.
  • kubectl tree: Shows ownership hierarchy. kubectl tree deployment anihpj-web → Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods. Visualizes the ownership chain.

Install Krew: follow instructions at krew.sigs.k8s.io. Then: kubectl krew install ctx ns neat tree.

8.3 Managing Multiple Clusters and Contexts

Always verify your current context before destructive commands. kubectl config current-context tells you which cluster you're targeting. Use kubectx (interactive context switcher) for fast switching with visual feedback. The CNPE exam will give you specific contexts per task — using the wrong context = zero points.

⚠️ The CNPE Exam Context Trap — How to Avoid Zero-Point Tasks

Every CNPE exam task specifies a kubectl context. If you stay on the wrong cluster, you execute perfectly but get ZERO points. Before typing ANY command, run kubectl config current-context first. It takes 1 second and has saved thousands of candidates from failing. Add this to your .bashrc:

# Show current k8s context in your prompt
export PS1="[\u@\h \W \$(kubectl config current-context 2>/dev/null)]\$ "
# Prompt: [user@host ~ cluster1-admin@cluster1]$
💡 kubeconfig Deep Dive — clusters, users, contexts

~/.kube/config has 3 sections: clusters (API server URLs + CA certs), users (client certs + keys), and contexts (cluster + user + namespace combinations). A context is a pointer: it references a cluster and a user. current-context is the active one. Merge kubeconfigs with: KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config:~/.kube/config2 kubectl config view --flatten > merged. View with: kubectl config view.

📖 kubeconfig Troubleshooting — "The connection to the server localhost:8080 was refused"

This is the most common kubectl error for beginners. It means kubectl can't find a valid kubeconfig. Here's the debug flowchart:

  1. Does the file exist? ls -la ~/.kube/config. If not, you never ran kubeadm init or copied the admin.conf.
  2. Is KUBECONFIG env var set? echo $KUBECONFIG. If set, it OVERRIDES ~/.kube/config. Unset it or point it to the right file.
  3. Are the paths in the config valid? kubectl config view — check certificate-authority, client-certificate, client-key paths. They must be absolute paths or relative to ~/.kube/.
  4. Is the server reachable? curl -k https://SERVER_IP:6443/healthz. If not, VPN or firewall might be blocking.
  5. Is the certificate still valid? kubectl config view --raw -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.certificate-authority-data}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -dates — check notAfter. K8s CA certs expire after 10 years.

8.5 Step-by-Step Deployment — From Zero to anihpj Running

Follow these steps in order. Each step builds on the previous. If a step fails, fix it before continuing — don't skip ahead.

💡 Step 1: Create the Namespace
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label ns anihpj app.kubernetes.io/part-of=anihpj environment=staging

Namespaces isolate resources. Label it so tools like Argo CD and Prometheus understand who owns it.

💡 Step 2: Create ConfigMap and Secret
# ConfigMap: Non-sensitive app configuration
kubectl create configmap anihpj-config -n anihpj \
  --from-literal=DEBUG=false \
  --from-literal=DB_HOST=postgres \
  --from-literal=DB_NAME=anihpj \
  --from-literal=REDIS_HOST=redis

# Secret: Sensitive data (base64 encoded, enable encryption at rest!)
kubectl create secret generic anihpj-secret -n anihpj \
  --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=s3cret-password \
  --from-literal=SECRET_KEY=django-insecure-abc123 \
  --from-literal=REDIS_PASSWORD=redis-secret

These inject configuration WITHOUT hardcoding values in Deployment YAML. The Deployment references them by name via envFrom.

💡 Step 3: Deploy PostgreSQL (StatefulSet + Service)
kubectl apply -f k8s/base/03-postgres-statefulset.yaml -n anihpj
kubectl apply -f k8s/base/04-postgres-service.yaml -n anihpj

PostgreSQL runs as a StatefulSet — each replica has a stable identity (postgres-0, postgres-1) and persistent storage via PVC. The Service creates DNS: postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local. Wait for it to be ready: kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/postgres-0 -n anihpj --timeout=120s.

Why StatefulSet, not Deployment? Databases need stable network identities, ordered startup/shutdown, and persistent storage per replica. Stateless apps like web servers don't need this — they use Deployments.

💡 Step 4: Deploy Redis (Deployment + Service)
kubectl apply -f k8s/base/05-redis-deployment.yaml -n anihpj
kubectl apply -f k8s/base/06-redis-service.yaml -n anihpj

Redis is stateless cache — a Deployment is fine. In production, use Redis Sentinel or Cluster for HA. DNS: redis.anihpj.svc.cluster.local.

💡 Step 5: Deploy anihpj Web Application (Deployment + Service)
kubectl apply -f k8s/base/07-anihpj-web-deployment.yaml -n anihpj
kubectl apply -f k8s/base/08-anihpj-web-service.yaml -n anihpj

The web Deployment runs 3 replicas with 2 containers per pod (Nginx + Gunicorn/Django). The Service makes it reachable at anihpj-web.anihpj.svc.cluster.local:8000.

💡 Step 6: Deploy Ingress — Expose to the Outside World
kubectl apply -f k8s/base/11-ingress.yaml -n anihpj

The Ingress routes external HTTP(S) traffic to the anihpj-web Service based on hostname (Host: anihpj.com) and path (/jobs/, /api/). For local testing without a domain, use port-forward instead.

😰 Common Deployment Failures — What Goes Wrong and Why
  • 🔴 ImagePullBackOff: Wrong image name, private registry without ImagePullSecret, or Docker Hub rate limit. Fix: kubectl describe pod <name> -n anihpj | grep -A5 Events.
  • 🔴 CrashLoopBackOff: Application crashes on startup. Missing ConfigMap/Secret env vars, DB not reachable, or permissions issue. Fix: kubectl logs <pod> -n anihpj --previous to see the crash logs.
  • 🔴 Pending (forever): Scheduler can't find a node. Insufficient CPU/memory, node taints not tolerated, or PVC can't bind. Fix: kubectl describe pod <name> -n anihpj | grep -A10 Events.
  • 🔴 Service has no endpoints: Selector doesn't match any pod labels. Fix: kubectl get endpoints -n anihpj — if column is empty, selector is wrong.

8.6 Verifying Everything — The Platform Engineer's Checklist

Don't just assume everything works. Verify each component methodically. This checklist is what you'd run in a production deployment pipeline.

#CheckCommandExpected Result
1All pods Runningkubectl get pods -n anihpjSTATUS: Running, READY: 1/1 or 2/2
2No crash loopskubectl get pods -n anihpj | grep -v RunningNo output (all pods Running)
3Services have endpointskubectl get endpoints -n anihpjEach Service has IP:port pairs
4Logs show startup successkubectl logs -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --tail=10No ERROR/FATAL lines
5Web app respondskubectl port-forward svc/anihpj-web 8080:8000 -n anihpj &
curl http://localhost:8080/healthz		HTTP 200 OK
6DB connectivitykubectl exec -it deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj -- python manage.py check --database default"System check identified no issues"
7Redis connectivitykubectl exec -it deploy/redis -n anihpj -- redis-cli PINGPONG
8Resource usagekubectl top pods -n anihpjAll pods show CPU/Memory values
9ConfigMap mountedkubectl exec deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj -- env | grep DB_HOSTDB_HOST=postgres
10Persistent storagekubectl exec postgres-0 -n anihpj -- df -h /var/lib/postgresql/dataPVC shows mounted with size
💡 Verification One-Liner — Check Everything in One Command
# Quick health check for the entire anihpj namespace
echo "=== Pods ===" && kubectl get pods -n anihpj && \
echo "=== Services ===" && kubectl get svc -n anihpj && \
echo "=== Endpoints ===" && kubectl get endpoints -n anihpj && \
echo "=== ConfigMaps ===" && kubectl get configmaps -n anihpj && \
echo "=== Secrets ===" && kubectl get secrets -n anihpj && \
echo "=== PersistentVolumeClaims ===" && kubectl get pvc -n anihpj

Run this after every deployment. If anything looks wrong, use kubectl describe and kubectl logs to investigate. The CNPE exam expects you to debug — not just deploy and hope.

⚠️ If Something Fails — The Platform Engineer's Debugging Protocol

1. Events first: kubectl describe pod <name> -n anihpj | tail -20 — Events tell you EXACTLY what went wrong and when.

2. Logs second: kubectl logs <pod> -n anihpj --tail=50 — Application-level errors. --previous shows logs from the last crashed instance.

3. Exec third: kubectl exec -it <pod> -n anihpj -- /bin/bash — Enter the container and debug live (check files, run commands, test connectivity).

4. Check dependencies: Is the DB pod running? Can the web pod resolve postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local? Run kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj -- nslookup postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local.

5. Scale to zero and back: Sometimes restarting is the fastest fix: kubectl scale deployment anihpj-web --replicas=0 -n anihpj && kubectl scale deployment anihpj-web --replicas=3 -n anihpj.

YOUR 6-CLUSTER LOCAL LAB

  │                     YOUR 6-CLUSTER PLATFORM LAB                          │

🏋️ Chapter 8 — Hands-On Practice Drills (10 Exercises)

The CNPE is a performance-based exam — you solve tasks in a live Linux terminal. Practice these drills in your lab environment until you can complete each within the target time.

⏱️ Target: 10 minutes
Drill 8.1 — Set Up Your 6-Cluster Lab

Create all 6 clusters and verify they're accessible.

  1. Create cluster1 (kubeadm): follow kubeadm setup guide
  2. Create clusters 2-4 (kind): kind create cluster --name dev, etc.
  3. Create cluster5: minikube start
  4. Create cluster6: k3d cluster create security
  5. Verify all: kubectl config get-contexts
💡 Hint: Use kind create cluster for clusters 2-4. kubectl config get-contexts shows all.
📝 View Solution 
kind create cluster --name dev
kind create cluster --name staging
kind create cluster --name prod
minikube start
k3d cluster create security
kubectl config get-contexts
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 8.2 — Switch Contexts Safely

Practice context switching and always verify before executing.

  1. Switch to cluster1: kubectl config use-context cluster1
  2. Verify: kubectl config current-context
  3. Switch to cluster3 (kind-staging)
  4. List nodes to confirm you're on the right cluster
💡 Hint: kubectl config current-context before EVERY command is the habit that saves you on exam day.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl config use-context kind-dev
kubectl config current-context
kubectl get nodes  # Should show kind-dev nodes only
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 8.3 — Deploy Full anihpj Stack to Your Lab

Deploy the complete anihpj application to cluster1.

  1. Switch to cluster1 context
  2. Create namespace: kubectl create ns anihpj
  3. Apply all base manifests: kubectl apply -f k8s/base/ -n anihpj
  4. Wait for all pods: kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n anihpj --timeout=120s
💡 Hint: Apply base manifests in order (00- to 13-). Or use kubectl apply -f k8s/base/ --recursive.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl config use-context cluster1-admin@cluster1
kubectl create ns anihpj
kubectl apply -f k8s/base/ --recursive -n anihpj
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -w
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 8.4 — Debug Using Logs, Describe, and Exec

Use the debugging trifecta on a running pod.

  1. Describe a pod: kubectl describe pod <name> -n anihpj
  2. View logs: kubectl logs <name> -n anihpj --tail=20
  3. Exec into pod: kubectl exec -it <name> -n anihpj -- /bin/bash
  4. Check environment variables inside: env | grep DB_
💡 Hint: Describe = Events + State. Logs = stdout/stderr. Exec = interactive shell.
📝 View Solution 
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl describe pod $POD -n anihpj | tail -20
kubectl logs $POD -n anihpj --tail=20
kubectl exec -it $POD -n anihpj -- env | grep DB_
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 8.5 — Port-Forward and Access the App Locally

Access the anihpj web app from your browser via port-forward.

  1. Port-forward: kubectl port-forward svc/anihpj-web 8080:8000 -n anihpj
  2. Open browser: http://localhost:8080/jobs/
  3. Test API: curl http://localhost:8080/api/jobs/
  4. Test health: curl http://localhost:8080/healthz
💡 Hint: Port-forward runs in the foreground. Use & to background it, or open a second terminal.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl port-forward svc/anihpj-web 8080:8000 -n anihpj &
curl http://localhost:8080/healthz
curl http://localhost:8080/api/jobs/
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 8.6 — Merge Multiple kubeconfig Files

Platform engineers manage dozens of clusters. Merge their kubeconfigs into one file.

  1. Export kubeconfigs: copy each cluster's kubeconfig to /tmp/cluster1.yaml, /tmp/cluster2.yaml, etc.
  2. Merge them: KUBECONFIG=/tmp/cluster1.yaml:/tmp/cluster2.yaml:/tmp/cluster3.yaml kubectl config view --flatten > ~/.kube/merged-config
  3. Backup original: cp ~/.kube/config ~/.kube/config.bak
  4. Replace with merged: cp ~/.kube/merged-config ~/.kube/config
  5. Verify all contexts: kubectl config get-contexts — should show all 6 clusters
💡 Hint: KUBECONFIG env var accepts colon-separated paths. --flatten merges them into one file.
📝 View Solution 
KUBECONFIG=/tmp/cluster1.yaml:/tmp/cluster2.yaml:/tmp/cluster3.yaml \
  kubectl config view --flatten > ~/.kube/merged-config
cp ~/.kube/config ~/.kube/config.bak
cp ~/.kube/merged-config ~/.kube/config
kubectl config get-contexts
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 8.7 — Install and Use kubectl Plugins (krew, ctx, ns)

Install Krew and essential plugins to boost your kubectl productivity.

  1. Install Krew from krew.sigs.k8s.io
  2. Install plugins: kubectl krew install ctx ns neat tree
  3. Switch context: kubectl ctx and pick from interactive list
  4. Switch namespace: kubectl ns and pick from list
  5. Clean YAML: kubectl neat pod anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj — removes status noise
💡 Hint: kubectl ctx is safer than kubectl config use-context — visual feedback prevents mistakes.
📝 View Solution 
# Install Krew (follow instructions at krew.sigs.k8s.io)
kubectl krew install ctx ns neat tree
kubectl ctx  # Interactive: select cluster
kubectl ns   # Interactive: select namespace
kubectl neat pod $(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o name | head -1) | head -20
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 8.8 — Deploy anihpj to 3 Clusters (Dev, Staging, Prod)

Apply the full anihpj stack to 3 different kind clusters.

  1. Switch to kind-dev: kubectl ctx kind-dev
  2. Deploy anihpj: kubectl apply -f k8s/overlays/dev/ -n anihpj
  3. Switch to kind-staging, deploy with k8s/overlays/staging/
  4. Switch to kind-prod, deploy with k8s/overlays/production/
  5. Verify each: kubectl get pods -n anihpj on each cluster
💡 Hint: Each overlay has different replica counts, resource limits, and DB configurations.
📝 View Solution 
# Dev
kubectl ctx kind-dev
kubectl apply -f k8s/overlays/dev/ -n anihpj

# Staging
kubectl ctx kind-staging
kubectl apply -f k8s/overlays/staging/ -n anihpj

# Production
kubectl ctx kind-prod
kubectl apply -f k8s/overlays/production/ -n anihpj

# Verify all

  kubectl ctx $ctx && kubectl get pods -n anihpj
done
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 8.9 — Delete a Cluster Completely and Recreate It

Practice fast cluster creation and deletion — a critical exam skill.

  1. Delete a kind cluster: kind delete cluster --name dev
  2. Verify it's gone: kubectl config get-contexts | grep dev
  3. Recreate: kind create cluster --name dev
  4. Re-deploy anihpj: apply base manifests
  5. Verify everything works: check pods, services, endpoints
💡 Hint: kind delete cluster is instant. Recreate takes ~30 seconds. Perfect for exam practice.
📝 View Solution 
kind delete cluster --name dev
kind create cluster --name dev
kubectl ctx kind-dev
kubectl apply -f k8s/base/ -n anihpj --recursive
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -w  # Watch pods start
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 8.10 — Troubleshoot a Broken Deployment (Simulated Failure)

Someone deployed anihpj with a wrong DB password. Debug and fix it.

  1. Create a Secret with wrong password: kubectl create secret generic anihpj-secret --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=wrongpass -n anihpj
  2. Deploy anihpj — web pods will crash (CrashLoopBackOff) because they can't connect to DB
  3. Debug: kubectl logs <web-pod> -n anihpj --previous — see "password authentication failed"
  4. Fix the Secret: kubectl create secret generic anihpj-secret --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=correctpass -n anihpj --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl replace -f -
  5. Restart Deployment: kubectl rollout restart deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj
  6. Verify recovery: pods should now be Running
💡 Hint: --previous shows logs from the crashed instance. rollout restart creates new pods with updated Secret.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl create secret generic anihpj-secret --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=wrongpass -n anihpj
kubectl apply -f k8s/base/ -n anihpj
# Wait for CrashLoopBackOff
kubectl logs $(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) -n anihpj --previous
# Fix: replace secret, restart
kubectl create secret generic anihpj-secret --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=correctpass -n anihpj \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl replace -f -
kubectl rollout restart deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -w  # Watch recovery

8.7 Day 2 Operations — Maintaining Your Lab Environment

Setting up a lab is easy. Keeping it running, clean, and useful for weeks of study is the real challenge. Here's your maintenance playbook.

💡 Daily Startup Script — Get All 6 Clusters Ready in One Command
#!/bin/bash
# lab-start.sh — Start all 6 clusters and verify
set -e

echo "=== Starting Lab Clusters ==="

# kind clusters (if Docker is running, they auto-start)
for cluster in dev staging prod; do
  if kind get clusters | grep -q "^$cluster$"; then
    echo "kind-$cluster: already exists"
  else
    kind create cluster --name $cluster
  fi
done

# minikube
minikube status &>/dev/null || minikube start

# k3d
k3d cluster list | grep -q security || k3d cluster create security

echo ""
echo "=== Current Contexts ==="
kubectl config get-contexts
echo ""
echo "⚠️  Current: $(kubectl config current-context)"
echo "✅ Lab ready!"
📖 Lab Resource Management — Don't Let Docker Eat Your Laptop

6 clusters = a LOT of containers. Here's how to manage resources:

  • Stop clusters you're not using: kind delete cluster --name dev and recreate later. Takes 30 seconds to restore.
  • Pause Docker: docker pause $(docker ps -q) freezes all containers. docker unpause $(docker ps -aq) to resume. CPU drops to zero while paused.
  • Monitor usage: docker stats --no-stream shows per-container CPU/memory. docker system df shows disk usage.
  • Clean up weekly: docker system prune -a -f --volumes. Removes unused images, containers, volumes. Frees GB of space.
  • Minimum lab: If resources are tight, run just 3 kind clusters + 1 k3d. That's ~2GB RAM vs ~6GB for all 6.
⚠️ Lab Backup Strategy — Protect Your Work

You'll invest dozens of hours in your lab. Don't lose your work:

  • Backup kubeconfig: cp ~/.kube/config ~/.kube/config.backup.$(date +%Y%m%d) — weekly. This is small but irreplaceable.
  • Backup your manifests: All anihpj YAML files should be in Git. git push daily. The lab is disposable; your code is not.
  • Backup etcd (kubeadm cluster): ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd-$(date +%Y%m%d).db — weekly. Test the restore: restore to a NEW data-dir and verify.
  • Disaster recovery test (monthly): Delete all kind clusters. Recreate from scratch. Re-deploy anihpj from Git. Time how long it takes. Target: under 15 minutes.

📖 Chapter 8 Summary: Your 6-cluster lab is the foundation for all hands-on practice. Cluster1 (kubeadm) for production-like scenarios, clusters 2-4 (kind) for GitOps multi-cluster workflows, cluster5 (minikube) for quick testing, and cluster6 (k3d) for security experiments. Master kubectl context switching — it's the skill that saves you from catastrophic mistakes on the CNPE exam.

Why Chapter 9 Matters on the CNPE Exam

The CNPE exam tests architecture decisions as applied knowledge — not multiple choice. You'll be given a scenario ("10 teams, PCI-DSS, growing to 50") and must justify your architecture. Your answer must cover: cluster count, isolation model, cloud provider choice, and namespace-as-a-service workflow. Every Domain 1 task expects you to EXPLAIN your decision, not just state it.

9.1 What Is Platform Architecture? — The Blueprint for Your IDP

Platform architecture is HOW you structure your clusters, networks, storage, and compute to support multiple teams and applications. It's the set of decisions that determine:

  • How many clusters? One big cluster shared by everyone, or many small clusters per team/environment?
  • How to isolate tenants? Namespaces (soft isolation) or virtual clusters (hard isolation)?
  • Cloud or on-prem? Managed K8s (EKS/AKS/GKE) or self-managed (kubeadm, Rancher)?
  • How do teams get resources? Ticket-based (manual ops) or self-service (namespace-as-a-service)?

😰 The Accidental Monolith — A Real Architecture Horror Story
  • 🔴 Year 1: Startup with 1 team, 1 cluster. "We'll add clusters later if we grow." Simple, works great.
  • 🔴 Year 2: 4 teams, still 1 cluster. Team A deploys a memory-hungry ML model → OOM kills Team B's production pods. First production outage.
  • 🔴 Year 3: 12 teams, still 1 cluster. PCI-DSS audit: "Your payment service shares a cluster with non-payment workloads. FAIL." Architecture rewrite takes 6 months and $500K.
  • 🟡 Lesson: Architecture decisions compound. What works for 1 team does NOT work for 12. Plan for growth from Day 1 — even if you start simple.

9.2 Cloud Native Design Principles — 12-Factor, Declarative, Immutable

Every platform architecture decision should align with cloud native principles. These aren't just buzzwords — they're battle-tested patterns that prevent the "it works on my machine" problem at platform scale.

📋
12-Factor App

Codebase (one repo per app), Dependencies (explicit, isolated), Config (in environment, not code), Backing Services (attached resources), Build/Release/Run (strict separation), Processes (stateless), Port Binding (self-contained), Concurrency (scale horizontally), Disposability (fast startup, graceful shutdown), Dev/Prod Parity (keep environments similar), Logs (event streams), Admin (one-off processes).

📝
Declarative

You declare DESIRED state ("I want 3 replicas of anihpj-web"), Kubernetes makes it ACTUAL state. You never say "create pod X on node Y." The platform figures out how. This is why GitOps works: Git holds desired state, the controller reconciles.

🧱
Immutable Infrastructure

Never modify running infrastructure. Don't SSH into a pod to "quickly fix something." Don't patch a running VM. Always: build new image → deploy new pod → destroy old. This guarantees reproducibility and eliminates configuration drift.

💡 How anihpj Embodies These Principles
  • 12-Factor: Config via ConfigMap/Secret (not hardcoded). Django reads os.environ['DB_HOST']. Logs go to stdout (not files inside container).
  • Declarative: All anihpj resources are YAML manifests in Git. Argo CD syncs them. No manual kubectl commands in production.
  • Immutable: New release = new Docker image tag (anihpj:v1.2.3). Old pods are replaced, never patched. kubectl rollout restart creates new pods.
  • Disposability: anihpj pods start in <5 seconds (Django + Gunicorn). Graceful shutdown catches SIGTERM, finishes in-flight requests, exits cleanly.

9.3 Single-Cluster vs Multi-Cluster Topologies

This is THE most consequential architecture decision you'll make. Let's compare them thoroughly.

  │                                                                         │
  │  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐                   │
  │  │ CLUSTER: DEV │  │ CLUSTER: STG │  │ CLUSTER: PROD │                   │
  │  │              │  │              │  │              │                    │
  │  │ NS: team-a   │  │ NS: team-a   │  │ NS: team-a   │                   │
  │  │ NS: team-b   │  │ NS: team-b   │  │ NS: team-b   │                   │

  │                                                                         │
  │  ✅ Dev cluster upgrade → prod unaffected                               │
  │  ✅ Blast radius limited: dev failure never touches prod                │
  │  ✅ Production gets dedicated nodes, higher specs                       │
  │  ⚠️ More clusters = more operational overhead (but tools like Argo CD   │
  │     make multi-cluster manageable)                                      │
  │                                                                         │
  │  Best for: 5+ teams, compliance, production isolation                   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
FactorSingle ClusterMulti-Cluster
Operational OverheadLow — one cluster to manage, upgrade, monitorHigher — N clusters × upgrades, monitoring, backup
Blast Radius🔴 One mistake affects EVERYONE🟢 Failure isolated to one cluster
CostLower — shared control plane, shared nodesHigher — separate control planes, separate nodes
IsolationSoft (Namespaces, RBAC, NetworkPolicies)Hard (separate kernel, separate etcd)
Upgrade Safety🔴 All-or-nothing upgrade. If kube-apiserver v1.30 breaks something, ALL teams affected.🟢 Canary upgrade: upgrade dev cluster first, observe for 1 week, then staging, then prod.
Compliance (PCI, HIPAA)🔴 Difficult — entire cluster in scope🟢 Dedicated compliant cluster, other clusters out of scope
Resource Sharing✅ Easy — teams share idle capacity❌ Harder — capacity per cluster, potential waste
anihpj Use CaseDev + Staging on one clusterProduction on dedicated cluster
🎉 anihpj Multi-Cluster Strategy — The Hybrid Approach
  • ✅ Cluster 1 (kind-dev): Development — all teams share one cluster. Fast iteration, low cost, blast radius acceptable (dev data is synthetic).
  • ✅ Cluster 2 (kind-staging): Staging — shared cluster with production-like NetworkPolicies and resource quotas. Catches config issues before prod.
  • ✅ Cluster 3 (kind-prod): Production — DEDICATED cluster. Separate nodes, strict NetworkPolicies, Velero backups, PDBs on every workload. No non-production workload touches this cluster EVER.
  • ✅ Why not 1 cluster? Production needs guaranteed resources and zero blast radius from dev experiments. A dev team testing a new operator should NEVER risk production stability.

9.4 Multi-Tenancy Patterns — Soft (Namespaces) vs Hard (vClusters/Kamaji)

Multi-tenancy answers: "How do we let multiple teams share infrastructure safely?" There are two fundamental approaches:

DimensionSOFT Multi-Tenancy (Namespaces)HARD Multi-Tenancy (vClusters)
Isolation LevelNamespace boundary: RBAC, NetworkPolicy, ResourceQuota, LimitRangeFull API server isolation: each tenant gets their own control plane (virtual K8s API server)
What's SharedAPI server, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager, nodes, kernelPhysical nodes and kernel only. Each tenant has OWN API server, OWN etcd (logical), OWN scheduler
CRD Isolation❌ CRDs are CLUSTER-scoped. Tenant A's CRD can conflict with Tenant B's.✅ Each vCluster has its own CRDs. No conflicts possible.
API Server Noisy Neighbor🔴 One tenant with 10,000 watches can degrade API server for ALL tenants🟢 Each tenant hits their OWN API server. No cross-tenant impact.
K8s Version per Tenant❌ All tenants share same K8s version (cluster-wide upgrade)✅ Each vCluster can run a DIFFERENT K8s version (e.g., Tenant A on 1.29, Tenant B on 1.30)
RBAC ModelClusterRoles + RoleBindings scoped to namespaces. Cluster-admin = root on everything.Each tenant gets cluster-admin on THEIR vCluster. Can't affect other tenants.
CostLower — share control plane resourcesHigher — each vCluster runs an API server (syncer process), ~50MB RAM per tenant
Best ForTrusted teams within same organization. 5-50 tenants.Untrusted tenants (SaaS), strict compliance, 50+ tenants needing CRDs, different K8s versions
💡 vCluster — Virtual K8s Inside Real K8s

vCluster (by Loft Labs) creates a fully functional virtual Kubernetes cluster INSIDE a host namespace. The tenant sees a real API server, can install CRDs, create ClusterRoles — all without touching the host cluster. Under the hood, vCluster runs a syncer that maps virtual resources to physical resources in the host namespace.

# Create a vCluster for Team Payments (PCI-DSS isolation)
vcluster create payments-vcluster --namespace payments --expose
# Tenant connects to THEIR virtual cluster:
vcluster connect payments-vcluster --namespace payments
# From the tenant's perspective: they have cluster-admin on their own cluster.
# From the host cluster perspective: it's just pods in the "payments" namespace.
🎉 anihpj Multi-Tenancy Strategy — Layered Isolation
  • ✅ Trusted internal teams (search, analytics): SOFT — Namespaces with ResourceQuota, NetworkPolicy, RBAC. Simple, fast, low overhead.
  • ✅ Payment processing (PCI-DSS): HARD — vCluster in dedicated namespace. Separate API server, strict NetworkPolicy (only egress to payment gateway IPs), audit logging enabled.
  • ✅ External contractor team: HARD — vCluster. They get cluster-admin on THEIR cluster but can't touch anything else. Revoke access = delete vCluster.
  • ✅ Platform team: Hard isolation via their OWN dedicated management cluster (kubeadm cluster). NO shared infrastructure with tenant workloads.

9.5 Namespace-as-a-Service — Self-Service Provisioning

The platform engineering dream: a developer clicks a button (or runs a CLI command) and gets a fully configured namespace with quotas, RBAC, NetworkPolicies, and monitoring — in 30 seconds. No ticket. No waiting. No platform engineer involved.
