📖 What Gets Auto-Provisioned Per Namespace

Every namespace request triggers creation of these 7 resources:

  1. Namespace: team-a-dev — labeled with team, environment, cost-center
  2. ResourceQuota: Max 10 pods, 4 CPU, 8GB RAM — prevents resource hogging
  3. LimitRange: Default CPU request 250m, limit 500m — every pod gets sensible defaults
  4. RBAC: RoleBinding to team's AD/OIDC group with edit access to their namespace only
  5. NetworkPolicy: Default-deny all ingress. Allow-list for cluster monitoring. Teams open what they need.
  6. ServiceAccount: team-a-sa — for their workloads, scoped to this namespace
  7. ServiceMonitor: Prometheus auto-discovers their services for scraping

9.6 Cloud Provider Integration — EKS vs AKS vs GKE vs Self-Managed

Which Kubernetes distribution should your platform run on? This decision impacts cost, operational overhead, upgrade strategy, and available features.

DimensionAWS EKSAzure AKSGCP GKESelf-Managed (kubeadm)
Control Plane Cost$0.10/hr (~$73/mo)FREE (you pay for worker nodes only)FREE for 1 zonal clusterInfrastructure cost only (VMs)
Control Plane SLA99.95%99.95% (with uptime SLA)99.5% (zonal) / 99.95% (regional)Your responsibility — whatever YOU build
Upgrade ProcessConsole/CLI: eksctl upgrade cluster. One minor version at a time.Console/CLI: az aks upgrade. Can skip minor versions.Auto-upgrade channel (opt-in). Regular/Stable/Rapid channels.Manual: kubeadm upgrade plan → kubeadm upgrade apply. Full control.
etcd BackupAWS manages etcd. No direct access. No snapshot capability.Azure manages etcd. No direct access.Automatic backups. Can restore to specific timestamp.FULL control — you manage etcd directly. Full snapshot/restore capability.
Add-on IntegrationDeep integration: IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA), AWS Load Balancer Controller, EBS/EFS CSIEntra ID (AAD) Pod Identity, Azure CNI (VNet integration), Azure Disk/File CSIWorkload Identity (IAM), GCP LB, persistent disk CSI, Cloud SQL proxyNONE — you install and configure everything (cert-manager, external-dns, ingress, CSI)
Node AutoscalingKarpenter (native), Cluster AutoscalerCluster Autoscaler (built-in)Cluster Autoscaler (built-in), Node Auto-ProvisioningKarpenter (self-install), Cluster Autoscaler (self-install)
Security PatchingAWS patches control plane. You patch worker nodes.Azure patches control plane. You patch worker nodes.Auto-upgrade channel patches BOTH control plane AND nodes (opt-in)YOU patch everything. CVE-2024-??? at 3AM = your problem.
Multi-Cloud❌ AWS-only❌ Azure-only❌ GCP-only✅ Run anywhere — same kubeadm on AWS, Azure, on-prem
Best For anihpjIf you're on AWS and want deep integrationIf you're on Azure with Microsoft ecosystemIf you want the most mature managed K8s with least opsIf you need multi-cloud portability or on-prem capability
⚠️ The Managed K8s Trade-Off You Never Think About Until It's Too Late

You CANNOT access etcd on EKS, AKS, or GKE. This means:

  • No etcdctl snapshot save — you can't take custom etcd backups
  • No etcdctl compact / etcdctl defrag — hope the cloud provider does it for you
  • Custom etcd configuration (e.g., changing snapshot frequency) — IMPOSSIBLE
  • For the CNPE exam, you PRACTICE etcd backup/restore on kubeadm. On managed K8s, you only practice what the cloud provider allows.

That's why our 6-cluster lab includes kubeadm — so you can actually touch etcd. Managed K8s abstracts it away, which is great for production but terrible for learning.

9.7 On-Prem vs Cloud vs Hybrid — Making the Case

FactorOn-PremisesCloud (Managed K8s)Hybrid
Latency✅ Sub-millisecond to local services⚠️ 1-50ms to cloud services, cross-AZ latencyCritical workloads on-prem, elastic workloads cloud
Compliance✅ Full physical control. Air-gapped possible.⚠️ Shared responsibility. Data in cloud provider's hands.✅ Sensitive data on-prem, everything else in cloud
Cost ModelCAPEX (buy hardware) + OPEX (maintain)OPEX only (pay per use) — predictable monthlyBaseline on-prem (CAPEX), burst to cloud (OPEX)
Elasticity❌ Weeks to add capacity (order hardware)✅ Minutes to add nodes (auto-scale)✅ Burst to cloud when on-prem runs out
Operational Overhead🔴 Your team manages hardware, hypervisors, networking, K8s, everything🟢 Cloud manages hardware, hypervisors, control plane. You manage workers + workloads.🟡 Both: manage on-prem infra + manage cloud infra
Best ForBanks, government, defense, manufacturing (air-gapped), stable workloadsSaaS, startups, e-commerce, variable workloads, most companiesEnterprises with existing data centers, regulated industries, latency-sensitive apps
💼 The Bank Scenario — When On-Prem Wins
  • 🏦 A regulated bank processes 100,000 transactions/second. Latency above 1ms costs millions in lost trades. Cloud cross-AZ latency is 1-2ms — unacceptable.
  • 🏦 PCI-DSS and local banking regulations require PHYSICAL control of servers. The bank's auditors won't accept "shared responsibility" — everything must be auditable on-prem.
  • 🏦 The bank already owns 3 data centers ($200M invested). Moving to cloud would waste that investment AND increase latency.
  • ✅ Decision: On-prem Kubernetes (kubeadm + Rancher) for trading platform. Cloud (AWS) for customer-facing mobile app and AI/ML training (spot instances). Hybrid architecture.

🧠 Deep Dive — Platform Architecture Core Concepts

📖 The Platform Architecture Maturity Model — How Platforms Evolve Over 5 Years

Platforms don't start complex. They EVOLVE through stages. Understanding this progression prevents over-engineering early and under-engineering late:

StageTeam SizeArchitectureKey ChallengeTypical Mistake
1. Organic
(Year 0-1)		1-3 teamsSingle cluster, no isolation. Dev=Prod parity is aspirational.Getting anything working at allThinking "we'll add structure later" — without labeling conventions, namespaces, or quotas, the cluster becomes unmappable
2. Structured
(Year 1-2)		3-10 teamsNamespaces with ResourceQuotas. RBAC per team. Separate dev/prod clusters.Noisy neighbors, RBAC complexityUnder-investing in self-service — platform team becomes a ticket bottleneck
3. Scaled
(Year 2-4)		10-50 teamsMulti-cluster per environment. vClusters for untrusted tenants. Namespace-as-a-service portal.Multi-cluster management, cost allocationNot investing in GitOps tooling — manual deployments become unsustainable at this scale
4. Optimized
(Year 4-5+)		50+ teamsPlatform as a Product. Golden paths. Developer portal (Backstage). FinOps integrated.Platform team culture, DevEx measurementBuilding features nobody asked for — platform team must act as product managers, not just engineers

Where anihpj fits: Stage 2 (Structured). We have separate dev/staging/prod clusters, namespace isolation, and are building toward namespace-as-a-service. The key is knowing Stage 3 patterns exist — so our architecture can evolve without a rewrite.

📖 Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) — Why You Need Them

Six months from now, someone will ask: "Why did we choose 3 clusters instead of 1?" Without an ADR, the answer is lost — the original architect left, and nobody remembers the reasoning. ADRs document the CONTEXT, DECISION, and CONSEQUENCES of every architecture choice:

# ADR-003: Multi-Cluster Topology for anihpj
## Context
anihpj serves 3 environments (dev, staging, prod) with PCI-DSS
requirements for payments processing. Team size growing from 3→10.

## Decision
We will use 3 separate K8s clusters (dev, staging, prod) with:
- Dev: Shared, soft isolation (namespaces), Flannel CNI
- Staging: Shared, soft isolation with production-like policies, Calico CNI
- Prod: Dedicated, hard isolation for payments, Cilium CNI

## Alternatives Considered
1. Single cluster with namespaces: Rejected — PCI-DSS scoping
   would put entire cluster in audit scope.
2. 5 clusters (per-team): Rejected — operational overhead
   outweighs isolation benefits at current team count.

## Consequences
- Positive: Clear blast radius boundaries, canary upgrades
- Negative: ~$220/mo additional (2 extra control planes)
- Neutral: Operations team needs multi-cluster tooling (Argo CD)

ADRs are lightweight — one markdown file per decision, stored in the same repo as your infrastructure code. Argo CD can even display them. The CNPE exam values architectural JUSTIFICATION, not just architectural CHOICES.

🎉 Team Topologies — How to Structure Your Platform Team
  • ✅ Stream-Aligned Teams: Each responsible for a business domain (payments, search, analytics). They own their services end-to-end. The platform serves THEM.
  • ✅ Platform Team: Builds and maintains the IDP. Their customers are the stream-aligned teams. They measure success by DevEx metrics (time-to-deploy, developer satisfaction).
  • ✅ Enabling Team: Helps stream-aligned teams adopt the platform. They write documentation, run workshops, and pair-program with application developers during onboarding.
  • ✅ Complicated Subsystem Team: Owns deeply specialized subsystems (e.g., the PCI-DSS compliant payments infrastructure). Few people can maintain it — dedicate a team to it.
  • ✅ The Anti-Pattern: A "DevOps Team" that all requests flow through. This is NOT platform engineering — it's a rebranded operations team. The platform should enable self-service, not create a new bottleneck.
⚠️ The Most Common Platform Architecture Mistake — and How to Avoid It

The mistake: Building a "perfect" platform before anyone uses it. The platform team spends 6 months building an IDP with Backstage, Argo CD, crossplane, service mesh, and developer portal — then discovers that developers don't want any of it. They wanted faster deployments, not a new UI to learn.

The fix — "Thinnest Viable Platform" (TVP): Start with the MINIMUM that solves the biggest pain point. If deployments take 3 days, start with Argo CD and a Git repo. If developers wait a week for a database, start with Crossplane database provisioning. Ship something in 2 weeks. Get feedback. Iterate. A platform nobody uses is not a platform — it's a hobby project.

The CNPE is a performance-based exam. Practice these drills until you can answer each within the target time.

Drill 9.1 — Design Cluster Topology for 3 Teams

Your company has 3 teams (payments, search, analytics). Payments needs PCI-DSS compliance. Design the cluster topology.

  1. Decide: single or multi-cluster? Justify your choice.
  2. Draw the topology on paper — how many clusters, what runs where
  3. For each cluster, list: who uses it, what isolation level, what special config
💡 Hint: PCI-DSS changes everything. Compliance boundaries are your primary design constraint.
📝 View Solution 
Two clusters:
Cluster A (Compliant): Payments only — dedicated nodes, vClusters,
  audit logging, encryption at rest, strict NetworkPolicies
Cluster B (General): Search + Analytics — namespaces with quotas,
  shared resources, standard security

Why not one cluster? PCI-DSS scoping: if payments shares ANY infra with
non-payment workloads, ALL of it is in scope for audit. $500K audit vs $50K.
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 9.2 — Compare Soft vs Hard Multi-Tenancy for 50 Teams

Your platform scales to 50 teams. Some are internal, some are external contractors. Compare approaches.

  1. List 3 scenarios where soft tenancy FAILS at this scale
  2. List 3 benefits of hard tenancy (vClusters) at this scale
  3. Recommend a hybrid approach with specific team placement
💡 Hint: CRD conflicts, API server load, K8s version fragmentation — all real at 50 teams.
📝 View Solution 
Soft fails: (1) 2 teams install conflicting CRDs (gateway-api versions),
(2) One team's 10k watch connections degrade API server for all 49 others,
(3) Cluster-admin risk — anyone with it sees all 50 teams' data.

Hard benefits: (1) Each team gets own CRDs, (2) API server isolation,
(3) Contractors get cluster-admin on THEIR cluster only.

Hybrid: Internal teams → namespaces (soft, low overhead).
External contractors + special compliance teams → vClusters (hard).
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 9.3 — EKS vs Self-Managed kubeadm on EC2

Compare EKS (managed control plane) vs running kubeadm on EC2 instances. Use 5 dimensions.

  1. Compare: cost, operational overhead, etcd access, upgrade process, multi-cloud portability
  2. You need etcd backup. Which option gives you etcdctl snapshot save?
  3. You might move to Azure next year. Which option is better?
💡 Hint: EKS charges for control plane ($73/mo). EC2 VMs for control plane cost similar but require management.
📝 View Solution 
EKS: Easier ops, no etcd access, AWS-only, $73/mo control plane, AWS patches.
kubeadm on EC2: Full etcd access, multi-cloud portable, YOU manage everything,
  similar cost (3 small VMs), full control over versions and patches.

For etcd snapshot: kubeadm ONLY. EKS doesn't expose etcd.
For multi-cloud: kubeadm. EKS locks you into AWS.
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 9.4 — Design Namespace-as-a-Service for anihpj

Design the auto-provisioning workflow that creates a fully configured namespace when a developer requests one.

  1. List all 7 resources that get auto-created
  2. Draw the flow: developer request → portal → Git → Argo CD → cluster
  3. What happens if the developer requests more CPU than their team's quota?
💡 Hint: The 7 resources are: Namespace, ResourceQuota, LimitRange, RoleBinding, NetworkPolicy, ServiceAccount, ServiceMonitor.
📝 View Solution 
Developer fills form: team=search, env=dev, cpu=4, mem=8Gi
→ Portal validates: team exists? quota within org limits?
→ Commits to Git: teams/search/dev/namespace.yaml + quota.yaml + rbac.yaml + netpol.yaml
→ Argo CD detects Git change → syncs to cluster
→ 30 seconds later: `kubectl get ns search-dev` → Active

Quota exceeded? Portal rejects request BEFORE committing to Git.
Shows: "Requested 16 CPU but team 'search' has 8 CPU remaining. Contact platform team."
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 9.5 — Prevent a Noisy Neighbor on Shared Cluster

Team A deploys a memory-hungry ML training job. It consumes all available RAM on shared nodes. Team B's production pods get OOM-killed. Fix it.

  1. What should have been configured to prevent this?
  2. List 3 specific Kubernetes resources that enforce limits
  3. How do you prevent CPU hogs (not just memory)?
💡 Hint: ResourceQuota at namespace level. LimitRange for defaults. QoS for OOM priority.
📝 View Solution 
Prevention: ResourceQuota limits TOTAL per namespace:
  requests.memory: 16Gi → Team A can't exceed 16GB total
LimitRange: DEFAULT requests/limits for any pod without them:
  defaultRequest.memory: 256Mi, default.memory: 512Mi
QoS: BestEffort pods OOM-killed first. Guaranteed pods survive.

CPU: limitRange sets default CPU limits. K8s THROTTLES CPU (not kill),
so Team A's ML job slows down but doesn't crash other pods.
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 9.6 — "One Cluster to Rule Them All" Debate

Your CTO says "One cluster to rule them all." Argue for AND against with 3 points each.

  1. Write 3 arguments FOR a single cluster
  2. Write 3 arguments AGAINST it
  3. Your final recommendation with specific guardrails
💡 Hint: For: cost, simplicity, resource sharing. Against: blast radius, compliance, upgrade risk.
📝 View Solution 
FOR: (1) Lower cost (one control plane), (2) Simpler to manage (one upgrade, one monitoring stack), (3) Better resource utilization (idle dev capacity used by staging).

AGAINST: (1) Single blast radius — control plane failure = everyone down, (2) PCI/hipaa scoping — entire cluster in audit scope, (3) No canary upgrades — K8s 1.30 bug hits everyone at once.

Recommendation: Single cluster ONLY with: strict ResourceQuotas, NetworkPolicies, PodSecurityStandards (restricted), and no compliance workloads. Add a second cluster for production when you hit 10+ teams.
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 9.7 — vCluster Isolation Analysis

vCluster creates virtual K8s clusters inside a host namespace. What isolation does it provide vs plain namespaces?

  1. What gets isolated WITH vCluster that doesn't with namespaces?
  2. What is still SHARED?
  3. When would you use vCluster instead of a separate physical cluster?
💡 Hint: vCluster isolates API server, CRDs, RBAC. Still shares nodes, kernel, CNI.
📝 View Solution 
Isolated: API server, CRDs, ClusterRoles, ClusterRoleBindings,
  admission webhooks, API priority & fairness, separate K8s version.

Shared: Physical nodes (kernel), CNI network, host filesystem,
  container runtime. A kernel panic affects ALL vClusters.

Use vCluster when: you need CRD isolation, different K8s versions,
  cluster-admin per tenant, but don't need physical isolation.
Use physical cluster when: you need kernel isolation, dedicated hardware,
  different CNI/network per tenant, air-gap requirements.

Design the network architecture for a multi-tenant platform with 20 teams. Each team needs to reach external APIs and specific internal services.

  1. What CNI plugin do you choose and why?
  2. Draw the NetworkPolicy structure: what's allowed by default? Blocked?

Default policies per namespace:
- Ingress: DENY all (teams explicitly allow their service ports)
- Egress: ALLOW DNS (53/udp to CoreDNS), DENY all else
- Teams add egress rules for their external dependencies

Stripe access:

A bank processes real-time trades. Latency above 1ms = lost money. PCI-DSS compliance required. Make the case for on-prem vs cloud.

  1. List 3 arguments for on-prem
  2. List 2 arguments where cloud could still help
  3. Recommend a hybrid architecture
💡 Hint: On-prem = latency + compliance. Cloud = elasticity + managed services (AI/ML, analytics).
📝 View Solution 
On-prem: (1) Sub-ms latency to trading systems — cloud cross-AZ adds 1-2ms,
(2) PHYSICAL control required by banking regulations and auditors,
(3) Existing $200M data center investment — moving is wasteful.

Cloud value: (1) ML training for fraud detection on spot instances (90% cheaper),
(2) Customer-facing mobile app with global CDN (CloudFront) for low latency worldwide.

Drill 9.10 — anihpj Multi-Environment Architecture

anihpj needs dev/staging/production environments. Design a multi-cluster topology and justify each cluster's purpose.

  1. How many clusters? Name them and assign purpose.
  2. What's different about each cluster's configuration?
  3. How does code flow from dev → staging → production?
💡 Hint: 3 kind clusters (dev, staging, prod). Each has different: replica counts, resource limits, monitoring strictness, NetworkPolicy strictness.
📝 View Solution 
kind-dev: 1 replica, BestEffort QoS, no PDBs, Flannel CNI (simple),

📖 Chapter 9 Summary: Architecture decisions compound. A well-designed multi-tenant platform with clear isolation boundaries (vClusters for untrusted, namespaces for trusted teams) scales to hundreds of developers. The single-cluster vs multi-cluster decision should be driven by compliance, blast radius, and team count — not by what's easiest today. Namespace-as-a-service turns platform engineering from a ticket-driven bottleneck into a self-service force multiplier. Cloud provider choice should be based on operational overhead tolerance and multi-cloud needs.

Chapter 10: Networking Architecture for Platforms

K8s networking model, CNI plugins, Services, Ingress, Gateway API, Service Mesh, mTLS, and NetworkPolicies — the circulatory system of your platform.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~3 hours🌐 Net

📖 Chapter Overview: Every packet in your platform travels through the networking layer. A misconfigured NetworkPolicy can expose your database to the internet. A wrong CNI choice can limit you to 5,000 services. A missing mTLS setup means internal traffic is plaintext. This chapter covers every networking decision a platform engineer makes — from CNI plugin selection to zero-trust NetworkPolicy design.

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand the K8s networking model: every pod gets a unique IP, all pods communicate without NAT
  • ✅ Choose the right CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium, Flannel, Weave) based on scale, security, and features
  • ✅ Design Service architectures (ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, ExternalName)
  • ✅ Configure Ingress controllers and understand when to use Gateway API instead
  • ✅ Implement zero-trust networking with NetworkPolicies (default-deny + allow-lists)
🎓 CNPE Relevance
Platform Architecture Domain 1 — 15% Networking Design CNI + Services + Mesh

10.1 Kubernetes Networking Model — The 4 Fundamental Rules

Kubernetes imposes a strict networking model that EVERY CNI plugin must implement:

1️⃣
Unique IP per Pod

Every pod gets its own IP address. Containers within a pod share this IP (localhost communication). No port conflicts between pods — each has its own network namespace.

2️⃣
No NAT for Pod-to-Pod

Pods communicate with each other using their real IPs. No network address translation between pods. Pod A (10.0.1.5) talks directly to Pod B (10.0.2.8) — the CNI handles routing.

3️⃣
Node-Pod Parity

Nodes and pods share the same network space. A node can reach any pod directly by its pod IP — no NAT. This simplifies debugging: from any node, ping 10.0.1.5 reaches that pod.

K8S NETWORKING — Pod-to-Pod Communication Across Nodes
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  POD-TO-POD COMMUNICATION — Same Node vs Different Node                  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  NODE 1 (10.0.0.1)                            NODE 2 (10.0.0.2)
  ┌────────────────────────┐                   ┌────────────────────────┐
  │  Pod A: 10.0.1.5       │                   │  Pod C: 10.0.2.8       │
  │  (anihpj-web)          │                   │  (anihpj-worker)       │
  │          │             │                   │          ▲             │
  │          │ veth pair   │                   │          │ veth pair   │
  │          ▼             │                   │          │             │
  │  ┌──────────────────┐  │                   │  ┌──────────────────┐  │
  │  │    cni0 bridge   │  │    VXLAN/Geneve   │  │    cni0 bridge   │  │
  │  │   10.0.1.0/24    │◄─┼───────────────────┼─►│   10.0.2.0/24    │  │
  │  └──────────────────┘  │    encapsulation  │  └──────────────────┘  │
  │          │             │                   │          │             │
  │          ▼             │                   │          ▼             │
  │  ┌──────────────────┐  │                   │  ┌──────────────────┐  │
  │  │      eth0        │  │                   │  │      eth0        │  │
  │  │   10.0.0.1/24    │◄─┼───────────────────┼─►│   10.0.0.2/24    │  │
  │  └──────────────────┘  │   physical network │  └──────────────────┘  │
  └────────────────────────┘                   └────────────────────────┘

  SAME NODE (Pod A → Pod B, same node):
    Pod A sends to 10.0.1.6 → veth pair → cni0 bridge → veth pair → Pod B
    NO encapsulation. Direct bridge forwarding. ~0.05ms latency.

  DIFFERENT NODE (Pod A → Pod C, cross-node):
    Pod A → cni0 → VXLAN encap (outer: 10.0.0.1→10.0.0.2, inner: 10.0.1.5→10.0.2.8)
    → eth0 → physical net → eth0 → VXLAN decap → cni0 → Pod C
    ~0.3-0.5ms latency (encapsulation overhead ~0.05ms)
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

10.2 CNI Plugins — Calico vs Cilium vs Flannel

The CNI plugin implements the K8s networking model. Your choice affects performance, security capabilities, and operational complexity.

DimensionFlannelCalicoCiliumWeave
How It RoutesVXLAN overlay or host-gw (L2)BGP (no overlay!) or VXLAN/IPIPeBPF — programs kernel directlyMesh overlay — every node peers with others (full mesh)
PerformanceGood (VXLAN overhead ~5%)Better (BGP: no encap overhead)Best (eBPF: kernel-native, bypasses iptables)Good (encrypted overlay, slight overhead)
NetworkPolicy❌ Not supported natively✅ Full support (iptables or eBPF)✅ L3/L4 + L7 (DNS, HTTP, Kafka)✅ Built-in (simple ingress/egress)
Encryption❌ No built-in❌ No built-in (WireGuard via config)✅ WireGuard / IPsec transparent✅ Built-in encrypted mesh (NaCl)
Observability❌ Minimal⚠️ Basic (Calico Enterprise)✅ Hubble (flows, latency, drops)✅ Weave Cloud / built-in metrics
Complexity⭐ Simplest — set and forget⭐⭐ Moderate — BGP needs config⭐⭐⭐ Highest — eBPF kernel ≥ 4.19⭐⭐ Moderate — mesh auto-configures
Best ForLearning, small clusters, no security requirementsProduction with NetworkPolicies, BGP for performanceHigh-perf + security + observability, 500+ node clustersEncrypted multi-cloud networking, simple setup with built-in security
💡 When to Upgrade from Flannel → Calico → Cilium

Start with Flannel when: learning K8s, small clusters (≤10 nodes), no security requirements, just need pods to talk.

Move to Calico when: you need NetworkPolicies (security), you have 10-100 nodes, you want BGP for better performance.

Move to Cilium when: 100+ nodes, need L7 policies (block SQL injection at kernel level!), need Hubble observability, want to replace kube-proxy + service mesh with one tool.

10.4 Ingress Controllers — Layer 7 HTTP Routing

An Ingress is a K8s resource that defines HTTP routing rules. An Ingress Controller is the actual software (NGINX, Traefik, etc.) that implements those rules. The controller watches for Ingress resources and configures itself accordingly.

ControllerStrengthsBest For
NGINX IngressMost popular (50K+ GitHub stars). Mature, well-documented. Extensive annotation system for customization.General purpose. Most tutorials use it. anihpj default choice.
TraefikAuto-discovery — detects new Services automatically. Built-in Let's Encrypt. Dashboard UI. Middleware system (rate limiting, auth).Dynamic environments where services change frequently.
HAProxyHighest raw throughput. Battle-tested L4/L7 proxy (20+ years).Ultra-high traffic (100K+ req/s). Latency-sensitive workloads.
ContourEnvoy-based. Gateway API native. Dynamic config via xDS protocol.Teams already using Envoy/Istio. Gateway API early adopters.
📖 anihpj Ingress Configuration — NGINX
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
  - hosts: [anihpj.com]
    secretName: anihpj-tls
  rules:
  - host: anihpj.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /jobs/
        pathType: Prefix
        backend: {service: {name: anihpj-web, port: {number: 8000}}}
      - path: /api/
        pathType: Prefix
        backend: {service: {name: anihpj-api, port: {number: 8000}}}
      - path: /admin/
        pathType: Prefix
        backend: {service: {name: anihpj-web, port: {number: 8000}}}
      - path: /healthz
        pathType: Exact
        backend: {service: {name: anihpj-web, port: {number: 8000}}}

10.5 Gateway API — The Next-Generation Ingress

Gateway API is the successor to Ingress. It's more expressive, role-oriented, and supports protocols beyond HTTP with dedicated route types for each protocol.

🌐
HTTPRoute

Layer 7 HTTP/HTTPS routing. Path matching, header-based routing, weighted traffic splitting (canary), request/response header manipulation, cross-namespace backend references. Most commonly used route type.

🔒
TLSRoute

TLS passthrough routing (no L7 inspection). Routes based on SNI hostname. Perfect for: mTLS-enabled services, databases with TLS, any service where the gateway should NOT terminate TLS.

⚡
TCPRoute + GRPCRoute

TCPRoute: Layer 4 TCP/UDP routing. Routes based on port. For non-HTTP protocols (Redis, Kafka, MySQL). GRPCRoute: gRPC-specific routing — method-level matching, gRPC status code-based retries.

FeatureIngress (Legacy)Gateway API (Modern)
ProtocolsHTTP/HTTPS onlyHTTP, HTTPS, TCP, UDP, gRPC, TLS (via HTTPRoute, TLSRoute, TCPRoute, GRPCRoute)
RoutingHost + Path onlyHost, path, headers, query params, method, weight (canary)
Role ModelOne-size-fits-all (dev changes Ingress)Infra admin (GatewayClass, Gateway) + App dev (HTTPRoute)
Traffic Splitting❌ Requires annotations (NGINX-specific)✅ Native weighted routing (canary deployments)
Cross-Namespace❌ Ingress only in same namespace as Service✅ HTTPRoute can reference Services in OTHER namespaces
MaturityGA since K8s 1.19 (stable)GA since K8s 1.27 (GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute). TLSRoute, GRPCRoute, TCPRoute still in progress.

10.6 Service Mesh — Istio vs Linkerd vs Cilium

A service mesh adds a dedicated infrastructure layer for service-to-service communication. Instead of each application implementing retries, timeouts, and TLS, the mesh handles it transparently — your code just makes HTTP calls to localhost.

FeatureIstio (Envoy)Linkerd (Rust)Cilium (eBPF)
ArchitectureSidecar proxy (Envoy) per podSidecar proxy (linkerd-proxy, Rust) per podSidecarless — eBPF in kernel
mTLS✅ Auto, per-pod identity (SPIFFE)✅ Auto, per-pod identity✅ Auto via WireGuard or IPsec
Traffic Splitting✅ DestinationRule (canary, A/B)✅ ServiceProfile (canary, retries)✅ L7 policies (HTTP, gRPC, Kafka)
Circuit Breaking✅ Outlier detection — evict failing backends after consecutive 5xx⚠️ Basic timeout-based✅ L7-aware per-endpoint detection
Retries & Timeouts✅ Per-route: max 3 retries, 2s timeout✅ Retry budget + per-route timeouts✅ HTTP retry, gRPC retry policies
Observability✅ Kiali dashboard, Jaeger tracing✅ Viz dashboard, built-in metrics✅ Hubble (flows, latency, drops)
Overhead⚠️ ~50-100MB per sidecar🟢 ~10-20MB per sidecar (Rust = efficient)🟢 Near-zero (kernel-native eBPF)
Complexity⭐⭐⭐ High⭐⭐ Medium⭐⭐ Medium (replaces CNI + kube-proxy + mesh)
Best ForEnterprise, multi-cluster, complex routingSimple, low-overhead, "just works"Performance-focused, consolidate networking stack
📖 Circuit Breaking — Protecting Your Platform from Cascading Failures

Problem: anihpj-web calls anihpj-api. anihpj-api becomes slow (database overload). Without circuit breaking: web keeps sending requests → threads pile up waiting for slow responses → web's thread pool exhausts → web ALSO becomes unresponsive → cascading failure.

Solution: The mesh monitors API success rate. When errors exceed threshold (5 consecutive 5xx), the circuit OPENS — requests immediately fail with 503 (fast failure). After 30s cooldown → HALF-OPEN (1 probe request). If probe succeeds → CLOSED (normal). If probe fails → stays OPEN.

Why this matters: A 2-second timeout × 100 requests/second = 200 threads blocked. Circuit breaking fails FAST (microseconds). The user sees degraded experience (some 503s) instead of a TOTAL outage. This is graceful degradation — not catastrophic failure. Every production service mesh must have circuit breaking configured.

10.7 mTLS — Mutual TLS for Zero-Trust Networking

Mutual TLS: Both client AND server present certificates. The server proves "I am postgres.anihpj.svc." The client proves "I am anihpj-web." Both verify each other's identity before any data flows. This prevents man-in-the-middle attacks and unauthorized services from connecting.

mTLS HANDSHAKE — What Happens When anihpj-web Connects to postgres
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    mTLS HANDSHAKE — 6 Steps                              │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  anihpj-web (Client)                           postgres (Server)
  ────────────────                              ─────────────────

  ① CLIENT HELLO ─────────────────────────────►
     "I support TLS 1.3"

  ②                               ◄───────────── SERVER HELLO + CERTIFICATE
                                               "I am postgres.anihpj.svc"
                                               (presents cert signed by mesh CA)

  ③ Client verifies server cert:
     - Is it signed by the mesh CA? ✓
     - Is the SAN "postgres.anihpj.svc"? ✓
     - Is it expired? No ✓

  ④ CLIENT CERTIFICATE ───────────────────────►
     "I am anihpj-web.anihpj.svc"
     (presents cert signed by mesh CA)

  ⑤                               Server verifies client cert:
                                               - Signed by mesh CA? ✓
                                               - SAN "anihpj-web.anihpj.svc"? ✓
                                               - Allowed to connect? (authz policy) ✓

  ⑥ ENCRYPTED DATA ──────────────────────────►
     ◄───────────────────────────────────────── ENCRYPTED DATA
     All traffic now encrypted with session keys

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  WITHOUT mTLS: Server proves identity. Client is ANONYMOUS.
  WITH mTLS: BOTH prove identity. Zero trust — no implicit trust on the network.
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

SPIFFE Identities: Service meshes use SPIFFE (Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone) to give each workload a cryptographic identity. Format: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/anihpj-web. This identity is embedded in the X.509 certificate. The mesh CA auto-issues short-lived certs (24-hour validity) and rotates them automatically. No human manages certs — the mesh handles the entire lifecycle.

What happens when a cert expires? With a service mesh: NOTHING. Certs rotate every 24 hours automatically. Without a mesh: TLS handshake fails → connection refused → application errors → production outage. This is why you never manually manage mTLS in production.

📖 mTLS Without a Service Mesh — cert-manager Approach

If you can't use a service mesh, cert-manager can provision mTLS certs. But you must configure your APPLICATION to load and verify them — Nginx, Django, PostgreSQL all need TLS config. This is 10× more work than a service mesh, which handles it transparently.

# cert-manager Certificate for mTLS
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata: {name: anihpj-web-mtls, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  secretName: anihpj-web-tls
  issuerRef: {name: cluster-issuer, kind: ClusterIssuer}
  usages: ["client auth", "server auth"]  # Both roles for mTLS
  dnsNames: ["anihpj-web.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"]

10.8 Network Policies — Your Pod-Level Firewall

⚠️ By default, all pod-to-pod traffic is ALLOWED. NetworkPolicies are DENY-by-default.

A namespace WITHOUT NetworkPolicies has ZERO network restrictions. Any pod can reach any other pod across any namespace. This is K8s' default — and it's dangerous in production.

NETWORKPOLICY — Default-Deny + Allow-List Pattern
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  NAMESPACE: anihpj — NetworkPolicy Zero-Trust Architecture               │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  STEP 1: Default-Deny ALL Ingress
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Policy: deny-all-ingress                                            │
  │  Effect: NOTHING can reach any pod in anihpj namespace                │
  │  Even pods in the SAME namespace are blocked!                         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  STEP 2: Allow-List Specific Traffic
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                      │
  │  ALLOW: anihpj-web → postgres:5432                                   │
  │  ┌──────────┐      ┌──────────┐                                      │
  │  │ anihpj-  │─TCP─►│ postgres │  ✅ Allowed (explicitly)              │
  │  │ web      │ port │ :5432    │                                      │
  │  └──────────┘ 5432 └──────────┘                                      │
  │                                                                      │
  │  ALLOW: monitoring → anihpj-web:8000/metrics                         │
  │  ┌──────────┐      ┌──────────┐                                      │
  │  │ Prometheus│─TCP─►│ anihpj-  │  ✅ Allowed (explicitly)              │
  │  │ (mon ns) │ port │ web:8000 │                                      │
  │  └──────────┘ 8000 └──────────┘                                      │
  │                                                                      │
  │  DENY: external internet → postgres:5432                             │
  │  ┌──────────┐      ┌──────────┐                                      │
  │  │ Internet │──X──►│ postgres │  ❌ BLOCKED (no allow rule)           │
  │  │ (0.0.0.0)│      │ :5432    │                                      │
  │  └──────────┘      └──────────┘                                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
📖 anihpj Complete NetworkPolicy Set
# 1. Default deny all ingress
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: deny-all-ingress, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  podSelector: {}  # Applies to ALL pods
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  # No ingress rules → deny everything

---
# 2. Allow web → postgres on port 5432
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-web-to-db, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: postgres}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: anihpj-web}}
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 5432}]

---
# 3. Allow monitoring from monitoring namespace
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-monitoring, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  podSelector: {}  # All anihpj pods
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {name: monitoring}}
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 8000}]

🧠 Deep Dive — Networking Core Concepts

📖 How CoreDNS Works — The DNS Brain of Your Cluster

Every time a pod resolves postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local, CoreDNS processes the query. Understanding this flow is critical for debugging "random" DNS failures:

# DNS resolution flow:
# 1. Pod's /etc/resolv.conf points to CoreDNS Service IP (10.96.0.10)
# 2. Pod sends DNS query: "What's the A record for postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local?"
# 3. CoreDNS checks its plugins in order:
#    a. errors → log any issues
#    b. health → is CoreDNS itself healthy?
#    c. ready → is CoreDNS ready to serve?
#    d. kubernetes → the K8s plugin: looks up "postgres" Service in "anihpj" namespace
#       → finds ClusterIP 10.96.200.50 → returns A record
#    e. cache → stores result for 30s (TTL)
#    f. forward → if not a cluster domain, forward to upstream DNS (/etc/resolv.conf)

# CoreDNS ConfigMap (kube-system)
kubectl get configmap coredns -n kube-system -o yaml
# Corefile:
# .:53 {
#     errors
#     health
#     ready
#     kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
#       pods insecure
#       fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
#     }
#     prometheus :9153
#     forward . /etc/resolv.conf
#     cache 30
#     loop
#     reload
#     loadbalance
# }

Common DNS issues and fixes: (1) NDOTS=5 problem: Pod's resolv.conf has ndots:5. Querying postgres (less than 5 dots) → K8s first tries postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local, then postgres.svc.cluster.local, etc. — 5 DNS queries before trying absolute. Fix: use FQDN (postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local) in app config, or reduce ndots. (2) CoreDNS crash: All pod-to-service communication breaks. Pods can't resolve ANY service names. Fix: CoreDNS runs as Deployment with anti-affinity — ensure 2+ replicas on different nodes.

📖 iptables vs eBPF — A Performance Deep Dive for Platform Engineers

Why does Cilium claim 10× performance over Calico/iptables? The answer is in the DATA STRUCTURES, not the marketing:

Dimensioniptables (Calico, kube-proxy)eBPF (Cilium)
Data StructureLinked list of rules traversed SEQUENTIALLY. Each packet walks ALL rules until match.Hash table in kernel. O(1) lookup regardless of rule count.
Rule Scaling1 Service = ~4 iptables rules (DNAT, SNAT, filter, chain). 1000 Services = 4000+ rules. Every packet traverses ALL 4000 rules.1 Service = 1 hash table entry. 1000 Services = 1000 entries. Lookup: constant time.
Update Speediptables-restore replaces ENTIRE ruleset atomically. Adding 1 rule = rewrite all 4000 rules. Spike at 100+ Services.eBPF map update: atomic key-value write. 1 Service change = 1 hash table update. Microseconds.
Packet PathNIC → netfilter (PREROUTING) → routing → netfilter (FORWARD) → netfilter (POSTROUTING) → NIC. Every netfilter hook traverses rules.NIC → eBPF program (attached to TC hook) → direct to socket. Bypasses netfilter entirely.
Observabilityiptables counters (iptables -L -v). Packet-level. No L7 visibility.eBPF programs emit events to Hubble. Per-packet, per-flow, L7 metadata (HTTP method, response code).
Real Impact at 1000 Services~4000 iptables rules. Rule walk: ~2-5ms per NEW connection. Latency P99 spikes during updates.~1000 hash entries. Lookup: ~0.001ms. No latency spikes during updates.

When does it matter? Under 50 Services, iptables is FINE. 50-500 Services, iptables works but updates become noticeable. 500+ Services, iptables becomes a performance bottleneck — every new connection pays the rule-walk tax. This is why Cilium exists: not because iptables is "bad," but because it doesn't scale. The CNPE exam might ask: "Your cluster has 2000 Services. Users report 2-second connection delays during rolling updates. What's likely the cause?" Answer: iptables rule updates during kube-proxy sync.

💡 kube-proxy Modes — How Service Traffic Gets Routed Under the Hood

kube-proxy has 3 modes, each with fundamentally different packet processing:

  • iptables (default): kube-proxy watches Services + Endpoints → writes iptables DNAT rules → kernel randomly picks backend pod. Limitation: random selection only — no round-robin, least-conn, or consistent hashing.
  • IPVS: kube-proxy creates IPVS virtual server. Linux kernel's IPVS module supports 10+ scheduling algorithms (rr, lc, sh, dh). 10× faster than iptables for 1000+ Services. Enable: --proxy-mode=ipvs. Requires kernel module: modprobe ip_vs.
  • userspace (legacy, deprecated): kube-proxy itself proxies every connection through user space. Slowest. NOT for production. Existed before iptables DNAT was reliable.
  • eBPF (Cilium replacement): Replaces kube-proxy entirely. Service lookup happens in eBPF at the socket level — before the packet even hits iptables. This is the future.

Drill 10.2 — Choose CNI for 500-Node Platform

Compare Calico vs Cilium for a platform with 500 nodes and 10,000 services.

  1. Which CNI handles 10K services without iptables slowdown?
  2. What observability does each provide?
  3. Final recommendation with justification
💡 Hint: iptables rules are O(n) — 10K services = 10K rules per node. IPVS is O(1). eBPF is even faster.
📝 View Solution 
Cilium wins at 500 nodes + 10K services:
- iptables: 10K services = 40K+ iptables rules. Rule walk = seconds.
- IPVS (Calico): O(1) lookup, but still iptables for NetworkPolicy.
- eBPF (Cilium): Replaces ALL iptables. Kernel-native. Hubble shows
  every packet flow. L7 policies for Kafka, HTTP, DNS.

Recommendation: Cilium for 500 nodes. The eBPF investment pays for
itself in performance + observability + L7 security.

Drill 10.3 — Gateway API vs Ingress Decision

anihpj is moving to a canary deployment model. You need to route 10% of traffic to v2 of the API.

  1. Can you do this with Ingress? How?
  2. Can you do this with Gateway API? How?
  3. Which is cleaner? Why?
💡 Hint: Ingress needs NGINX-specific canary annotations. Gateway API has native weighted routing in HTTPRoute.
📝 View Solution 
Ingress: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true"
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-weight: "10"  (NGINX-specific)

Gateway API (HTTPRoute):
  backendRefs:
  - name: anihpj-api-v1, weight: 90
  - name: anihpj-api-v2, weight: 10

Gateway API is cleaner: native, portable across controllers, no
vendor-specific annotations. This is why Gateway API is the future.

Drill 10.4 — Egress NetworkPolicy for Stripe API

anihpj-api needs to call api.stripe.com:443. Write the egress NetworkPolicy. All other egress should be blocked.

💡 Hint: Egress rules use policyTypes: [Egress] and egress: section. For FQDN, CiliumNetworkPolicy supports toFQDNs.
📝 View Solution 
# Default deny egress
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: deny-egress, namespace: anihpj}
spec: {podSelector: {}, policyTypes: [Egress]}

# Allow DNS (required for FQDN resolution)
# Allow Stripe (with Cilium for FQDN-based policy):
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
spec:
  endpointSelector: {matchLabels: {app: anihpj-api}}
  egress:
  - toEndpoints: [{matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns}}]
    toPorts: [{ports: [{port: "53", protocol: UDP}]}]
  - toFQDNs: [{matchName: api.stripe.com}]
    toPorts: [{ports: [{port: "443"}]}]

Drill 10.5 — Service Mesh vs NetworkPolicy

What does a Service Mesh add that plain NetworkPolicies can't do? List 5 things.

💡 Hint: Think beyond allow/deny — mesh adds reliability, observability, and traffic control.
📝 View Solution 
1. mTLS (automatic cert provisioning + rotation)
2. Traffic splitting (canary: 90% v1, 10% v2)
3. Retries + circuit breaking + timeouts
4. Distributed tracing (every hop instrumented)
5. L7 metrics (HTTP 200 vs 500, per-endpoint latency)

NetworkPolicy = allow/deny (L3/L4 firewall).
Service Mesh = allow/deny + reliability + observability + security.

Drill 10.6 — NodePort in Production

NodePort range is 30000-32767. Why is this problematic for production?

  1. List 3 reasons why NodePort is bad for production
  2. What should you use instead?
💡 Hint: Think security, port conflicts, and load balancing.
📝 View Solution 
1. Opens port on EVERY node (security — bypasses cloud firewall)
2. Limited range (2768 ports) — collision risk with many services
3. No intelligent load balancing (random node → random pod)

Use LoadBalancer (cloud LB) or Ingress (L7 routing).
NodePort is for DEVELOPMENT and learning only.

Drill 10.7 — cert-manager TLS Flow

Draw the flow from Ingress creation to TLS certificate renewal with cert-manager + Let's Encrypt.

  1. What resources are created? In what order?
  2. How does renewal work automatically?
💡 Hint: Flow: Ingress (with annotation) → Certificate resource → Order → Challenge (HTTP-01/DNS-01) → cert issued → stored in Secret.
📝 View Solution 
1. Create Ingress with annotation: cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt
2. cert-manager creates Certificate CRD (auto from Ingress)
3. cert-manager creates Order (Let's Encrypt ACME)
4. cert-manager creates Challenge (HTTP-01 or DNS-01)
5. Let's Encrypt validates challenge → issues certificate
6. cert-manager stores cert in Secret (anihpj-tls)
7. NGINX Ingress mounts Secret → serves HTTPS

Renewal: cert-manager checks cert expiry daily. 30 days before
expiry → auto-renews using same flow. Zero manual intervention.
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 10.8 — mTLS Certificate Expiry

mTLS between anihpj-web and anihpj-db. What happens if the cert expires?

💡 Hint: Service mesh auto-rotates certs. Manual mTLS (cert-manager) needs renewal config.
📝 View Solution 
With service mesh (Istio/Linkerd): certs auto-rotate every 24 hours.
  Expiry is never an issue — mesh issues short-lived certs continuously.

With manual cert-manager: cert expires → TLS handshake fails →
  web can't connect to db → HTTP 500 errors on every request.
  Fix: cert-manager auto-renews (30 days before expiry) if configured.

Without any system: cert expires → connection refused → production
  OUTAGE. Never manually manage mTLS certs in production.
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 10.9 — Two Ingress Controllers Conflict

NGINX Ingress and Traefik are both installed. 50% of requests return 404. Why?

💡 Hint: Both controllers watch ALL Ingress resources by default. ingressClassName selects which controller handles it.
📝 View Solution 
Both NGINX and Traefik watch ALL Ingress objects.
Each creates its own config. External LB split-traffics 50/50 between them.

Result: 50% of requests hit NGINX (which knows about all Ingresses),
50% hit Traefik (which also knows about all). But if one controller
doesn't understand the other's annotations → 404.

Fix: Set `ingressClassName: nginx` on Ingress resources so only
NGINX handles them. Or: `--watch-ingress-without-class=false`
so controllers ignore Ingresses without their class.
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 10.10 — eBPF vs iptables Performance

Cilium uses eBPF instead of iptables. What performance benefit does this give at scale (1000+ services)?

💡 Hint: iptables rules are sequential lists. eBPF programs are hash tables in the kernel. O(n) vs O(1).
📝 View Solution 
iptables: 1000 services = ~4000 iptables rules (DNAT + SNAT + filter).
  Every packet traverses ALL rules sequentially (O(n)).
  At 10K services, rule walk takes milliseconds → latency spikes.

eBPF: Hash table lookup in kernel (O(1)). Same speed for 10 services
  or 10,000. Also: eBPF bypasses netfilter entirely — packets go
  directly from NIC to socket without traversing iptables chains.

Result: At 10K services, eBPF is 10-100× faster for service routing.
Plus Hubble gives you per-packet observability that iptables can't.

📖 Chapter 10 Summary: Platform networking is about connecting things securely. NetworkPolicies enforce zero-trust at the pod level. Service mesh adds mTLS, observability, and traffic control. Gateway API is the future of ingress routing. Choose CNI based on scale (Flannel for simple, Calico for policies, Cilium for performance + eBPF). Your networking decisions determine your platform's security posture and performance ceiling.

PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims, StorageClasses, CSI drivers, StatefulSets, cloud storage integration, and backup with Velero — where your data lives.

📖 Chapter Overview: Containers are ephemeral — they come and go. But DATA must persist. PostgreSQL databases, Redis snapshots, user uploads, log archives — these survive pod restarts, node failures, and cluster upgrades. This chapter covers K8s storage from PV to Velero backup.

🎓 CNPE Relevance
Platform Architecture Domain 1 — 15% Storage Design PV/PVC/CSI
Why Chapter 11 Matters on the CNPE Exam

The CNPE exam tests storage as applied configuration. Expect tasks like: "Create a PVC with StorageClass fast-ssd, 20GB, ReadWriteOnce for PostgreSQL. Then resize it to 50GB." You must know: PVC YAML syntax, StorageClass naming, access mode implications, and CSI driver requirements. Also tested: Velero backup/restore commands, StatefulSet volumeClaimTemplates, and PVC debugging (Pending status causes).

11.1 Storage Fundamentals — PV, PVC, StorageClass, CSI

K8S STORAGE — How a Pod Gets Persistent Storage
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │               KUBERNETES STORAGE ARCHITECTURE                             │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ADMIN                             USER (Dev)                    K8S + CLOUD
  ─────                             ──────────                    ───────────

  ┌──────────────┐                  ┌──────────────┐
  │ StorageClass │                  │ Persistent   │
  │ (provisioner)│                  │ VolumeClaim  │
  │              │                  │ (PVC)        │
  │ "fast-ssd":  │                  │              │
  │ provisioner: │                  │ "I need 20GB │
  │ ebs.csi.aws  │                  │  ReadWrite   │
  │              │                  │  Once (RWO)" │
  └──────┬───────┘                  └──────┬───────┘
         │                                 │
         │    ┌────────────────────────────┘
         │    │  PVC references StorageClass by name
         │    ▼
         │  ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐
         │  │ CSI Driver   │────►│ Persistent   │────►│ aws ebs      │
         │  │ (ebs.csi.aws)│     │ Volume (PV)  │     │ create-volume│
         │  │              │     │              │     │ 20GB, gp3    │
         │  │ Provisions   │     │ 20GB, gp3    │     │ us-east-1a   │
         │  │ the volume   │     │ us-east-1a   │     │ vol-abc123   │
         │  └──────────────┘     └──────┬───────┘     └──────┬───────┘
         │                              │                    │
         │                              │  PV references     │
         │                              │  the cloud volume  │
         │                              ▼                    │
         │                        ┌──────────────┐           │
         │                        │ POD: postgres│           │
         │                        │              │           │
         │                        │ mounts PVC   │           │
         │                        │ at /var/lib/ │◄──────────┘
         │                        │ postgresql/  │  Cloud volume
         │                        │ data         │  attached to node
         │                        └──────────────┘
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  StorageClass → CSI Driver → Cloud Volume → PV → PVC → Pod Mount
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
📦
PV (PersistentVolume)

A cluster-scoped resource representing actual storage. Like a node in the cluster — it exists independently of any pod. Admin-managed OR dynamically provisioned by CSI.

🎫
PVC (PersistentVolumeClaim)

A namespace-scoped request for storage. "I need 20GB, ReadWriteOnce, from StorageClass fast-ssd." K8s binds PVC to a matching PV. Like a pod requesting CPU — PVC requests storage.

⚙️
StorageClass

Defines "classes" of storage. "fast-ssd" (gp3, 3000 IOPS), "slow-hdd" (sc1, 250 IOPS). Each class has a provisioner (CSI driver). Enables dynamic provisioning: PVC → StorageClass → CSI → cloud volume.

11.2 Access Modes — RWO, ROX, RWX, RWOP

ModeReadWriteNodesBackend Requiredanihpj Use
RWO (ReadWriteOnce)✅✅1 node onlyBlock storage (EBS, Azure Disk, GCE PD)PostgreSQL (single pod writes)
ROX (ReadOnlyMany)✅❌Many nodesAny shared filesystemStatic assets shared across web pods (read-only)
RWX (ReadWriteMany)✅✅Many nodesShared filesystem (EFS, Azure Files, NFS)User file uploads (all web pods write)
RWOP (ReadWriteOncePod)✅✅1 pod onlyBlock storage (CSI with SINGLE_NODE_SINGLE_WRITER)PostgreSQL (guaranteed — only 1 pod writes, even on same node)

11.3 Dynamic Provisioning — Storage On Demand

Without dynamic provisioning: admin creates PV manually → user creates PVC → K8s binds them. With dynamic provisioning: user creates PVC with StorageClass → CSI driver auto-creates PV AND cloud volume. No admin involvement.

# StorageClass defines HOW to provision
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata: {name: fast-ssd}
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
parameters:
  type: gp3
  iops: "3000"
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer  # Wait until pod scheduled (zone-aware!)
allowVolumeExpansion: true  # PVC can be resized
---
# PVC requests storage USING that class
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: {name: postgres-data, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  storageClassName: fast-ssd
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources: {requests: {storage: 20Gi}}

11.4 StatefulSet Storage — Stable Identity + Persistent Data

StatefulSets are designed for stateful applications. Each pod replica gets a STABLE identity (postgres-0, postgres-1) and its OWN PVC. If postgres-0 is rescheduled to a different node, its PVC follows it (same cloud volume, re-attached).

💡 volumeClaimTemplates — PVC per Replica

Unlike Deployments (where all pods share one PVC template), StatefulSets use volumeClaimTemplates: each replica gets its OWN PVC: postgres-data-postgres-0, postgres-data-postgres-1. These PVCs OUTLIVE the pod — deleting the StatefulSet does NOT delete PVCs (you must clean them up manually).

11.5 Cloud Storage Options

ServiceTypeAccess ModeMulti-AZ?PerformanceBest For
AWS EBS (gp3)BlockRWO❌ Single AZ3000 IOPS baseDatabases, single-instance stateful apps
AWS EFSFile (NFS)RWX✅ Multi-AZBursting (scales with size)Shared file uploads, CMS assets
Azure DiskBlockRWO❌ Single AZVaries by SKUDatabases on AKS
Azure FilesFile (SMB/NFS)RWX✅ Multi-AZPremium tierShared storage on AKS
GCE Persistent DiskBlockRWO / ROX⚠️ Regional PD (multi-zone)Varies by typeDatabases on GKE

11.6 Backup with Velero — Protect Your Data

Velero backs up K8s objects (YAML manifests) AND persistent volumes (snapshots) to S3-compatible storage. It can restore entire namespaces or individual resources.

# Backup entire anihpj namespace (objects + PV snapshots)
velero backup create anihpj-daily --include-namespaces anihpj

# Schedule daily backups with 7-day retention
velero schedule create anihpj-daily \
  --schedule="0 2 * * *" \
  --include-namespaces anihpj \
  --ttl 168h

# Restore entire namespace
velero restore create --from-backup anihpj-daily

# Restore only postgres PVC
velero restore create --from-backup anihpj-daily \
  --include-resources persistentvolumeclaims/postgres-data

11.7 anihpj-db Storage Design — Complete Reference

anihpj's PostgreSQL database is the most critical stateful component. Here's the complete storage architecture:

📖 PostgreSQL StatefulSet — Full Storage Configuration
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: postgres
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  serviceName: postgres
  replicas: 1  # Single master (use Patroni/CloudNativePG for HA)
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: postgres}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: postgres}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef: {name: anihpj-secret, key: DB_PASSWORD}
        - name: PGDATA
          value: /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5432
        volumeMounts:
        - name: postgres-data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
        resources:
          requests: {cpu: "500m", memory: "1Gi"}
          limits: {cpu: "2", memory: "4Gi"}
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: postgres-data
    spec:
      storageClassName: fast-ssd  # AWS gp3, 3000 IOPS
      accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 20Gi
📦
Storage Spec

20GB gp3 EBS volume, 3000 IOPS, ReadWriteOnce. Resizable to 50GB (StorageClass: allowVolumeExpansion: true). Encrypted at rest (AWS KMS).

🔄
Backup Schedule

Velero: Daily at 2AM UTC, 30-day retention. S3 bucket: anihpj-velero-backups. etcd: Hourly CronJob on control plane, stored alongside Velero backups.

🎯
RPO / RTO

RPO=1 hour: Max 1 hour of data loss (Velero hourly + WAL archiving). RTO=30 min: 15 min to provision new PVC + 10 min to restore from Velero + 5 min smoke tests.

⚠️ Production Hardening — What's Missing from This Basic Setup
  • HA: Single replica = single point of failure. Production needs Patroni (auto-failover), CloudNativePG operator, or managed RDS.
  • WAL Archiving: Not configured. Without WAL archiving, RPO is "last Velero backup" (up to 24 hours). With WAL archiving to S3, RPO drops to seconds (point-in-time recovery).
  • Connection Pooling: No PgBouncer. Every Django worker opens a new PostgreSQL connection. With 10 workers × 3 pods = 30 connections. PgBouncer reduces this to ~5 persistent connections.
  • Monitoring: No Postgres Exporter. Production needs: connection count, replication lag, cache hit ratio, slow queries.

🧠 Deep Dive — Storage Core Concepts

📖 Block vs File vs Object Storage — What to Use When

These 3 storage types are fundamentally different in HOW they store data and WHAT they're good for. Your database performance depends on choosing correctly:

DimensionBlock Storage (EBS, Azure Disk)File Storage (EFS, Azure Files)Object Storage (S3, GCS)
How Data is OrganizedRaw blocks — like a blank hard drive. You create a filesystem (ext4, xfs) on top.Hierarchical files + folders. Multiple clients mount the same filesystem.Flat namespace of objects (files) with metadata. No hierarchy. Accessed via HTTP API.
Access MethodMounted as a device (/dev/nvme1n1) → formatted → mounted as directoryMounted as NFS/SMB share → appears as normal directoryHTTP API: GET /bucket/photo.jpg. No mounting — app uses SDK.
Concurrent AccessRWO — ONE node reads/writes. No concurrent access.RWX — MANY nodes read/write simultaneously.N/A — accessed via API. Infinite concurrent readers.
Latency✅ Sub-millisecond (local SSD). ~1-3ms (network-attached).⚠️ 5-10ms (network filesystem overhead).❌ 50-200ms (HTTP round-trip). Not for real-time access.
Performance✅ 100K+ IOPS (io2). Consistent, predictable.⚠️ Burst credits. Performance scales with size.✅ Infinite throughput (parallel GETs). Variable latency.
Best ForDatabases (PostgreSQL, MySQL), any write-heavy workload requiring low latencyShared configs, CMS uploads, home directories, ML model sharingBackups, static assets, logs, data lakes, container images
K8s Access ModeReadWriteOnce (RWO)ReadWriteMany (RWX)N/A — use S3 SDK or CSI driver (e.g., Mountpoint for S3)

The database rule: NEVER use file storage (EFS/NFS) for databases. The network filesystem adds 5-10ms latency to every disk operation. A single PostgreSQL query does 100s of disk reads — 100 × 5ms = 500ms query time. Block storage: 100 × 0.5ms = 50ms. This is a 10× difference in database performance.

📖 How CSI Drivers Work — The Plugin That Connects K8s to Cloud Storage

CSI (Container Storage Interface) is a standardized gRPC API between K8s and storage providers. Before CSI, every cloud provider had code INSIDE Kubernetes (in-tree). CSI extracted that code into external plugins:

# CSI Driver Architecture:
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
# │  Kubernetes Control Plane                            │
# │  ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────┐   │
# │  │ kube-controller│◄──►│ CSI Controller Plugin     │   │
# │  │ -manager      │    │ (ebs-csi-controller pod)  │   │
# │  │               │    │ Handles: CreateVolume,     │   │
# │  │               │    │ DeleteVolume,              │   │
# │  │               │    │ ControllerPublishVolume    │   │
# │  └──────────────┘    └──────────┬───────────────┘   │
# └─────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────┘
#                                   │ gRPC
# ┌─────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────┐
# │  Worker Node                    │                    │
# │  ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────▼───────────────┐   │
# │  │ kubelet      │◄──►│ CSI Node Plugin            │   │
# │  │              │    │ (ebs-csi-node DaemonSet)   │   │
# │  │              │    │ Handles: NodeStageVolume,   │   │
# │  │              │    │ NodePublishVolume,          │   │
# │  │              │    │ NodeUnpublishVolume         │   │
# │  └──────────────┘    └──────────┬───────────────┘   │
# │                                 │                    │
# │                          ┌──────▼──────────┐        │
# │                          │ /var/lib/kubelet│        │
# │                          │ /pods/.../mount │        │
# │                          │ (pod's volume)  │        │
# │                          └─────────────────┘        │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

# The flow when a pod requests a PVC:
# 1. User creates PVC → kube-controller-manager sees it
# 2. Controller calls external-provisioner sidecar
# 3. Provisioner calls CSI Controller: CreateVolume
# 4. CSI Controller calls AWS API: ec2 create-volume
# 5. AWS creates EBS volume → volume ID returned
# 6. CSI Controller creates PV object in K8s
# 7. Scheduler assigns pod to node
# 8. kubelet calls CSI Node Plugin: NodeStageVolume → NodePublishVolume
# 9. CSI Node Plugin calls AWS API: ec2 attach-volume
# 10. Volume appears as /dev/nvme1n1 on the node
# 11. CSI Node Plugin formats (if needed) + mounts to pod's directory
# 12. Pod starts → /var/lib/postgresql/data is the EBS volume!

Debugging tip: If a PVC is stuck Pending, check CSI controller pod logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l app=ebs-csi-controller. If a pod can't mount, check CSI node pod logs on that node: kubectl logs -n kube-system ebs-csi-node-xxxxx. The CSI logs tell you EXACTLY which step failed.

📖 Velero Under the Hood — How Backup and Restore Actually Work

Velero doesn't just "copy files." It orchestrates a complex process involving K8s API objects, cloud volume snapshots, and S3 storage:

  1. Backup (K8s objects): Velero queries the API server → serializes all objects (Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, etc.) as JSON → uploads to S3 as a tarball.
  2. Backup (Persistent Volumes): Velero calls the CSI driver's VolumeSnapshot API → cloud provider creates a snapshot of the EBS volume → snapshot ID stored in the backup metadata.
  3. Restore (K8s objects): Velero downloads the tarball from S3 → deserializes JSON → creates objects via the K8s API. It respects owner references — if you restore a Deployment, it doesn't create duplicate pods.
  4. Restore (PVs): Velero creates a new EBS volume FROM the snapshot → creates a new PV pointing to it → creates a PVC → pod mounts it. The restored pod sees the EXACT data from backup time.

Critical detail: Velero restores CLUSTER-SCOPED resources too (ClusterRoles, CRDs, etc.). If you backup namespace "anihpj" but that namespace uses a ClusterRole, Velero backs up both. This prevents "my restore works but RBAC is broken."

🏋️ Chapter 11 — Hands-On Practice Drills (10 Exercises)

⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 11.1 — Create PVC for anihpj-db

Create a PVC: 20GB, RWO, StorageClass "fast-ssd". What happens if StorageClass doesn't exist?

💡 Hint: PVC stays Pending with warning: "storage class fast-ssd not found."
📝 View Solution
kubectl apply -f pvc.yaml
kubectl get pvc -n anihpj
# STATUS: Pending (storageclass.storage.k8s.io "fast-ssd" not found)
# Fix: kubectl apply -f storageclass.yaml (create the StorageClass first)
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 11.2 — Pod Deleted, PVC Survives?

anihpj-db-0 pod is deleted. Does the PVC get deleted? Does the data survive?

💡 Hint: PVC lifecycle is INDEPENDENT of pod lifecycle. StatefulSet PVCs outlive pod deletion.
📝 View Solution
kubectl delete pod postgres-0 -n anihpj
# Pod restarts (StatefulSet maintains desired count).
# PVC postgres-data-postgres-0 still EXISTS.
# Data intact — same PVC, same cloud volume.

# To DELETE the PVC:
kubectl delete pvc postgres-data-postgres-0 -n anihpj
# ⚠️ This DELETES the cloud volume (data gone forever).
# StatefulSet does NOT auto-delete PVCs — manual cleanup required.
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 11.3 — RWX Storage for File Uploads

5 anihpj-web replicas need to write user-uploaded files. Which cloud storage service and access mode?

💡 Hint: Multiple pods writing → need ReadWriteMany (RWX). AWS = EFS, Azure = Azure Files.
📝 View Solution
AWS: EFS (Elastic File System) — NFS, multi-AZ, RWX.
Azure: Azure Files — SMB/NFS, multi-AZ, RWX.
GCP: Filestore — NFS, multi-zone, RWX.

Access mode: ReadWriteMany.
Do NOT use EBS (RWO) — only 1 node can mount it.
5 web pods on different nodes → EBS fails.
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 11.4 — Velero Backup Failed

"volume snapshot not supported." Why? How do you fix it?

💡 Hint: CSI driver must support VolumeSnapshot. Not all drivers do. Check with kubectl get volumesnapshotclass.
📝 View Solution
Reason: StorageClass uses a CSI driver WITHOUT snapshot support.
OR: No VolumeSnapshotClass defined.

Fix 1: Install VolumeSnapshot CRDs + VolumeSnapshotClass.
Fix 2: If CSI doesn't support snapshots, use Velero's Restic
  (filesystem-level backup instead of volume snapshots):
  velero backup create anihpj --default-volumes-to-restic
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 11.5 — StatefulSet vs Deployment for PostgreSQL

3 reasons why StatefulSet is better for databases.

💡 Hint: Stable identity, persistent storage per pod, ordered scaling.
📝 View Solution
1. Stable identity: postgres-0, postgres-1 (needed for replication).
   Deployment pods have random names (postgres-7f3a-abcde).

2. Persistent storage per replica: volumeClaimTemplates gives
   each pod its OWN PVC. Deployment shares one PVC template.

3. Ordered startup/shutdown: postgres-0 starts first (master),
   then postgres-1 (replica). Deployment starts all at once.

4. (Bonus) PVC survives pod rescheduling: pod moves to new node,
   same cloud volume re-attaches. Data intact.
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 11.6 — PVC Stuck Pending

PVC shows "Pending" for 1 hour. Debug the issue. List 5 possible causes.

💡 Hint: kubectl describe pvc → check Events. Common: StorageClass not found, provisioner not running, zone mismatch.
📝 View Solution
1. StorageClass doesn't exist (or name typo in PVC)
2. CSI driver pod not running (ebs-csi-controller in kube-system)
3. volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer + no pod using PVC yet
4. Zone mismatch: pod in us-east-1a, StorageClass only in us-east-1b
5. Cloud quota exceeded: max EBS volumes per region/account reached

Debug: kubectl describe pvc postgres-data -n anihpj | grep -A10 Events
⏱️ Target: 2 minutes
Drill 11.7 — Resize PVC from 20GB to 50GB

Is it online? What's required?

💡 Hint: StorageClass needs allowVolumeExpansion: true. Most CSI drivers support online resize.
📝 View Solution
# Check if StorageClass allows expansion
kubectl get sc fast-ssd -o yaml | grep allowVolumeExpansion

# Edit PVC (increase size)
kubectl edit pvc postgres-data -n anihpj
# Change: spec.resources.requests.storage: 50Gi

# Check status
kubectl get pvc -n anihpj
# CAPACITY: 50Gi (resize in progress → file system expand)

# Online: YES for gp3 EBS, Azure Disk, GCE PD.
# Offline: NOT needed — CSI driver expands online.
# After volume resize: restart pod to make it see new size,
# then run filesystem resize inside: resize2fs /dev/nvme1n1
⏱️ Target: 2 minutes
Drill 11.8 — CSI vs In-Tree Provisioner

Why did K8s move from in-tree provisioners to CSI?

💡 Hint: In-tree = code inside K8s. CSI = external plugin. Think release cycles and vendor independence.
📝 View Solution
In-tree: Cloud provider code INSIDE Kubernetes core.
  Problem: AWS EBS driver updates = wait for K8s release.
  Problem: Bloated K8s binary (every cloud's code included).

CSI: External plugin, independent release cycle.
  Fix: AWS releases EBS CSI driver weekly, not tied to K8s.
  Fix: Vendors maintain their OWN drivers. K8s stays lean.

K8s 1.29+ all in-tree provisioners are REMOVED.
Use CSI drivers exclusively for cloud storage.
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 11.9 — etcd Snapshot vs Velero Backup

What does each restore? If you lose the entire AWS region, which one do you need?

💡 Hint: etcd = cluster state (deployments, services, secrets). Velero = namespaces + PV snapshots.
📝 View Solution
etcd snapshot: Restores CLUSTER STATE — Deployments, Services,
  ConfigMaps, Secrets, RBAC. Does NOT restore PV data.

Velero: Restores NAMESPACES (K8s objects) + PV SNAPSHOTS (data).

Lose entire region → restore Velero backup to NEW cluster in
  different region. Velero restores K8s objects + PV data from S3.
  etcd backup alone can't restore PV data.
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 11.10 — Backup Strategy for anihpj

Design a backup strategy: RPO=1 hour, RTO=30 minutes.

💡 Hint: Combine etcd snapshots + Velero schedules. Test restore monthly.
📝 View Solution
RPO=1 hour:
- Velero Schedule: hourly backup of anihpj namespace + PV snapshots
- etcd snapshot: hourly (CronJob on control plane)

RTO=30 minutes:
- Velero restore to new cluster: ~10 min for objects + PV data
- etcd restore (if needed): ~5 min
- DNS cutover: ~2 min
- Smoke tests: ~10 min

Total: ~27 minutes (within 30-min RTO)

Monthly restore test: restore production backup to staging cluster.
Verify: data integrity, app starts, API responds. Document results.

📖 Chapter 11 Summary: PVs represent storage. PVCs request it. StorageClasses automate provisioning. StatefulSets give stable identity + per-replica PVCs. Velero backs up everything — K8s objects + PV data — to S3. Your backup strategy defines your disaster recovery capability. RPO and RTO are business decisions, not technical ones.

Platform Architecture Domain 1 — 15% Cost Optimization FinOps
