12.1 Resource Requests & Limits — The Foundation of Scheduling

Requests = guaranteed minimum. The scheduler uses requests to decide where to place pods. Limits = maximum allowed. Container is THROTTLED (CPU) or KILLED (memory) if exceeded.

QoS ClassRequest = Limit?OOM ScoreKilled OrderBest For
Guaranteed✅ Yes — req == limit for CPU AND Memory-998 (highest priority)3rd (LAST)Production databases, critical services
Burstable⚠️ No — req < limit, or only one setBased on usage ratio2ndWeb apps, APIs — most workloads
BestEffort❌ No requests or limits set1000 (lowest priority)1st (FIRST)Development, batch jobs, non-critical
⚠️ Memory vs CPU — Different Enforcement

Memory: Exceed limit → OOMKilled. Container is TERMINATED. CPU: Exceed limit → THROTTLED. Container slows down but STAYS RUNNING. This is critical: memory limits are a HARD KILL SWITCH. CPU limits are a SOFT BRAKE.

12.2 Scheduling Strategies — Node Selector, Affinity, Taints

StrategyHow It WorksStrictnessUse Case
nodeSelectorSimple key=value match. Pod runs ONLY on nodes with matching labels.Hard requirement"Run GPU workloads only on gpu=true nodes"
nodeAffinityrequiredDuringScheduling (hard) or preferredDuringScheduling (soft). More expressive than nodeSelector.Hard or Soft"Prefer SSD nodes but OK with HDD"
podAffinityCo-locate pods: "Schedule me near pods with label app=redis"Hard or SoftWeb pod near cache for low latency
podAntiAffinitySpread pods: "DON'T schedule me on same node as pods with label app=anihpj-web"Hard or SoftHA: 3 replicas on 3 different nodes/zones
Taints & TolerationsNode TAINTS repel pods. Pod TOLERATIONS allow them on tainted nodes. Taint: "gpu=true:NoSchedule" repels ALL pods without matching toleration.HardDedicated nodes for specific teams or workloads
💡 anihpj Scheduling Example
# Spread anihpj-web across AZs for HA
affinity:
  podAntiAffinity:
    requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
    - labelSelector:
        matchLabels: {app: anihpj-web}
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
# Result: 3 replicas → 3 different AZs (if available)

12.3 Topology Spread Constraints — Fine-Grained Distribution

More flexible than podAntiAffinity. maxSkew controls how UNEVEN pod distribution can be. While podAntiAffinity says "never co-locate", topologySpreadConstraints says "distribute evenly within tolerance."

TOPOLOGY SPREAD — maxSkew in Action (6 replicas, 3 zones)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  maxSkew=1: "At most 1 pod difference between any two zones"            │
  │                                                                         │
  │  zone-a: 2 pods  │  zone-b: 2 pods  │  zone-c: 2 pods   ✅ Balanced     │
  │  zone-a: 3 pods  │  zone-b: 2 pods  │  zone-c: 1 pod    ❌ Skew=2       │
  │  → Scheduler fixes: schedules next pod to zone-c                       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  maxSkew=2: "At most 2 pod difference" (more relaxed)                   │
  │                                                                         │
  │  zone-a: 4 pods  │  zone-b: 2 pods  │  zone-c: 0 pods   ✅ Skew=2 (OK)  │
  │  → This allows unbalanced distribution when zones have different capacity│
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
💡 anihpj Topology Spread — Even Distribution Across AZs
topologySpreadConstraints:
- maxSkew: 1
  topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
  whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway  # Soft: try to spread, but schedule anyway
  labelSelector:
    matchLabels: {app: anihpj-web}
# With 6 replicas, 3 zones: 2 per zone (maxSkew=1 satisfied)
# With 6 replicas, 2 zones: 3 per zone (maxSkew=1 satisfied)
# If zone fails: ScheduleAnyway allows pods on remaining zones

whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule = hard requirement. If constraint can't be met, pod stays Pending. Use ScheduleAnyway for availability over perfect distribution.

Key difference from podAntiAffinity: podAntiAffinity says "DON'T put me with pod X" (binary). Topology spread says "evenly distribute pods matching label Y" (quantitative). For HA, use BOTH: anti-affinity keeps replicas apart, spread keeps the distribution balanced.

12.4 Priority & Preemption — Who Gets Evicted First

High-priority pods can EVICT lower-priority pods to get scheduled. PriorityClass defines priority levels (e.g., high-priority=1000, default=0). A pending high-priority pod can preempt (evict) a running low-priority pod to claim its node.

💡 PriorityClass Example — Protect Critical Workloads
# Define priority levels
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata: {name: anihpj-critical}
value: 1000000  # Highest — preempts everything
globalDefault: false
description: "Critical anihpj infrastructure"
---
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata: {name: anihpj-production}
value: 1000
globalDefault: false
---
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata: {name: anihpj-development}
value: 100
globalDefault: true  # Default for all pods without explicit priority

# Use in pod:
spec:
  priorityClassName: anihpj-production
PREEMPTION FLOW — How a Critical Pod Claims a Full Node
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  SCENARIO: Node worker-1 is FULL. anihpj-critical pod needs to run.     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  NODE worker-1 (CPU: 4/4 used, Memory: 8/8Gi used)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Running Pods:                                                       │
  │  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐       │
  │  │ anihpj-web-1    │  │ analytics-batch │  │ test-pod        │       │
  │  │ priority: 1000  │  │ priority: 100   │  │ priority: 0     │       │
  │  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ① anihpj-critical pod created (priority: 1000000, needs 2 CPU)
  ② Scheduler checks all nodes → all full
  ③ Scheduler evaluates preemption candidates:
     - anihpj-web-1 (priority 1000): can't preempt (equal or higher)
     - analytics-batch (priority 100): ✅ VICTIM — lower priority → EVICT
     - test-pod (priority 0): ✅ VICTIM — lower priority → EVICT
  ④ Scheduler evicts analytics-batch + test-pod (SIGTERM)
  ⑤ Node now has 2 CPU free → anihpj-critical is SCHEDULED

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  RULE: Pod can ONLY preempt pods with LOWER priority.
  Same priority? No preemption. Higher priority? No preemption.
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
⚠️ Preemption WARNING — Evicted Pods Are NOT Rescheduled by Default

When a pod is preempted, it's DELETED (not rescheduled). If it was created by a Deployment, the Deployment controller will create a replacement — but that replacement might also be preempted. Pods without a controller (bare pods) are GONE FOREVER. Always use Deployments/StatefulSets. Preemption also triggers PDB violations — if evicting a pod violates minAvailable, preemption is BLOCKED.

12.5 Node Management — Cordon, Drain, PDBs

🚧
Cordon

Mark node as unschedulable. No NEW pods. Existing pods keep running. kubectl cordon worker-1. Reversible: kubectl uncordon.

🚚
Drain

Evict ALL pods, then cordon. Pods gracefully terminated and rescheduled. kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data.

🛡️
PDB (PodDisruptionBudget)

Minimum pods that MUST stay running during VOLUNTARY disruptions (drain, upgrade). minAvailable: 2 for 3 replicas = only 1 can be drained at a time. Does NOT protect against involuntary failures (node crash).

📖 Drain Troubleshooting — When kubectl drain Gets Stuck

Symptom: kubectl drain worker-1 hangs for minutes. Nothing happens.

Common causes and fixes:

  • PDB blocking: Drain would violate PDB. Fix: kubectl get pdb -A to find blocking PDB. Scale up replicas temporarily, or (temporarily) delete PDB → drain → recreate PDB.
  • DaemonSet pods: Drain ignores DaemonSet pods by default. Always use --ignore-daemonsets flag.
  • Pods without controllers: "Bare" pods (not owned by Deployment/StatefulSet) can't be evicted. Fix: kubectl drain --force to delete them (they're gone forever!).
  • EmptyDir volumes: Pods using emptyDir can't be evicted (data would be lost). Fix: --delete-emptydir-data flag (data IS lost).
  • Pod termination grace period expired: Pod didn't exit within terminationGracePeriodSeconds. Fix: --grace-period=0 --force (force kill, last resort).
💡 PDB YAML — Protect Your Workloads from Voluntary Disruptions
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web-pdb
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  minAvailable: 2  # At least 2 pods must stay running
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
# With 3 replicas: drain can evict at most 1 pod.
# The 2nd pod would violate minAvailable → drain BLOCKED.
# But if a NODE CRASHES (involuntary): PDB doesn't protect.
# maxUnavailable: 1 is an alternative (same effect: 2 pods stay).

PDB vs Node Crash: PDB only applies to VOLUNTARY disruptions (kubectl drain, cluster autoscaler scale-down, node upgrade). If a node CRASHES (involuntary), PDB is IGNORED — pods on the dead node are NOT protected. This is intentional: availabilty > PDB guarantees when hardware fails.

12.6 Cluster Autoscaler vs Karpenter — Node Scaling

FeatureCluster AutoscalerKarpenter
How It WorksWatches for Pending pods. If no node fits, adds a node from a node group (AWS ASG).Watches for Pending pods. Selects the OPTIMAL instance type/size in real-time. Provisions node directly.
Instance SelectionFixed node groups (t3.medium OR t3.large). Can't mix.Dynamic — chooses from 600+ instance types. Bin-packs pods optimally.
Speed~2-5 minutes (ASG launch + join)~30-60 seconds (direct EC2 launch)
Cost OptimizationLimited — uses predefined node groups✅ Bin-packing minimizes waste. Supports spot-first then on-demand fallback.
Best For anihpjSimple, predictable workloads. Few instance types.Production — fastest scaling, lowest cost, handles burst traffic.

12.7 Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) — Right-Size Your Pods

VPA analyzes historical CPU/memory usage and recommends (or auto-sets) resource requests. If a pod requests 1GB but only uses 100MB, VPA catches the waste.

ModeBehaviorPod Restart?Best For
OffComputes recommendations ONLY. Displays in kubectl describe vpa. Does NOT change anything.❌ NeverSafe first step. Learn what VPA would recommend before letting it act.
InitialSets resource requests ONCE when a pod is first created. Does NOT update running pods.❌ Never (only affects new pods)New Deployments — sensible defaults from the start.
AutoEVICTS running pods and recreates them with updated requests. Continuously adjusts.⚠️ YES — on every updateProduction with PDBs and proper readiness probes to handle restarts.
RecreateSame as Auto but more aggressive about pod lifecycle.⚠️ YESWhen you need immediate right-sizing.
💡 VPA YAML — Monitor and Right-Size anihpj-web
apiVersion: autoscaling.k8s.io/v1
kind: VerticalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web-vpa
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  targetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: anihpj-web
  updatePolicy:
    updateMode: "Off"  # Start with Off — observe recommendations first
  resourcePolicy:
    containerPolicies:
    - containerName: anihpj-web
      minAllowed:       # NEVER go below this (safety floor)
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      maxAllowed:       # NEVER go above this (safety ceiling)
        cpu: 2
        memory: 4Gi
      controlledResources: ["cpu", "memory"]
# After 1 week of Off mode:
# kubectl describe vpa anihpj-web-vpa
# Recommendation: CPU 250m, Memory 384Mi
# Current: CPU 1, Memory 2Gi (4-5× over-provisioned!)
⚠️ VPA Auto Mode Risks — Know Before You Enable
  • Pod restart: VPA Auto EVICTS pods to apply new resource values. If you have 3 replicas and VPA updates all 3 simultaneously → brief outage. Use PDBs.
  • Cannot be combined with HPA on same resource: Don't use VPA for CPU + HPA for CPU on the same Deployment. VPA for memory + HPA for CPU is OK.
  • OOMKilled during update: If VPA lowers memory too aggressively, pods might OOM. Set minAllowed as a safety net.
  • StatefulSets: VPA Auto on StatefulSets is riskier — pod identity matters. Use Off mode + manual updates for databases.

12.8 FinOps & Cost Management — Showback vs Chargeback

ConceptWhat It IsTool
ShowbackShow teams their costs WITHOUT charging them. Creates awareness.Kubecost, OpenCost
ChargebackACTUALLY bill teams based on their resource consumption.Kubecost + cloud billing API
Cost AllocationTag resources (namespace labels → cost centers). kubectl label ns team-a cost-center=1234.Kubecost namespace view
Right-SizingIdentify over-provisioned resources. VPA recommends lower requests.VPA recommender

12.9 Spot Instances — Up to 90% Cheaper, But Can Vanish

Spot instances are spare cloud capacity sold at deep discount. AWS gives a 2-minute warning before termination. Use for: stateless workloads (web pods, workers, batch jobs). NEVER use for: databases, stateful services. Combine with PDBs and fast startup times to handle interruptions gracefully.

💡 Karpenter Spot Provisioner — Spot-First with On-Demand Fallback
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1beta1
kind: NodePool
metadata: {name: spot-burst}
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      requirements:
      - key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type
        operator: In
        values: ["spot", "on-demand"]  # Spot preferred, on-demand fallback
      - key: kubernetes.io/arch
        operator: In
        values: ["amd64"]
      nodeClassRef: {name: default}
  limits:
    cpu: 64  # Max 64 CPU across all spot nodes
  disruption:
    consolidationPolicy: WhenUnderutilized
    expireAfter: 720h  # Replace nodes after 30 days
  weight: 100  # Higher weight = preferred
---
# Separate on-demand NodePool as safety net
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1beta1
kind: NodePool
metadata: {name: on-demand-safe}
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      requirements:
      - key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type
        operator: In
        values: ["on-demand"]
  weight: 1  # Lower weight = use only when spot unavailable
🎉 Handling Spot Interruption — The anihpj Resilience Pattern
  • ✅ 2-minute warning: AWS sends termination notice → K8s taints node (NoExecute) → pods get SIGTERM.
  • ✅ Graceful shutdown: Django/Gunicorn: stop accepting new connections, finish in-flight requests, exit (5-10 seconds).
  • ✅ PDB protection: minAvailable ensures at least some pods stay running during mass interruption.
  • ✅ Karpenter replacement: Detects spot interruption → provisions replacement node BEFORE the spot node terminates (node taint timing gives it 2 minutes).
  • ✅ Pod Topology Spread: Spreads pods across AZs. Spot interruption in us-east-1a → pods in 1b and 1c still serving. Zero downtime.
  • ✅ Celery workers: task_acks_late=True — if worker dies mid-task, task re-queued to another worker. No lost work.
📖 Spot Best Practices — The Platform Engineer's Checklist
  • Diversify instance types: Don't request just t3.medium. Request t3, t3a, m5, m5a, c5 families. More types = lower interruption rate.
  • Mix AZs: Spot capacity varies per AZ. Spread across all AZs to minimize simultaneous interruptions.
  • Monitor interruption rate: If >5% of spot nodes are interrupted daily, increase on-demand percentage or investigate instance diversification.
  • Fallback plan: Karpenter's spot-first + on-demand fallback ensures workloads ALWAYS run. Higher cost briefly, but no outage.
  • Test regularly: Use AWS Fault Injection Simulator to trigger spot interruptions in staging. Verify your pods handle it correctly.

12.10 anihpj Cost Optimization Strategy

Reserved Instances (baseline): PostgreSQL (StatefulSet), Redis — always-on, predictable load. 1-year reserved = 40% savings. Spot Instances (burst): anihpj-web pods, Celery workers — stateless, can restart quickly. 90% savings. Karpenter (auto-scaling): Spot-first, on-demand fallback when spot unavailable. Bin-packing minimizes waste. Kubecost: Per-namespace cost breakdown. Team A spends $800/mo on compute. Team B spends $200. Data-driven conversations about efficiency.

🧠 Deep Dive — Compute, Scheduling & Cost Core Concepts

📖 How Linux cgroups Enforce K8s Resource Limits — The Kernel Mechanism

When you set resources.limits.memory: 512Mi, K8s doesn't have its own enforcement engine. It delegates to Linux cgroups (control groups) — a kernel feature that limits, accounts for, and isolates resource usage. Understanding this explains WHY memory limits kill containers and CPU limits only throttle:

# What K8s does when you create a pod with memory limit 512Mi:
# 1. kubelet tells containerd: "Create container with memory limit 512Mi"
# 2. containerd creates a cgroup for this container:
#    /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/kubepods/burstable/pod-<UID>/<container-ID>/
# 3. containerd writes 512Mi to the cgroup's memory.limit_in_bytes file
# 4. Linux kernel enforces: if container exceeds 512Mi → OOM killer triggers
# 5. OOM killer sends SIGKILL to the container process → container exits
# 6. kubelet sees container exit → reports OOMKilled to API server

# See it yourself:
POD_UID=$(kubectl get pod anihpj-web-xxx -o jsonpath='{.metadata.uid}')
ls /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/kubepods/burstable/pod$POD_UID/
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/kubepods/burstable/pod$POD_UID/memory.limit_in_bytes
# 536870912 (= 512Mi)

# CPU throttling works differently:
# cgroup cpu.max = "50000 100000" means:
#   - 50000 microseconds of CPU per 100000 microsecond period
#   - = 50% of one CPU core
#   - Container CAN burst above this, but gets throttled back
#   - NO KILL — just slower execution

Critical insight: Memory limits are a HARD WALL. CPU limits are a RUBBER BAND. This is why production databases need Guaranteed QoS (request=limit) — you never want the OOM killer deciding PostgreSQL's fate. And this is why CPU limits can be set higher than requests — throttling is safer than killing.

📖 Scheduler Scoring Algorithm — The Math Behind Pod Placement

The K8s scheduler doesn't randomly pick nodes. It runs through a scoring pipeline where each plugin assigns 0-100 points. The node with the highest weighted total wins:

Scoring PluginWhat It ScoresHigher = Better WhenWeight
NodeResourcesFitLeastAllocated: scores nodes with MORE free resources higher. MostAllocated (for bin-packing): scores nodes with LESS free resources higher.LeastAllocated for spreading workloads. MostAllocated for cost optimization (fill nodes before adding new ones).1
ImageLocalityDoes the node already have the container image cached? Full image = 10 points. No image = 0 points.Large images (ML models, Java apps). Saves 30-60s image pull time.1
PodTopologySpreadHow evenly are pods distributed across topology domains (zones, nodes)? Balanced = high score.HA-critical workloads that must survive zone failures.2
NodeAffinityDoes the node match preferred affinity rules? Matched = 100. Not matched = 0.Workloads with hardware requirements (GPU, SSD).1
TaintTolerationThis runs in the FILTERING phase (not scoring). If pod doesn't tolerate a taint, node is eliminated BEFORE scoring.N/A — taints are binary (pass/fail).N/A

Final Score = Σ (plugin_score × plugin_weight). Example: NodeResourcesFit(80) × 1 + ImageLocality(10) × 1 + PodTopologySpread(60) × 2 = 80 + 10 + 120 = 210. The scheduler picks the node with the highest total. Ties are broken randomly. You can see this in action: kubectl describe pod <name> | grep -A10 Events shows "Scoring" events with the winner.

📖 Karpenter Architecture — Why It's Faster Than Cluster Autoscaler

Karpenter doesn't just "autoscale faster." It fundamentally rethinks node provisioning:

DimensionCluster AutoscalerKarpenter
Decision MakingWatches for Pending pods. Checks if ANY node in ANY node group can fit it. If not → adds 1 node to the largest-matching node group.Watches for Pending pods. Evaluates ALL 600+ EC2 instance types in real-time. Selects the OPTIMAL type/size/zone for the EXACT pod requirements.
Node CreationIncreases ASG desired count → AWS launches EC2 instance → instance boots → kubelet registers → node joins. 2-5 minutes.Calls EC2 RunInstances API directly → instance boots → kubelet registers → node joins. 30-60 seconds.
Bin-PackingSimple: one pod at a time. If Pod A needs 2 CPU and nodes are full → add new node. Pod B needs 1 CPU (5 min later) → checks if it fits existing nodes → fits on new node. But that node is t3.large (2 CPU) for 2+1=3 CPU pods — wasted 1 CPU.Batch scheduling: queues pending pods for 10 seconds. Simulates packing them onto existing + potential new nodes. Chooses the configuration with minimum waste + minimum cost.
ConsolidationBasic: if node is underutilized for 10 min → drains and terminates. One node at a time.Advanced: identifies nodes that can be REPLACED by cheaper nodes. If 3 t3.medium nodes (2 CPU each, $0.0416/hr) could be replaced by 1 m5.xlarge (4 CPU, $0.192/hr) → consolidates. Saves money.
Spot HandlingLimited: spot node groups. If spot unavailable, pods stay Pending until on-demand group scales up.Native: "Spot-first, on-demand fallback" in ONE NodePool. No separate node groups needed. 90% cost savings on variable workloads.

When Karpenter makes sense for anihpj: Production cluster with bursty traffic (peak = 3× baseline). Karpenter provisions spot nodes for the burst, consolidates them when traffic drops, and falls back to on-demand if spot is unavailable. Result: 60-70% cost reduction vs static node groups. When NOT to use Karpenter: tiny clusters (<5 nodes) where the operational complexity isn't justified. Cluster Autoscaler is simpler and works fine at small scale.

💡 FinOps Maturity Model — From Wasteful to World-Class

FinOps isn't just about tools. It's a cultural practice that matures over time:

StageWhat HappensToolsanihpj Status
0. No VisibilityAWS bill arrives. "Why is it $5000 this month?" Nobody knows. Engineering and finance don't talk.AWS Cost Explorer (monthly surprise).🚫 Avoid this
1. ShowbackCosts are VISIBLE. Each team sees their spend. Nobody is billed — just informed. "Team A, your workloads cost $3200 this month."Kubecost namespace view. AWS tags → cost allocation.✅ Current goal
2. ChargebackTeams are BILLED for their usage. Creates accountability. "Team A's cost center is charged $3200." Teams optimize because it affects their budget.Kubecost + cloud billing API + internal invoicing.🔜 Next quarter
3. OptimizationSystematic waste elimination. Spot instances for stateless. Reserved for baseline. Right-sizing via VPA. Idle resource termination.Karpenter spot-first, VPA recommender, Kubecost savings recommendations.🔜 This year
4. Unit EconomicsCost per business metric. "$0.003 per API call." "$0.12 per job posting." Engineers optimize cost per unit, not total spend.Custom dashboards (Grafana + Prometheus metrics ÷ Kubecost spend).🔮 Future

📝 View Solution

Drill 12.4 — Node Drain Stuck (PDB Blocking)

kubectl drain is stuck. kubectl describe node shows PDB blocking. What's the fix?

💡 Hint: PDB prevents eviction if it would violate minAvailable. Either wait, scale up, or force.
📝 View Solution
Check PDB: kubectl get pdb -n anihpj
PDB says minAvailable: 2 for 3 replicas.
Drain tries to evict 2 pods → violates minAvailable → blocked.

Fixes:
1. Scale Deployment up to 4 replicas → drain can evict 2 (4-2=2, OK)
2. Temporarily delete PDB → drain → recreate PDB
3. Force drain: kubectl drain --disable-eviction (WARNING: ignores PDB!)
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 12.5 — Cluster Autoscaler vs Karpenter

anihpj has burst traffic (3× normal at peak). Which autoscaler and why?

💡 Hint: Karpenter provisions nodes faster and chooses optimal instance types.
📝 View Solution
Karpenter wins for burst traffic:
- 30-60s node provisioning vs 2-5 min (ASG)
- Dynamic instance selection (choose most cost-effective)
- Spot-first then on-demand fallback
- Bin-packing minimizes wasted capacity

Cluster Autoscaler: OK for steady workloads, pre-defined node groups.
Karpenter: Better for variable/burst workloads, cost optimization.
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 12.6 — Find Which Team Costs $5000

AWS bill shows $5000/month for K8s. How do you find which team/namespace is responsible?

💡 Hint: kubectl top pods → aggregate by namespace. Kubecost shows per-namespace cost breakdown.
📝 View Solution
1. Install Kubecost: helm install kubecost kubecost/cost-analyzer
2. Open Kubecost dashboard → Namespace view
3. Sort by cost: team-a: $3200 (64%), team-b: $1200 (24%), team-c: $600 (12%)
4. Drill into team-a → find which workloads cost most

Alternative: kubectl top pods -A | sort -k3 -rn | head -20
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 12.7 — Over-Provisioned Resources

Team requests 8GB RAM per pod but uses only 500MB. What tool identifies this? How do you fix?

💡 Hint: VPA recommender shows recommended vs actual usage. VPA auto mode fixes it.
📝 View Solution
Identify: VPA recommender → shows:
  Container: anihpj-web
  Recommendation: CPU: 100m, Memory: 512Mi
  Current request: Memory: 8Gi (16x over-provisioned!)

Fix:
- VPA Off mode: show recommendations, manually update Deployments
- VPA Auto mode: auto-updates requests (evicts pod, recreates with new values)
- Warning: VPA Auto causes pod restart!
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 12.8 — Spot Instance Termination

Spot instance terminated mid-job. How does the anihpj Celery worker handle this?

💡 Hint: 2-minute warning → SIGTERM → graceful shutdown. Celery acks late. Job re-queued.
📝 View Solution
1. AWS sends 2-minute termination notice
2. K8s node gets taint: node.kubernetes.io/instance-type=spot:NoExecute
3. K8s sends SIGTERM to Celery worker pod
4. Celery worker: finishes current task, rejects re-queue, exits
5. Karpenter launches replacement node (on-demand if spot unavailable)
6. New Celery worker starts on new node → picks up re-queued task

Requirements:
- Celery: task_acks_late=True (re-queue on worker failure)
- PodDisruptionBudget: minAvailable for workers
- Fast startup: worker container starts in 5-10 seconds
⏱️ Target: 2 minutes
Drill 12.9 — 3 Replicas, 2 Nodes

podAntiAffinity requires 3 replicas on 3 different nodes, but cluster has only 2 nodes. What happens?

💡 Hint: requiredDuringScheduling = hard. 2 replicas run, 1 stays Pending. preferredDuringScheduling = soft → all 3 run.
📝 View Solution
requiredDuringScheduling (hard): 2 pods running, 1 Pending forever.
kubectl describe pod shows: "0/2 nodes are available:
  2 node(s) didn't match pod anti-affinity rules."

preferredDuringScheduling (soft): all 3 pods running.
Scheduler prefers separate nodes but settles for 2+1.

Production fix: scale nodes to 3, OR use preferredDuringScheduling
with maxSkew in topologySpreadConstraints.
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 12.10 — Cost Optimization Strategy

Design cost optimization: reserved for baseline, spot for burst, auto-fallback to on-demand.

💡 Hint: Karpenter provisioner: spot-first, on-demand fallback. Reserved Instances for DB.
📝 View Solution
Baseline (always running): PostgreSQL (RDS Reserved, 1yr, 40% off),
  Redis (ElastiCache Reserved). Predictable, stable.

Burst (variable): anihpj-web, Celery workers. Karpenter:
  - requirements: [instance-type: spot, on-demand]
  - weight: spot=100, on-demand=1 (spot preferred, fallback)
  - 90% cost savings on burst workloads

Monitoring: Kubecost shows per-team, per-namespace costs.
Alert: if spot interruption rate > 5%, increase on-demand percentage.

Total estimated savings: 60-70% vs all on-demand.

📖 Chapter 12 Summary: Scheduling determines WHERE pods run. Resource management determines HOW MUCH they consume. Cost management determines WHAT it all costs. A platform engineer balances all three — performance (right-sizing without throttling), efficiency (bin-packing without waste), and economics (spot instances + reserved = 60-70% savings).

Why Chapter 13 Matters on the CNPE Exam

You WILL be asked to: write an Argo CD Application YAML, configure sync policies (prune, selfHeal), debug OutOfSync states, set up ApplicationSets for multi-cluster, and choose between Sealed Secrets vs External Secrets for GitOps secret management. 13.1 What Is GitOps? — Git as the Single Source of Truth

GitOps is an operational model where Git is the single source of truth for your entire platform. Instead of running kubectl apply manually, you commit YAML to Git. An agent inside the cluster (Argo CD or Flux) watches Git and syncs the cluster to match. This means:

GITOPS FLOW — Push to Git, Agent Syncs to Cluster
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                        GITOPS DELIVERY FLOW                              │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  DEVELOPER                          GIT                        K8S CLUSTER
  ─────────                          ───                        ───────────

  ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ ① Write  │────►│ ② Commit │────►│ ③ Git     │     │ ④ Argo CD detects    │
  │ YAML     │     │ & Push   │     │   repo    │────►│    change in Git      │
  │ manifests│     │ to Git   │     │ updated   │     │    (polls every 3min) │
  └──────────┘     └──────────┘     └──────────┘     └──────────┬───────────┘
                                                                │
                                     ┌──────────────────────────┘
                                     │ ⑤ Argo CD compares Git (desired)
                                     │    vs Cluster (actual)
                                     ▼
                          ┌──────────────────────┐
                          │ ⑥ DIFFERENCE FOUND?   │
                          │ Git: replicas=3       │
                          │ Cluster: replicas=2   │
                          └──────────┬───────────┘
                                     │ YES — OUT OF SYNC
                                     ▼
                          ┌──────────────────────┐
                          │ ⑦ Argo CD applies    │
                          │ kubectl apply -f     │
                          │ Cluster now: 3 pods  │
                          └──────────┬───────────┘
                                     │
                                     ▼
                          ┌──────────────────────┐
                          │ ⑧ Argo CD reports    │
                          │ "Synced" → Healthy   │
                          └──────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  KEY: Developer never touches the cluster. CI system has NO cluster creds.
  Argo CD LIVES in the cluster and PULLS from Git. This is pull-based GitOps.
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
🎉 GitOps vs Traditional CI/CD — Why GitOps Wins
  • ✅ Traditional (Push): CI pipeline runs kubectl apply. CI needs cluster credentials. If CI is compromised → attacker gets cluster access.
  • ✅ GitOps (Pull): Argo CD lives IN the cluster. Pulls from Git. CI has ZERO cluster access. If CI is compromised → attacker can only push to Git, which is auditable and reversible.
  • ✅ Self-Healing: Someone runs kubectl edit deployment and changes replicas. Argo CD detects drift within 3 minutes → reverts to Git state. The cluster is ALWAYS converging toward Git.
  • ✅ Audit Trail: Every change to the cluster goes through Git. git log shows who changed what, when, and why. No more "who ran kubectl apply at 3 AM?"

13.2 GitOps Principles — The 4 Pillars

📝
1. Declarative

Everything is expressed as YAML/JSON in Git. No imperative commands (kubectl scale). System state is declared, not scripted. "I want 3 replicas" — not "run this script to create 3 replicas."

📚
2. Versioned

Git history = audit log. Every change has a commit hash, author, timestamp, and message. Rollback = git revert. No separate change management database needed.

🔄
3. Pull-Based

Agent INSIDE cluster pulls from Git. No external system pushes to the cluster. This inverts the security model — the cluster reaches OUT to get its desired state.

🤖
4. Continuously Reconciled

Agent constantly compares desired (Git) vs actual (cluster). Any difference triggers correction. Not just on deploy — ALWAYS. Drift is auto-corrected within minutes.

13.3 Repo Structure — Monorepo vs Polyrepo & App of Apps

PatternStructureProsConsBest For
MonorepoOne repo: platform/teams/{a,b,c}/*.yamlSingle source of truth, easy cross-team changesLarge repos, permission granularitySingle platform team managing everything
PolyrepoPer-team repos: team-a/infra, team-b/infraTeam autonomy, smaller repos, OWNERS filesCross-team consistency harder, more repos to manageMultiple autonomous teams
💡 App of Apps Pattern — The Key to Scaling GitOps

The App of Apps pattern: one ROOT Argo CD Application deploys CHILD Applications. Each child represents an environment, team, or service. The root app watches a directory — adding a new YAML file to that directory auto-creates a new child Application.

# Root Application — watches apps/ directory
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: root-app
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/anihpj/infrastructure.git
    path: argocd/apps/          # ← watches THIS directory
    targetRevision: main
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: argocd
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
# Any YAML in argocd/apps/ → auto-created as Argo CD Application
# Add: argocd/apps/anihpj-dev.yaml → Argo CD creates "anihpj-dev" app
💡 Sync Waves & Phases — Controlling Deployment Order

Argo CD syncs resources in order: first by phase (PreSync → Sync → PostSync), then by wave within each phase (lower numbers first, negatives allowed). This ensures dependencies deploy before dependents:

# PostgreSQL must exist BEFORE anihpj-web
# postgres-statefulset.yaml:
metadata:
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-1"  # Deploy FIRST

# redis-deployment.yaml:
metadata:
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "0"   # Deploy SECOND

# anihpj-web-deployment.yaml:
metadata:
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "1"   # Deploy LAST (depends on DB + Redis)

# Within same wave: resources sync in PARALLEL (fast!)
# Across waves: sync SEQUENTIALLY (dependency order)
# Total order: wave -1 → wave 0 → wave 1 → ... (higher numbers)

Sync phases: PreSync (run migrations, create secrets) → Sync (apply manifests) → PostSync (run smoke tests, send notifications). Hooks in each phase can be Jobs or Pods that must succeed before the next phase starts.

13.4 Argo CD — Application, Sync, and Health

An Argo CD Application defines WHAT to deploy (Git repo + path), WHERE to deploy (cluster + namespace), and HOW to sync (auto/manual, prune, selfHeal).

😰 The 3 AM kubectl Edit — How selfHeal Saved Production
  • 🔴 3:00 AM: On-call engineer gets paged. Production is slow. They SSH to a node and run kubectl edit deployment anihpj-web — change replicas from 3 to 10. Traffic spike handled. Engineer goes back to sleep.
  • 🔴 3:03 AM: Argo CD detects drift: Git says replicas=3, cluster says replicas=10. selfHeal: true → Argo CD reverts the change. Replicas drop back to 3. Traffic spike RETURNS.
  • 🔴 3:05 AM: Engineer gets paged AGAIN. Replicas are back at 3. Engineer edits again → 3 minutes later, Argo CD reverts again. Infinite loop.
  • 🟡 The RIGHT fix: Edit the Deployment YAML in Git → set replicas: 10 → commit → Argo CD syncs. Now Git says 10, cluster says 10. Problem permanently solved. selfHeal prevents bandaids — it forces you to fix the SOURCE.
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata: {name: anihpj-prod, namespace: argocd}
spec:
  project: production  # Must match an AppProject
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/anihpj/infrastructure.git
    path: k8s/overlays/production
    targetRevision: main
  destination:
    server: https://prod-cluster.example.com  # Target cluster
    namespace: anihpj
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true    # Delete resources that exist in cluster but NOT in Git
      selfHeal: true # Auto-fix drift: if someone edits in cluster, revert to Git
    syncOptions:
    - CreateNamespace=true
    retry:
      limit: 5
      backoff: {duration: 10s, factor: 2, maxDuration: 3m}

13.5 Argo CD — AppProject for RBAC Scope

AppProjects restrict which clusters, namespaces, and resource types an Application can deploy to. Without AppProjects, any Application can deploy anywhere — a security risk.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AppProject
metadata: {name: production, namespace: argocd}
spec:
  sourceRepos: [https://github.com/anihpj/infrastructure.git]
  destinations:
  - namespace: anihpj
    server: https://prod-cluster.example.com
  clusterResourceWhitelist:
  - group: '*'  # Allow only specific cluster-scoped resources
    kind: 'Namespace'

13.6 ApplicationSets — Templated Deployments for Multi-Cluster

ApplicationSets generate Argo CD Applications from templates. One ApplicationSet can deploy anihpj to dev, staging, AND production — each with different configurations.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata: {name: anihpj, namespace: argocd}
spec:
  generators:
  - list:
      elements:
      - env: dev
        cluster: https://dev-cluster.example.com
        replicas: "1"
      - env: staging
        cluster: https://staging-cluster.example.com
        replicas: "2"
      - env: production
        cluster: https://prod-cluster.example.com
        replicas: "3"
  template:
    metadata: {name: 'anihpj-{{env}}'}
    spec:
      project: production
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/anihpj/infrastructure.git
        path: 'k8s/overlays/{{env}}'
        targetRevision: main
      destination:
        server: '{{cluster}}'
        namespace: anihpj
      syncPolicy:
        automated: {prune: true, selfHeal: true}
1
Manual kubectl
kubectl apply -f
No audit. No rollback.
2
Scripted Deploy
CI runs kubectl.
CI has cluster creds.
3
Basic GitOps
Argo CD polls Git.
Manual sync button.
4
Auto-Sync GitOps
selfHeal + prune.
Cluster auto-converges.
5
Multi-Cluster GitOps
Hub-and-spoke.

13.7 Flux CD — GitRepository, Kustomization, HelmRelease

Flux CD takes a different approach than Argo CD. Instead of "Applications," Flux uses dedicated CRDs for each concern. Here's what a Flux deployment looks like:

# 1. GitRepository — WHERE is the source?
apiVersion: source.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: GitRepository
metadata: {name: anihpj, namespace: flux-system}
spec:
  interval: 3m  # Check Git every 3 minutes
  url: https://github.com/anihpj/infrastructure.git
  ref: {branch: main}
---
# 2. Kustomization — WHAT to apply?
apiVersion: kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: Kustomization
metadata: {name: anihpj-prod, namespace: flux-system}
spec:
  interval: 5m
  path: ./k8s/overlays/production
  prune: true  # Delete resources removed from Git
  sourceRef:
    kind: GitRepository
    name: anihpj
  healthChecks:  # Wait for these to be healthy before reporting success
  - apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: anihpj-web
    namespace: anihpj
---
# 3. HelmRelease — Deploy a Helm chart
apiVersion: helm.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v2beta1
kind: HelmRelease
metadata: {name: anihpj-redis, namespace: flux-system}
spec:
  interval: 10m
  chart:
    spec:
      chart: redis
      version: 18.x.x
      sourceRef:
        kind: HelmRepository
        name: bitnami
  values:
    architecture: standalone
    auth:
      password: s3cret  # Use SOPS or Sealed Secrets!
🔄 Argo CD
  • CRD: Application (all-in-one resource)
  • UI: Rich web dashboard — see all apps, health, sync status
  • Multi-Cluster: Native — one Argo CD instance manages many clusters
  • Sync: Polls Git every 3 minutes (configurable)
  • RBAC: AppProject restricts which clusters/namespaces apps deploy to
  • CNPE Focus: Heavily tested on the exam
📂 Flux CD
  • CRDs: GitRepository + Kustomization + HelmRelease (composable)
  • UI: CLI-first. No built-in web UI. Can add Weave GitOps dashboard.
  • Multi-Cluster: Flux installed per cluster. Each reconciles independently.
  • Sync: Configurable interval per resource. Image update automation built-in.
  • RBAC: Native K8s RBAC per CRD — more granular control
  • CNPE Focus: Know the CRDs and how Flux differs from Argo CD

13.8 Secrets in GitOps — Encrypted, Synced, Never Plaintext

ToolHow It WorksGit-Safe?ComplexityBest For
Sealed SecretsEncrypts K8s Secret with cluster's public key. Only that cluster can decrypt. Encrypted YAML is safe to commit.✅ Yes⭐⭐GitOps — encrypted secrets live next to app manifests in Git
SOPSEncrypts YAML/JSON with cloud KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS). Decrypt on deploy (Argo CD Vault Plugin or Flux SOPS).✅ Yes⭐⭐Teams already using cloud KMS; multi-cloud
External Secrets OperatorNO secrets in Git. Syncs from AWS/GCP/Azure secret stores INTO K8s Secrets. ExternalSecret CRD defines what to sync.✅ (nothing in Git)⭐⭐⭐Enterprise — secrets managed in cloud secret managers, not Git at all

13.9 Infrastructure GitOps — Crossplane & Terraform via Flux

GitOps isn't just for applications. Infrastructure-as-Code can also be GitOps-managed. Crossplane provisions cloud infrastructure (RDS, S3, IAM) as K8s CRDs — managed by Argo CD/Flux like any other K8s resource. Terraform can be run via Flux's TF-controller — Git commit triggers terraform plan → manual approval → terraform apply.

13.10 Multi-Cluster GitOps — Hub-and-Spoke Architecture

HUB-AND-SPOKE — One Argo CD Manages Many Clusters

  │                 HUB-AND-SPOKE GITOPS ARCHITECTURE                        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

                    ┌──────────────────────────┐
                    │     GIT REPOSITORY       │

                    │                          │
                    │  apps/dev/               │

                    │  apps/production/        │
                    └────────────┬─────────────┘

                    ┌────────────▼─────────────┐

                    │  (Management / Control)   │
                    │                          │
                    │  ┌──────────────────────┐│
                    │  │ Argo CD              ││

                    │  └──────────┬───────────┘│

                                  │
          ┌───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┐
          │                       │                       │

  ┌───────────────┐     ┌───────────────┐     ┌───────────────┐

  └───────────────┘     └───────────────┘     └───────────────┘

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  HUB: runs Argo CD. Has credentials for ALL spoke clusters.
  SPOKE: workload clusters. Argo CD deploys TO them.
  GITOPS DISASTER RECOVERY: Hub cluster burns down → spin up new K8s cluster

🧠 Deep Dive — GitOps Core Concepts

📖 How Argo CD Sync Works Internally — The Reconciliation Loop

When Argo CD says "Synced," a complex reconciliation process just completed. Understanding this is critical for debugging sync failures:

  1. Compare (every 3 min): Argo CD fetches the latest commit from Git (targetRevision). It runs kubectl apply --dry-run equivalent to generate the DESIRED manifest. Then it queries the K8s API for the ACTUAL state. Diff = desired - actual.
  2. If diff is empty: App is "Synced." No action needed. This is the steady state — 99% of the time.
  3. If diff is non-empty: App is "OutOfSync." Argo CD shows the diff in the UI (green = added, red = removed). If automated.selfHeal: true, Argo CD automatically applies the diff. If automated.prune: true, resources that exist in the cluster but NOT in Git are DELETED.
  4. After applying: Argo CD waits for resources to become healthy. A Deployment is "Healthy" when status.availableReplicas == spec.replicas. A Pod is "Healthy" when its status is Running. Custom health checks can be defined via Lua scripts in the argocd-cm ConfigMap.
  5. Sync phases: PreSync (hooks run) → Sync (apply manifests in wave order) → PostSync (hooks run). If any phase fails → App shows "Unknown" or "Degraded."

Why this matters: When an Application shows "OutOfSync" but you haven't changed anything, someone modified the cluster directly. Argo CD's diff shows EXACTLY what changed. When it shows "Degraded," a resource failed its health check — check kubectl describe on the failing resource, not Argo CD logs.

📖 ApplicationSet Generators — How They Work Under the Hood

ApplicationSets don't just "generate" Applications. Each generator type works differently, and understanding this helps you debug when Applications don't appear:

GeneratorHow It WorksUse CaseWatch Out For
ListStatic list of elements. ApplicationSet controller iterates over each element, renders the template, creates one Application per element.Fixed environments: dev, staging, production. Each element has different cluster/namespace/values.Elements are hardcoded. Adding a new environment = edit the ApplicationSet YAML.
ClusterQueries Argo CD's list of connected clusters. Creates one Application PER cluster automatically. If you add a new cluster to Argo CD → new Application appears without editing the ApplicationSet."Deploy anihpj to every cluster I connect to Argo CD." Bootstrap new clusters automatically.All clusters get the SAME configuration. Use cluster labels in the template for per-cluster customization.
GitWatches a Git directory. Each subdirectory = one Application. Add a new directory → new Application auto-created. The Git repo IS the list of elements.Teams self-service: create a directory in teams/ → Argo CD deploys it. No ApplicationSet edits needed.Directory structure must match template expectations. Git permission model must be correct.
MatrixCombines TWO generators (Cartesian product). List × Cluster = one Application per environment per cluster.anihpj deployed to 3 environments × 4 regions = 12 Applications from one ApplicationSet.Explosion risk: 10 elements × 10 clusters = 100 Applications. Set limits on generator size.
💡 How Flux CD Source Controller Works — Git Polling & Artifact Storage

Flux doesn't just "pull from Git." The source-controller is a dedicated component that manages GitRepository and HelmRepository resources:

  1. Poll: Every spec.interval (e.g., 3m), source-controller does git fetch to check for new commits. Not a full clone — a lightweight fetch.
  2. Artifact: When changes are detected, source-controller clones/pulls the repo, archives it as a .tar.gz, and stores it as a K8s Artifact (referenced by URL). The artifact is stored in a persistent volume or OCI registry.
  3. Notification: Source-controller updates the GitRepository status with the latest commit SHA and artifact URL. Other controllers (kustomize-controller, helm-controller) WATCH GitRepository resources for changes.
  4. Reconciliation: Kustomization controller detects the new artifact → downloads it → runs kustomize build → applies to cluster. HelmRelease controller detects new artifact → downloads chart → runs helm upgrade --install.

Key difference from Argo CD: Flux stores the ENTIRE repo as an artifact (tar.gz in-cluster). Argo CD clones the repo in-memory on each sync. Flux's approach means you can reconcile even when Git is temporarily unavailable — as long as the artifact is cached.

🏋️ Chapter 13 — Hands-On Practice Drills (10 Exercises)

⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 13.1 — Write an Argo CD Application for anihpj

Create an Argo CD Application that deploys anihpj from GitHub to your cluster.

  1. Write the Application YAML: source repo, path, destination
  2. Configure auto-sync with prune and selfHeal
  3. Apply and verify sync status
💡 Hint: argocd app create or write Application CRD. Check status with argocd app get anihpj-prod.
📝 View Solution
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata: {name: anihpj-prod, namespace: argocd}
spec:
  project: default
  source: {repoURL: https://github.com/anihpj/infrastructure.git, path: k8s/base, targetRevision: main}
  destination: {server: https://kubernetes.default.svc, namespace: anihpj}
  syncPolicy: {automated: {prune: true, selfHeal: true}}

kubectl apply -f application.yaml
argocd app get anihpj-prod
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 13.2 — Detect and Fix Drift

Argo CD Application shows "OutOfSync." You check: cluster has 3 replicas, Git says 2. What happened? How does Argo CD fix it?

💡 Hint: Someone manually ran kubectl scale. Argo CD selfHeal auto-reverts. Without selfHeal, it shows OutOfSync.
📝 View Solution
Cause: Someone ran kubectl scale deployment anihpj-web --replicas=3
Argo CD detected: DESIRED (Git) = 2, ACTUAL (Cluster) = 3 → OutOfSync

Without selfHeal: shows OutOfSync, waits for manual sync
With selfHeal: auto-reverts to 2 replicas within 3 minutes

Fix: kubectl scale deployment anihpj-web --replicas=2
OR: git revert the commit that changed replicas
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 13.3 — Argo CD vs Flux CD

Compare across 5 dimensions: UI, sync mechanism, CRDs, multi-cluster, complexity.

💡 Hint: Argo CD = Application CRD + rich UI. Flux = GitRepository + Kustomization + HelmRelease + CLI-first.
📝 View Solution
1. UI: Argo CD has rich web UI. Flux is CLI-first (no built-in UI).
2. Sync: Argo CD polls Git every 3 min. Flux polls at configurable interval.
3. CRDs: Argo CD uses Application CRD. Flux uses GitRepository+Kustomization+HelmRelease.
4. Multi-cluster: Argo CD natively connects to multiple clusters. Flux installed per cluster.
5. Complexity: Argo CD simpler to start. Flux more composable for advanced scenarios.
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 13.4 — ApplicationSet for 3 Environments

Deploy anihpj to dev, staging, prod on 3 clusters using an ApplicationSet with list generator.

💡 Hint: Use list generator with elements for each environment. Template uses {{env}}, {{cluster}}, {{replicas}}.
📝 View Solution
generators:
- list:
    elements:
    - {env: dev, cluster: https://dev.local, replicas: "1"}
    - {env: staging, cluster: https://stg.local, replicas: "2"}
    - {env: production, cluster: https://prod.local, replicas: "3"}
template:
  metadata: {name: 'anihpj-{{env}}'}
  spec:
    destination: {server: '{{cluster}}', namespace: anihpj}
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 13.5 — Secrets: Sealed Secrets vs External Secrets vs SOPS

Compare 3 secret management approaches for GitOps.

💡 Hint: Sealed Secrets = encrypted YAML in Git. SOPS = cloud KMS encrypted. External Secrets = nothing in Git, sync from cloud.
📝 View Solution
Sealed Secrets: Encrypt with cluster key → commit encrypted YAML → controller decrypts in cluster.
  Pro: simple, self-contained. Con: secrets still in Git (encrypted).

SOPS: Encrypt with AWS KMS → commit encrypted → Argo CD decrypts via plugin.
  Pro: uses existing KMS keys, multi-cloud. Con: needs plugin config.

External Secrets: ExternalSecret CRD → ESO fetches from AWS Secrets Manager → creates K8s Secret.
  Pro: NO secrets in Git. Auto-rotation. Con: more complex setup, cloud dependency.
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 13.6 — AppProject Restrictions

Create an AppProject that limits anihpj deployments to the "anihpj" namespace on the production cluster only.

💡 Hint: Use destinations + clusterResourceWhitelist to restrict what the project can deploy.
📝 View Solution
spec:
  destinations:
  - namespace: anihpj
    server: https://prod-cluster.example.com
  sourceRepos: [https://github.com/anihpj/infrastructure.git]
  # Cannot deploy to other namespaces or clusters
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 13.7 — GitOps Disaster Recovery

Production cluster burned down. Walk through recovery using GitOps.

💡 Hint: All desired state is in Git. Spin up new cluster → install Argo CD → point to same Git repo → everything re-syncs.
📝 View Solution
1. Provision new K8s cluster (EKS, kind, kubeadm — any)
2. Install Argo CD: kubectl apply -f argocd-install.yaml
3. Apply root Application pointing to Git repo
4. Argo CD syncs ALL applications from Git
5. Wait for sync → all pods running → health checks pass
6. Update DNS to point to new load balancer
7. Verify: same Git, same cluster state

RTO: ~15-30 min for small clusters, ~1hr for large
No backup restoration needed — Git IS the backup!
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 13.8 — Sync Waves for Dependencies

PostgreSQL must deploy BEFORE anihpj-web. Configure Argo CD sync waves.

💡 Hint: Add annotation argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-1" to DB, "0" to web. Lower numbers sync first.
📝 View Solution
# PostgreSQL (sync first):
metadata:
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-1"

# Redis (sync second):
metadata:
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "0"

# anihpj-web (sync last — depends on DB + Redis):
metadata:
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "1"

# Argo CD syncs in wave order: -1 → 0 → 1 → ... → higher.
# Within same wave: sync in parallel.
⏱️ Target: 2 minutes
Drill 13.9 — Manual Cluster Edit vs GitOps

Someone ran kubectl edit deployment anihpj-web and changed the image tag. Argo CD reverts it. Why?

💡 Hint: selfHeal: true → Argo CD detects drift → reverts to Git state within 3 minutes.
📝 View Solution
Argo CD syncPolicy.automated.selfHeal: true
→ Every 3 minutes: compare cluster vs Git
→ Difference detected → apply Git version
→ Revert the manual edit

Without selfHeal: application shows OutOfSync, waits for manual intervention.
With selfHeal: application auto-corrects. Git is ALWAYS the truth.
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 13.10 — Multi-Cluster GitOps Architecture

Design a hub-and-spoke GitOps architecture: 1 control cluster + 3 workload clusters.

💡 Hint: Hub runs Argo CD. Spokes are target clusters. ApplicationSets deploy to all 3 with per-environment config.
📝 View Solution
Hub cluster (management):
- Runs Argo CD with access to all 3 spoke clusters
- Root ApplicationSets define what goes where
- RBAC: AppProjects restrict per-environment access

Spoke clusters (workload):
- No Argo CD installed (just the workloads)
- Argo CD on hub pushes to spoke clusters
- Each spoke has different: replica counts, resource limits, CNI

Git repo structure:
argocd/
  appsets/
    anihpj-appset.yaml  (deploys to all 3)
  projects/
    dev-project.yaml
    staging-project.yaml
    production-project.yaml

📖 Chapter 13 Summary: GitOps makes deployments auditable, reproducible, and self-healing. Argo CD is the de facto standard for K8s GitOps. The App of Apps pattern scales to hundreds of applications. ApplicationSets deploy to multiple clusters with templates. Secrets can live in Git (encrypted) or be synced from external stores. Multi-cluster GitOps uses hub-and-spoke: one Argo CD manages many clusters. If a cluster burns down, spin up a new one and Argo CD recreates everything from Git.

Chapter 14: CI/CD Pipeline Design

GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Tekton, Argo Workflows, image building strategies, artifact promotion, and pipeline security — the delivery backbone of your platform.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~3 hours⚡ CI/CD🔧 Pipeline

📖 Chapter Overview: The CI/CD pipeline is the automated path from developer laptop to production. CI builds and tests every commit. CD deploys (with approval gates for production). This chapter covers pipeline stages, tooling choices, image building, artifact promotion, and security scanning — all tested in CNPE Domain 2 (25%).

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Design CI/CD pipelines: Lint → Test → Build → Scan → Push → Deploy
  • ✅ Choose pipeline tools: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Tekton, Argo Workflows
  • ✅ Build container images securely without Docker daemon (Kaniko, Buildpacks)
  • ✅ Implement artifact promotion with immutable tags and attestations
  • ✅ Secure pipelines: SAST, secret scanning, dependency scanning
🎓 CNPE Relevance
GitOps & CD Domain 2 — 25% Pipeline Design CI/CD Integration

14.1 CI vs CD vs Continuous Deployment — Know the Difference

🔨
Continuous Integration

Build + test on EVERY push. Verify code compiles, tests pass, linting clean. Goal: catch issues within minutes of commit. "Does this code break anything?"

🚀
Continuous Delivery

Auto-deploy to staging. Production deploy requires MANUAL approval. Every commit that passes CI is "deliverable." "Could we deploy this right now?"

🤖
Continuous Deployment

Auto-deploy to production WITHOUT manual approval. Every passing commit goes to prod. Requires: comprehensive tests, feature flags, automated rollback. "If it passes, it ships."

14.2 Pipeline Stages — The Standard CI/CD Flow

CI/CD PIPELINE — From Code to Production
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              anihpj CI/CD PIPELINE — 7 Stages                            │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────────┐
  │ Lint │→│ Test │→│Build │→│ Scan │→│ Push │→│ Deploy│→│ Verify   │
  │flak8 │ │pytest│ │Docker│ │Trivy │ │ ECR  │ │ ArgoCD│ │Healthcheck│
  │ 30s  │ │ 2min │ │ 3min │ │ 1min │ │ 30s  │ │ 2min  │ │ 30s      │
  └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────────┘
      │        │        │        │        │
      ▼        ▼        ▼        ▼        ▼
    ❌ Fail = STOP pipeline immediately (fail fast)
    ✅ Pass = continue to next stage

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  TOTAL PIPELINE TIME: ~9 minutes (with caching and parallelization)
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

14.3 GitHub Actions — Workflows, Jobs, Matrix

GitHub Actions runs workflows in response to events (push, PR, schedule). Each workflow has jobs that can run in parallel. Matrix strategies test across multiple Python/Django versions.

name: anihpj CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  lint: {runs-on: ubuntu-latest, steps: [{uses: actions/checkout@v4}, {run: pip install flake8 && flake8 .}]}
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy: {matrix: {python: ['3.11', '3.12']}}
    steps: [{uses: actions/checkout@v4}, {uses: actions/setup-python@v5, with: {python-version: '${{matrix.python}}'}}, {run: pip install -r requirements.txt && pytest}]
  build:
    needs: [lint, test]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [{uses: actions/checkout@v4}, {run: docker build -t anihpj:${{github.sha}} .}]

14.4 GitLab CI — Stages, Artifacts, Environments

GitLab CI uses .gitlab-ci.yml with stages, job artifacts (passing files between stages), and environment tracking. Unlike GitHub Actions (event-driven YAML), GitLab CI has a more structured pipeline model with explicit stage ordering.

# .gitlab-ci.yml for anihpj
stages: [lint, test, build, scan, deploy]

lint:
  stage: lint
  script: [pip install flake8, flake8 .]

test:
  stage: test
  script: [pip install -r requirements.txt, pytest]
  artifacts: {paths: [test-results/], expire_in: 7 days}
  parallel:
    matrix: [{PYTHON_VERSION: ["3.11", "3.12"]}]

build:
  stage: build
  image: gcr.io/kaniko-project/executor:debug
  script:
    - /kaniko/executor --context=$CI_PROJECT_DIR --destination=$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA
  only: [main]

deploy-staging:
  stage: deploy
  script: [argocd app sync anihpj-staging]
  environment: {name: staging}
  only: [main]

deploy-production:
  stage: deploy
  script: [argocd app sync anihpj-production]
  environment: {name: production}
  when: manual  # Manual approval for production!

14.5 Tekton — K8s-Native CI/CD

Tekton runs INSIDE your K8s cluster. Everything is a CRD — no external CI server needed. Task = single reusable step, Pipeline = sequence of Tasks, Trigger = event listener for webhooks:

# Task: A single reusable step (like a function)
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1
kind: Task
metadata: {name: pytest}
spec:
  params: [{name: python-version, type: string}]
  steps:
  - name: test
    image: python:$(params.python-version)
    script: |
      pip install -r requirements.txt
      pytest --junitxml=results.xml
---
# Pipeline: Sequence of Tasks (like a workflow)
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1
kind: Pipeline
metadata: {name: anihpj-ci}
spec:
  params: [{name: repo-url}, {name: image-tag}]
  tasks:
  - name: lint
    taskRef: {name: flake8}
  - name: test
    taskRef: {name: pytest}
    params: [{name: python-version, value: "3.12"}]
    runAfter: [lint]  # Sequential: lint → test
  - name: build-and-push
    taskRef: {name: kaniko}
    params: [{name: IMAGE, value: registry.example.com/anihpj:$(params.image-tag)}]
    runAfter: [test]
---
# Trigger: Event listener that creates PipelineRuns on webhook
apiVersion: triggers.tekton.dev/v1beta1
kind: TriggerTemplate
spec:
  resourcetemplates:
  - apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1
    kind: PipelineRun
    spec:
      pipelineRef: {name: anihpj-ci}
      params: [{name: image-tag, value: $(tt.params.git-sha)}]

14.6 Argo Workflows — DAG-Based Workflow Engine

Argo Workflows defines workflows as DAGs (Directed Acyclic Graphs) or step sequences. Unlike Tekton (pipeline-focused), Argo Workflows excels at data processing, ML training, and complex dependency graphs where steps can run in parallel:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Workflow
metadata: {generateName: anihpj-ml-pipeline-}
spec:
  entrypoint: train-and-deploy
  templates:
  - name: train-and-deploy
    dag:
      tasks:
      - name: preprocess
        template: preprocess-data
      - name: train-model-a
        depends: preprocess  # Runs AFTER preprocess
        template: train
        arguments: {parameters: [{name: model, value: "A"}]}
      - name: train-model-b
        depends: preprocess
        template: train
        arguments: {parameters: [{name: model, value: "B"}]}
      # train-model-a and train-model-b run IN PARALLEL (DAG!)
      - name: evaluate
        depends: "train-model-a && train-model-b"  # Runs after BOTH complete
        template: evaluate
      - name: deploy
        depends: evaluate
        template: deploy-best-model
  - name: train
    inputs: {parameters: [{name: model}]}
    container: {image: python:3.12, command: [python, train.py, --model, "{{inputs.parameters.model}}"]}

14.7 Image Building — Kaniko, Buildpacks, Buildah

BuilderNeeds Docker Daemon?Root Required?Best For
Kaniko❌ No — runs in container❌ No (rootless possible)CI/CD in K8s clusters. Standard choice for GitLab CI + K8s.
Buildpacks❌ No — auto-detects language❌ NoDevelopers who don't write Dockerfiles. Auto-detects Python/Django, creates optimized image with best-practice layers automatically.
Buildah❌ No — daemonless✅ Usually root (rootless possible)Red Hat ecosystem. Podman-compatible.
DinD✅ Needs Docker daemon✅ Requires privileged⚠️ Legacy. Security risk (privileged container). Use Kaniko instead.

14.8 Image Tagging — Git SHA vs SemVer

StrategyExampleProsConsBest For
Git SHAanihpj:a1b2c3dImmutable. Traceable to exact commit (git show a1b2c3d). Unique per build. Never conflicts.Not human-readable. Can't tell if a1b2c3d is newer than e5f6g7h without git.CI/CD pipelines. Every commit gets a unique tag. The standard for internal deployments.
SemVeranihpj:v1.2.3Human-readable. Communicates meaning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Users understand version relationships.Mutable (a new build can be tagged v1.2.3, overwriting the old). Requires version management discipline.Public releases. API versioning. When humans need to understand what changed.
Hybridanihpj:v1.2.3-a1b2c3dBest of both: human-readable + traceable. The tag tells you WHAT version AND exactly WHICH build.Slightly longer. Still mutable at the tag level (but traceable via SHA).Production releases. Standard for most platforms. docker pull anihpj:v1.2.3-a1b2c3d
Digestanihpj@sha256:abc123...CRYPTOGRAPHICALLY immutable. The hash IS the content. Impossible to tamper with.Not human-readable at all. Long. Hard to type.K8s deployments. image: anihpj@sha256:abc... guarantees you always run the exact bytes you tested.

Golden rule for production: Pin by digest (@sha256:...). Tag with Git SHA + SemVer for humans (:v1.2.3-a1b2c3d). NEVER use :latest — it's a pointer to whatever the last push was, and you have no idea what that is tomorrow.

14.9 Artifact Promotion — Dev → Staging → Production

Build ONCE, promote many times. The image that passed staging tests is the EXACT same image (by SHA256 digest) deployed to production. This is the foundation of deployment confidence:

ARTIFACT PROMOTION — Same Image, Different Registries
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                ARTIFACT PROMOTION — Build Once, Promote Many             │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐
  │ BUILD    │───►│ SCAN     │───►│ PROMOTE  │───►│ DEPLOY   │
  │          │    │          │    │          │    │          │
  │ anihpj:  │    │ Trivy:   │    │ Copy to  │    │ Prod uses │
  │ abc123   │    │ PASS ✓   │    │ staging  │    │ @sha256:  │
  │          │    │          │    │ registry │    │ abc123... │
  └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └────┬─────┘    └──────────┘
                                       │
                              ┌────────▼────────┐
                              │ GATE: Smoke Tests│
                              │ All pass? →      │
                              │ Promote to prod  │
                              └────────┬────────┘
                                       │
                              ┌────────▼────────┐
                              │ PRODUCTION       │
                              │ Same sha256      │
                              │ Tested = Deployed│
                              └──────────────────┘
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Gates at each stage: Dev → Trivy scan (0 CRITICAL) → Staging → Smoke tests (all pass) → Manual approval → Production. Each promotion adds an attestation (scan results, test results, approval). The production deployment uses the EXACT same digest that passed all gates. If you rebuild, you lose the chain of trust.

14.10 Pipeline Security — SAST, DAST, Secret Scanning

🔍
SAST (Static Analysis)

Scans source code WITHOUT executing it. Finds: SQL injection patterns, hardcoded secrets, insecure functions. Tools: Bandit (Python), SonarQube, Semgrep. Runs in seconds, catches issues before they reach production.

🌐
DAST (Dynamic Analysis)

Tests RUNNING application from outside — like an attacker would. Sends malicious payloads, probes endpoints, checks for OWASP Top 10 (XSS, CSRF, injection). Tools: OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite. Finds runtime vulnerabilities that SAST misses — like misconfigured CORS headers or exposed debug endpoints.

🔐
Secret Scanning

Detects credentials accidentally committed. GitHub secret scanning (built-in, free), truffleHog (scans git history for high-entropy strings), git-secrets (pre-commit hook). Block commit if AWS key pattern detected.

📦
Dependency Scan

Known CVEs in pip/npm packages. Safety (Python), Snyk, Dependabot. Every dependency is a potential attack vector. Log4Shell (2021) showed why this matters — one vulnerable logging library compromised thousands of apps.

🐳
Container Scan

CVEs in base image OS packages. Trivy scans Alpine/Debian packages + language deps. CRITICAL CVE in base image = rebuild with updated base. Tools: Trivy, Grype, Clair.

✅
Image Signing

Cryptographically verify images came from your CI. Cosign + Sigstore. Pipeline signs image with OIDC token → K8s admission controller verifies signature before running. Prevents supply chain attacks.

⚠️ The SAST Triage Decision — 47 Findings, Now What?

SAST found 47 vulnerabilities. Don't blindly block the pipeline — that creates alert fatigue and slows development. Instead: (1) CRITICAL + exploitable in production: BLOCK. Fix immediately. (2) HIGH + potentially exploitable: BLOCK. Investigate within 24 hours. (3) MEDIUM: WARN. Fix in next sprint. (4) LOW / false positive: WARN. Suppress with .trivyignore or SARIF baseline. Goal: security without grinding development to a halt.

14.11 anihpj CI/CD Pipeline — Complete Reference

GitHub Actions workflow: lint (flake8) → test (pytest, Django test) → build (Kaniko) → scan (Trivy) → push (ECR) → deploy (update image tag in Git). Argo CD detects the Git change and syncs to the cluster. No CI system has cluster access — the CI only updates Git. The cluster pulls from Git via Argo CD. This separation is the essence of secure GitOps CI/CD.

Why this separation matters: If CI is compromised, the attacker can push malicious code to Git — but that's AUDITABLE and REVERSIBLE. If CI had cluster credentials, the attacker could deploy anything directly — NO audit trail, NO reversal. The CI→Git→Argo CD→Cluster chain ensures every change is visible in Git history.

🧠 Deep Dive — CI/CD Core Concepts

📖 How Kaniko Builds Images Without Docker — Userspace Image Construction

Kaniko doesn't need a Docker daemon because it reimplements Dockerfile execution entirely in userspace:

  1. No Docker socket: Kaniko runs as a regular container. It never touches /var/run/docker.sock. Instead, it directly manipulates the filesystem — unpacking base image layers, executing RUN commands, and snapshotting the results.
  2. Layer extraction: Each FROM instruction downloads base image layers from the registry. Kaniko unpacks them into its own filesystem using the OCI image spec — no containerd or Docker daemon involved. Everything happens in userspace.
  3. Filesystem snapshotting: After each Dockerfile instruction (RUN, COPY), Kaniko takes a filesystem snapshot. The DIFFERENCE between snapshots = the new layer. It computes the sha256 and creates layer metadata — all without a container runtime.
  4. Push directly to registry: Kaniko uploads the layers + manifest directly to the registry via HTTP. The registry sees a perfectly valid OCI image. It doesn't know or care that Docker wasn't used.

Why this matters for platform security: Every -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock mount in CI is a root-level security risk. Kaniko eliminates this attack vector entirely — no privileged containers, no Docker socket, no host kernel access needed to build images.

📖 How Buildpacks Auto-Detect Your Language — The Detection Pipeline

Buildpacks don't just "guess" your language. They use a structured multi-phase pipeline:

  1. Detect phase: Each buildpack checks if it applies. Python buildpack looks for requirements.txt, setup.py, or Pipfile. Node.js buildpack looks for package.json. If the detection file exists → this buildpack participates.
  2. Build phase: Each participating buildpack contributes layers. Python buildpack: installs Python runtime, runs pip install, sets Gunicorn as start command. Each step becomes a separate layer — automatically optimized for caching.
  3. Rebasing (the killer feature): When the base image gets a security patch, Buildpacks can "rebase" — swap the base layers WITHOUT rebuilding your app layers. A CVE fix that requires a full Docker rebuild takes seconds with Buildpacks.

anihpj example: pack build anihpj --builder heroku/builder:22 — Buildpacks auto-detects Python/Django, installs Python 3.12, runs pip install, configures Gunicorn. No Dockerfile written. The result follows all best practices (non-root user, minimal layers, proper CMD) — without you knowing what those are.

💡 SLSA Framework — Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts

SLSA ("salsa") rates your build pipeline's trustworthiness: "Can I trust that this image actually came from this source code?"

LevelRequirementWhat It Preventsanihpj Status
SLSA 1Build is scripted (CI/CD). Provenance shows how it was built.Manual build mistakes.✅ GitHub Actions
SLSA 2Hosted platform + version control. Build logs are auditable.Post-build tampering.✅ GitHub + Git history
SLSA 3Isolated (hermetic) build. Signed provenance (Cosign + Sigstore).Build process compromise.⚠️ Needs hermetic builds
SLSA 4Two-person review. Reproducible builds. Parameterless + hermetic.Insider threats. Supply chain attacks at highest level.🔮 Requires org-wide changes

CNPE relevance: Know that SLSA 3+ requires hermetic builds, signed provenance (Cosign + Sigstore OIDC), and build isolation. Kaniko + GitHub Actions OIDC + Cosign signing gets you to SLSA 3 without massive infrastructure changes.

Drill 14.1 — GitHub Actions Workflow for anihpj

Write a workflow: lint (flake8), test (pytest), build (docker), scan (Trivy).

💡 Hint: Each step is a job or step. Use needs for dependencies. runs-on: ubuntu-latest.
📝 View Solution
jobs:
  lint: {runs-on: ubuntu-latest, steps: [{uses: actions/checkout@v4}, {run: pip install flake8 && flake8 .}]}
  test: {needs: lint, steps: [{run: pip install -r requirements.txt && pytest}]}
